67.doc: Computer Vision & Multimodal Learning Systems (Dive Deep)
67.title: Overview
67.content: Computer vision encompasses algorithms, architectures, and pipelines designed to extract high-level semantic understanding, geometric structure, and generative control from digital images and videos. This document establishes an end-to-end technical reference spanning classical feature engineering, dense spatial segmentation, state-of-the-art transformer backbones, attention visualization, and multimodal generative architectures. The field has evolved from hand-crafted filters, corners, edges, and local descriptors into learned convolutional, transformer-based, generative, and multimodal systems. Classical methods remain valuable because they are interpretable, data-efficient, and useful for geometric reasoning. Deep models dominate modern perception because they learn hierarchical representations directly from data.

68.doc: Computer Vision & Multimodal Learning Systems (Dive Deep)
68.title: Part 1: Classical Computer Vision & Feature Engineering

69.doc: Computer Vision & Multimodal Learning Systems (Dive Deep)
69.title: Computer vision hierarchy
69.content: Processing pipelines in computer vision are traditionally categorized into three hierarchical levels: . | Low-level vision (image-to-image): Operations such as filtering, blurring, sharpening, edge extraction, and optical-flow estimation that transform or analyze primitive pixel data. | Intermediate-level vision (image-to-features): Extraction of symbolic features, contours, regions, and local descriptors from preprocessed image patches to support object recognition and 3D interpretation. | High-level vision (features-to-analysis): Semantic clustering, classification, activity recognition, scene understanding, and intent interpretation. | . Raw image | v Low-level vision - filtering - gradients - edges - optical flow | v Intermediate-level vision - corners - contours - regions - local descriptors | v High-level vision - classification - detection - segmentation - scene understanding . This hierarchy is a useful mental model, although modern deep networks often learn several levels jointly rather than following it explicitly.

70.doc: Computer Vision & Multimodal Learning Systems (Dive Deep)
70.title: Local feature detectors and descriptors
70.content: Local features provide compact representations that can be matched across changes in viewpoint, scale, rotation, and illumination. A local feature pipeline generally has two components: . | Detector: finds repeatable image locations, such as corners, blobs, or extrema. | Descriptor: converts the local neighborhood into a vector or binary signature for matching. | . Scale-Invariant Feature Transform (SIFT) . Scale-Invariant Feature Transform, or SIFT, detects scale-space extrema using a Difference of Gaussians (DoG) pyramid. Keypoints are filtered to remove low-contrast responses and edge artifacts. Descriptors are built from gradient orientation histograms over local sub-regions, producing a 128-dimensional vector. ai.googleblog . Image | v Gaussian pyramid | v Difference of Gaussians | v Scale-space extrema | v Keypoint localization and filtering | v Orientation assignment | v 128-dimensional SIFT descriptor . SIFT is robust to scale and rotation, but it is computationally more expensive than modern binary-feature methods. Affine SIFT (ASIFT) . Affine SIFT, or ASIFT, extends SIFT by simulating a comprehensive set of camera-axis orientation parameters—commonly described as latitude and longitude—before applying standard SIFT. This provides stronger invariance to affine viewpoint changes than SIFT alone. ASIFT is useful when the camera viewpoint changes substantially, but it multiplies the number of images that must be processed and therefore increases computation. Speeded-Up Robust Features (SURF) . Speeded-Up Robust Features, or SURF, approximates Hessian-matrix determinants using box filters evaluated rapidly through integral images, also called summed-area tables. SURF produces 64-dimensional descriptors and was designed to be faster than SIFT while retaining reasonable robustness. | Method | Descriptor type | Typical dimension | Main strength | . | SIFT | Floating-point gradient histogram | 128 | Strong scale and rotation robustness | . | ASIFT | SIFT over simulated viewpoints | 128 | Strong affine invariance | . | SURF | Floating-point descriptor | 64 | Faster Hessian-based detection | . | ORB | Binary descriptor | 256 bits | Fast, lightweight, license-friendly | . Oriented FAST and Rotated BRIEF (ORB) . Oriented FAST and Rotated BRIEF, or ORB, combines the FAST keypoint detector with a BRIEF binary descriptor. It adds multi-scale image pyramids and orientation assignment to improve rotation invariance. ORB is widely used in real-time systems because binary descriptors are efficient to compute and match. FAST detector | v Multi-scale pyramid | v Orientation assignment | v Rotated BRIEF descriptor | v Binary feature matching . ORB is often preferred for embedded and real-time applications where SIFT or SURF may be too slow or license-restricted.

71.doc: Computer Vision & Multimodal Learning Systems (Dive Deep)
71.title: Edge detection and image enhancement
71.content: Canny edge detection . Canny edge detection is a multi-stage edge detector: . | Apply Gaussian smoothing to suppress noise. | Compute image gradients, commonly with Sobel operators. | Apply non-maximum suppression along gradient directions. | Apply hysteresis thresholding using high and low thresholds to connect edge segments. | . \[G_x = \frac{\partial I}{\partial x}, \qquad G_y = \frac{\partial I}{\partial y}\] \[G = \sqrt{G_x^2 + G_y^2}, \qquad \theta = \arctan\left(\frac{G_y}{G_x}\right)\] where: . | $I$ is the input image. | $G_x$ and $G_y$ are horizontal and vertical gradients. | $G$ is gradient magnitude. | $\theta$ is gradient direction. | . Non-maximum suppression keeps only local maxima along the gradient direction. Hysteresis thresholding connects weak edges to strong edges, reducing fragmented edge maps. Harris corner detector . The Harris corner detector identifies points where intensity changes significantly in multiple directions. It computes a structure tensor from local image gradients: . \[M = \sum_{x,y} w(x,y) \begin{bmatrix} I_x^2 & I_x I_y \\ I_x I_y & I_y^2 \end{bmatrix}\] where: . | $I_x$ and $I_y$ are image gradients. | $w(x,y)$ is a windowing function, often Gaussian. | . The Harris response is commonly computed as: . \[R = \det(M) - k \cdot \text{trace}(M)^2\] where $k$ is a sensitivity parameter, often around 0.04 to 0.06. Corners produce large positive Harris responses because the eigenvalues of $M$ are both large. Edges produce one large and one small eigenvalue. Flat regions produce two small eigenvalues. Structural Similarity Index (SSIM) . Structural Similarity Index, or SSIM, evaluates perceived structural degradation between two images by comparing luminance, contrast, and structure. SSIM values fall within $[-1, 1]$, where $1$ denotes identical structure. \[\text{SSIM}(x,y) = \frac{ (2\mu_x\mu_y + C_1)(2\sigma_{xy} + C_2) }{ (\mu_x^2 + \mu_y^2 + C_1)(\sigma_x^2 + \sigma_y^2 + C_2) }\] where: . | $x$ and $y$ are image patches. | $\mu_x$ and $\mu_y$ are local means. | $\sigma_x^2$ and $\sigma_y^2$ are local variances. | $\sigma_{xy}$ is local covariance. | $C_1$ and $C_2$ stabilize division. | . SSIM is generally more perceptually meaningful than mean squared error (MSE), although neither metric perfectly captures human perception.

72.doc: Computer Vision & Multimodal Learning Systems (Dive Deep)
72.title: Geometric alignment
72.content: Homography . A homography relates two views of the same planar surface in 3D space. It is a $3 \times 3$ projective transformation: . \[\begin{bmatrix} x' \\ y' \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} \sim H \begin{bmatrix} x \\ y \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}\] where: . | $(x, y)$ is a point in the first image. | $(x’, y’)$ is the corresponding point in the second image. | $H$ is a $3 \times 3$ homography matrix. | $\sim$ denotes equality up to scale. | . A homography has eight degrees of freedom after scale normalization. At least four non-collinear point correspondences are required to estimate it. RANSAC . Random Sample Consensus, or RANSAC, estimates geometric models while rejecting outliers. Repeat: 1. Randomly select minimum number of correspondences 2. Estimate homography 3. Count inliers within error threshold 4. Keep model with most inliers 5. Refit model using all inliers . RANSAC is robust to incorrect feature matches, but it is stochastic and may require many iterations when the outlier ratio is high.

73.doc: Computer Vision & Multimodal Learning Systems (Dive Deep)
73.title: Part 2: Dense Prediction, Object Detection, and Segmentation

74.doc: Computer Vision & Multimodal Learning Systems (Dive Deep)
74.title: Object detection fundamentals
74.content: Object detection answers two questions: . | What objects are present? | Where are they located? | . Traditional detectors often use sliding windows, hand-crafted features, and classifiers. Modern detectors use convolutional or transformer backbones, learned region proposals or object queries, and differentiable losses.

75.doc: Computer Vision & Multimodal Learning Systems (Dive Deep)
75.title: Focal loss and RetinaNet
75.content: Single-stage detectors evaluate dense grids of candidate anchor boxes but suffer from extreme class imbalance during training, where background regions dominate foreground objects. Focal loss dynamically scales cross-entropy loss based on prediction confidence to down-weight easy background examples. ai.googleblog . Given the model’s estimated probability $p_t$ for the ground-truth class, focal loss is: . \[\text{FL}(p_t) = -\alpha_t(1 - p_t)^\gamma \log(p_t)\] where: . | $p_t$ is the predicted probability for the ground-truth class. | $\alpha_t$ balances class frequencies. | $\gamma$ is the focusing parameter. | Larger $\gamma$ reduces the contribution of easy examples. | . RetinaNet uses $\alpha = 0.25$ and $\gamma = 2$ in its original formulation. ai.googleblog . Easy background example: p_t close to 1 (1 - p_t)^gamma close to 0 Loss contribution small Hard foreground example: p_t low (1 - p_t)^gamma close to 1 Loss contribution large .

76.doc: Computer Vision & Multimodal Learning Systems (Dive Deep)
76.title: Semantic segmentation
76.content: Semantic segmentation assigns a class label to every pixel. Input image | v Encoder / backbone | v Multi-scale feature extraction | v Decoder / upsampling | v Per-pixel class probabilities . DeepLab V3 . DeepLab V3 uses atrous, or dilated, convolutions to expand the receptive field without reducing spatial resolution. It also uses Atrous Spatial Pyramid Pooling (ASPP) with dilation rates $$ to capture multi-scale contextual features. ai.googleblog . Input image | v Backbone CNN | v ASPP with dilated convolutions | v Feature fusion | v Upsampling | v Per-pixel segmentation mask . Atrous convolution inserts gaps between kernel elements, allowing the network to enlarge its receptive field without adding parameters or reducing resolution.

77.doc: Computer Vision & Multimodal Learning Systems (Dive Deep)
77.title: Panoptic segmentation
77.content: Panoptic segmentation unifies semantic segmentation and instance segmentation. It assigns a class label to every pixel and distinguishes individual object instances for countable categories such as people, cars, and animals. ai.googleblog . | Task | Output | . | Semantic segmentation | One class label per pixel | . | Instance segmentation | One mask per object instance | . | Panoptic segmentation | Non-overlapping masks with class labels for both things and stuff | . MaX-DeepLab . MaX-DeepLab is a fully end-to-end panoptic segmentation model that directly predicts class-labeled masks using a mask transformer. It removes many hand-designed intermediate components, such as anchor design, box assignment, non-maximum suppression, and thing-stuff merging. ai.googleblog . Its dual-path architecture combines: . | A convolutional pixel path. | A global memory path. | Dual-path transformer blocks that allow CNN layers to read from and write to global memory. ai.googleblog | . Input image | +--> CNN pixel path ----+ | +--> Global memory path-+ | v v Dual-path transformer blocks | v Stacked-hourglass decoder | v Mask set + class predictions | v Panoptic segmentation output . MaX-DeepLab directly predicts $N$ masks and $N$ classes, optimized with a Panoptic Quality-style objective and one-to-one matching between predicted and ground-truth masks. ai.googleblog . Google reported that MaX-DeepLab achieved 51.3% Panoptic Quality on the COCO test-dev set without test-time augmentation, a 7.1% Panoptic Quality gain over Axial-DeepLab in the box-free regime. ai.googleblog .

78.doc: Computer Vision & Multimodal Learning Systems (Dive Deep)
78.title: Part 3: Vision Transformers and Modern Architectures

79.doc: Computer Vision & Multimodal Learning Systems (Dive Deep)
79.title: Vision Transformer (ViT)
79.content: Vision Transformers adapt the standard natural-language-processing transformer encoder to image recognition by processing non-overlapping flattened image patches. ai.googleblog . Input image | +-- Split into patches --> [Patch 1, Patch 2, ..., Patch N] | +-- Linear projection --> Patch embeddings + learnable [class] token | +-- Position encoding --> Add spatial information | +-- Transformer encoder --> Multi-head self-attention + MLP blocks | +-- Classification head --> Read [class] token output . For an image of size $H \times W \times C$, patch size $P$, and embedding dimension $D$, the number of patches is: . \[N = \frac{H}{P} \times \frac{W}{P}\] Each patch is flattened and linearly projected into a $D$-dimensional token embedding. Self-attention computes relationships among all patch tokens: . \[\text{Attention}(Q,K,V) = \text{softmax}\left(\frac{QK^T}{\sqrt{d_k}}\right)V\] where: . | $Q$, $K$, and $V$ are query, key, and value matrices. | $d_k$ is the key dimension. | . The main trade-off is that standard self-attention has quadratic complexity in the number of tokens: . \[O(N^2)\] This becomes expensive for high-resolution images or small patch sizes.

80.doc: Computer Vision & Multimodal Learning Systems (Dive Deep)
80.title: Detection Transformer (DETR)
80.content: DETR casts object detection directly as a set-prediction problem, eliminating hand-crafted components such as anchor generation and non-maximum suppression. It uses a convolutional backbone, a transformer encoder-decoder, and a fixed set of $N$ learned object queries. ai.googleblog . Input image | v CNN backbone | v Transformer encoder | v Transformer decoder | +-- Object query 1 --> box + class +-- Object query 2 --> box + class +-- ... +-- Object query N --> box + class . DETR uses bipartite matching with the Hungarian algorithm to assign each prediction to at most one ground-truth object. This removes duplicate detections and avoids non-maximum suppression.

81.doc: Computer Vision & Multimodal Learning Systems (Dive Deep)
81.title: DeNoising DETR (DINO)
81.content: DeNoising DETR, or DINO, improves DETR-style detectors by introducing denoising training. During training, the model receives noised ground-truth boxes and learns to reconstruct the original boxes, improving query initialization and convergence. Ground-truth boxes | v Add controlled noise | v Noisy box queries | v Transformer decoder | v Reconstructed boxes . DINO retains the end-to-end set-prediction formulation while improving training stability and detection performance.

82.doc: Computer Vision & Multimodal Learning Systems (Dive Deep)
82.title: MLP-Mixer
82.content: MLP-Mixer is an all-MLP vision architecture. Instead of using self-attention, it alternates: . | Token-mixing MLPs across patch positions. | Channel-mixing MLPs across feature channels. | . Input patches | v Patch normalization | v Token-mixing MLP | v Channel-mixing MLP | v Repeated blocks | v Classification head . MLP-Mixer demonstrates that attention is not strictly required for strong image classification, although transformers generally remain more flexible for many vision-language and dense-prediction tasks.

83.doc: Computer Vision & Multimodal Learning Systems (Dive Deep)
83.title: Part 4: Generative Computer Vision Models

84.doc: Computer Vision & Multimodal Learning Systems (Dive Deep)
84.title: Autoencoders
84.content: An autoencoder learns a compressed latent representation of an input and reconstructs the input from that representation. Input image x | v Encoder E(x) | v Latent code z | v Decoder D(z) | v Reconstruction x_hat . The reconstruction objective is commonly: . \[\mathcal{L}_{\text{recon}} = \|x - D(E(x))\|^2\] Autoencoders are useful for denoising, compression, anomaly detection, and representation learning. A standard autoencoder does not necessarily learn a well-structured generative latent space.

85.doc: Computer Vision & Multimodal Learning Systems (Dive Deep)
85.title: Variational Autoencoders (VAEs)
85.content: A Variational Autoencoder parameterizes an approximate latent distribution $q_\phi(z \mid x)$ by predicting a mean $\mu$ and variance $\sigma^2$. To enable backpropagation through stochastic sampling, it uses the reparameterization trick: . \[z = \mu + \sigma \odot \epsilon, \qquad \epsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I)\] where: . | $z$ is the latent variable. | $\mu$ is the predicted mean. | $\sigma$ is the predicted standard deviation. | $\epsilon$ is sampled noise. | $\odot$ denotes element-wise multiplication. | . The VAE optimizes the Evidence Lower Bound (ELBO): . \[\mathcal{L}_{\text{VAE}} = \mathbb{E}_{q_\phi(z \mid x)} \left[ -\log p_\theta(x \mid z) \right] + D_{\text{KL}} \left( q_\phi(z \mid x) \parallel p(z) \right)\] where: . | $p_\theta(x \mid z)$ is the decoder likelihood. | $p(z)$ is the prior, commonly $\mathcal{N}(0, I)$. | $D_{\text{KL}}$ is the Kullback-Leibler divergence. | . The first term encourages accurate reconstruction. The KL term regularizes the latent distribution toward the prior.

86.doc: Computer Vision & Multimodal Learning Systems (Dive Deep)
86.title: Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs)
86.content: A Generative Adversarial Network trains two networks in competition: . | A generator $G$ maps noise $z$ to an image. | A discriminator $D$ distinguishes real images from generated images. | . Noise z | v Generator G | v Fake image | +--> Discriminator D --> real or fake | Real image ------------------^ . The original minimax objective is: . \[\min_G \max_D \mathbb{E}_{x \sim p_{\text{data}}} [\log D(x)] + \mathbb{E}_{z \sim p_z} [\log(1 - D(G(z)))]\] where: . | $x$ is a real image. | $z$ is a latent noise vector. | $G(z)$ is a generated image. | $D(x)$ is the discriminator’s probability that $x$ is real. | . GANs can produce sharp images but are notoriously unstable. Common problems include mode collapse, non-convergence, vanishing gradients, and sensitivity to hyperparameters.

87.doc: Computer Vision & Multimodal Learning Systems (Dive Deep)
87.title: Diffusion models
87.content: Diffusion models generate data by learning to reverse a fixed Markov chain of forward Gaussian noising steps. Starting from a data sample $x_0$, noise is progressively added across $T$ timesteps to produce $x_1, \ldots, x_T$. ai.googleblog . Forward diffusion: x_0 -> x_1 -> x_2 -> ... -> x_T Reverse denoising: x_T -> x_T-1 -> ... -> x_1 -> x_0 . The forward process is commonly: . \[q(x_t \mid x_{t-1}) = \mathcal{N} \left( x_t; \sqrt{1 - \beta_t}x_{t-1}, \beta_t I \right)\] where: . | $\beta_t$ is a variance schedule. | $x_t$ is the noisy sample at timestep $t$. | . The model learns the reverse process: . \[p_\theta(x_{t-1} \mid x_t)\] typically by predicting the noise added at each step. Diffusion models generally produce high-quality samples and train more stably than GANs, but they require multiple denoising steps at inference, increasing latency.

88.doc: Computer Vision & Multimodal Learning Systems (Dive Deep)
88.title: MaskGIT
88.content: MaskGIT is a masked generative image transformer. It first encodes an image into discrete visual tokens, then generates an image by iteratively predicting and unmasking tokens. Image | v Visual tokenizer | v Masked token sequence | v Transformer predicts masked tokens | v Iterative unmasking | v Generated image . MaskGIT can generate images with fewer sampling iterations than autoregressive token models because it predicts multiple tokens in parallel at each step.

89.doc: Computer Vision & Multimodal Learning Systems (Dive Deep)
89.title: Part 5: Attention Mechanisms and Explainability

90.doc: Computer Vision & Multimodal Learning Systems (Dive Deep)
90.title: Channel and spatial attention
90.content: Attention modules help convolutional networks emphasize informative channels and spatial locations. Bottleneck Attention Module (BAM) . The Bottleneck Attention Module computes attention at network bottlenecks using parallel channel and spatial sub-modules. It suppresses irrelevant low-level background features and emphasizes task-relevant information. Feature map F | +--> Channel attention --> M_c | +--> Spatial attention --> M_s | v Refined feature map F' = F + F * M_c * M_s . Convolutional Block Attention Module (CBAM) . CBAM applies channel attention followed by spatial attention. Feature map F | v Channel attention - average pooling - max pooling - shared MLP | v Spatial attention - channel-wise pooling - convolution - sigmoid | v Refined feature map . Channel attention answers: “Which feature channels matter?” . Spatial attention answers: “Which image locations matter?” .

91.doc: Computer Vision & Multimodal Learning Systems (Dive Deep)
91.title: Grad-CAM
91.content: Gradient-weighted Class Activation Mapping, or Grad-CAM, produces coarse localization heatmaps by computing gradients of a target class score $y^c$ with respect to feature maps $A^k$ from a chosen convolutional layer. ai.googleblog . The importance weight for feature map $k$ is: . \[\alpha_k^c = \frac{1}{Z} \sum_i \sum_j \frac{\partial y^c}{\partial A_{i,j}^k}\] where: . | $y^c$ is the score for class $c$. | $A_{i,j}^k$ is activation at spatial position $(i,j)$ in feature map $k$. | $Z$ is the number of spatial positions. | . The final heatmap is: . \[L_{\text{Grad-CAM}}^c = \text{ReLU} \left( \sum_k \alpha_k^c A^k \right)\] ReLU retains only features with a positive influence on the target class. Input image | v CNN feature maps | v Target-class gradients | v Global-average-pooled weights | v Weighted feature-map combination | v ReLU | v Class activation heatmap . Grad-CAM is useful for debugging, but it is an explanation method, not proof of causality.

92.doc: Computer Vision & Multimodal Learning Systems (Dive Deep)
92.title: Saliency maps
92.content: Saliency maps highlight input pixels that most influence a model’s prediction. A simple saliency method computes the gradient of the class score with respect to the input image: . \[S = \left| \frac{\partial y^c}{\partial x} \right|\] where: . | $y^c$ is the score for class $c$. | $x$ is the input image. | $S$ is the saliency map. | . Large gradient magnitudes indicate input locations where a small change would most affect the class score.

93.doc: Computer Vision & Multimodal Learning Systems (Dive Deep)
93.title: Part 6: Multimodal Learning

94.doc: Computer Vision & Multimodal Learning Systems (Dive Deep)
94.title: Contrastive Language-Image Pre-training (CLIP)
94.content: Contrastive Language-Image Pre-training, or CLIP, jointly trains an image encoder and a text encoder on web-scale image-caption pairs using a symmetric contrastive loss. It maximizes cosine similarity between matching image-text pairs while minimizing similarity across incorrect pairings in the batch. ai.googleblog . Image batch: [I1, I2, ..., IN] Text batch: [T1, T2, ..., TN] Similarity matrix: T1 T2 T3 I1 [ high low low ] I2 [ low high low ] I3 [ low low high] . For a batch of $N$ image-text pairs, the image-to-text contrastive loss is: . \[\mathcal{L}_{I \rightarrow T} = -\frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^{N} \log \frac{ \exp(\text{sim}(I_i, T_i)/\tau) }{ \sum_{j=1}^{N} \exp(\text{sim}(I_i, T_j)/\tau) }\] where: . | $I_i$ is an image embedding. | $T_j$ is a text embedding. | $\text{sim}$ is cosine similarity. | $\tau$ is a learned temperature parameter. | . CLIP enables zero-shot classification by comparing an image embedding with text embeddings for candidate labels.

95.doc: Computer Vision & Multimodal Learning Systems (Dive Deep)
95.title: BLIP
95.content: Bootstrapping Language-Image Pre-training, or BLIP, extends CLIP’s dual-encoder alignment with a unified encoder-decoder mixture architecture. It supports both multimodal understanding tasks, such as retrieval and classification, and generative tasks, such as captioning and visual question answering. ai.googleblog . Image + text | v Shared multimodal backbone | +--> Image-text contrastive learning | +--> Image-text matching | +--> Language modeling / captioning . BLIP also introduces synthetic caption bootstrapping: it generates captions for web images, filters noisy text, and uses the improved data to enhance pre-training.

96.doc: Computer Vision & Multimodal Learning Systems (Dive Deep)
96.title: Segment Anything Model (SAM)
96.content: The Segment Anything Model, or SAM, is a promptable segmentation foundation model. It can produce segmentation masks from prompts such as points, boxes, or text, depending on the deployment configuration. Image + prompt | v Image encoder | v Prompt encoder | v Mask decoder | v Segmentation masks . SAM is useful for interactive segmentation, dataset annotation, and video object segmentation when combined with a memory-based tracker such as XMem.

97.doc: Computer Vision & Multimodal Learning Systems (Dive Deep)
97.title: Part 7: Applications

98.doc: Computer Vision & Multimodal Learning Systems (Dive Deep)
98.title: Image alignment
98.content: Feature-based image alignment uses local features and geometric model estimation: . Image A and Image B | v Detect keypoints | v Compute descriptors | v Match descriptors | v Estimate homography with RANSAC | v Warp Image B to Image A . This is the foundation of panorama stitching, document alignment, augmented reality, and image registration.

99.doc: Computer Vision & Multimodal Learning Systems (Dive Deep)
99.title: Neural style transfer
99.content: Neural style transfer combines: . | Content representation from one image. | Style representation from another image. | Optimization or feed-forward generation to synthesize a stylized output. | . Content image | +--> Content loss | Style image | +--> Style loss | v Generated image . The original optimization approach minimizes content reconstruction error while matching Gram-matrix statistics of style features.

100.doc: Computer Vision & Multimodal Learning Systems (Dive Deep)
100.title: Human pose estimation
100.content: Human pose estimation detects body keypoints and connects them into a skeleton. Input image | v Human detector | v Keypoint heatmaps | v Keypoint decoding | v Skeleton . Applications include fitness analysis, sports analytics, animation, augmented reality, and human-computer interaction.

101.doc: Computer Vision & Multimodal Learning Systems (Dive Deep)
101.title: Video object segmentation
101.content: Video object segmentation tracks and segments an object across frames. First-frame mask | v SAM segmentation | v XMem memory module | v Per-frame object mask . SAM provides strong promptable segmentation, while a memory module such as XMem helps maintain object identity across frames.

102.doc: Computer Vision & Multimodal Learning Systems (Dive Deep)
102.title: Part 8: Limitations and Open Questions

103.doc: Computer Vision & Multimodal Learning Systems (Dive Deep)
103.title: Computational complexity
103.content: Attention-based mechanisms such as standard Vision Transformers and dense transformer decoders incur quadratic complexity relative to spatial resolution or token count: . \[O(N^2)\] where $N$ is the number of tokens. This makes high-resolution images, video, and dense prediction expensive.

104.doc: Computer Vision & Multimodal Learning Systems (Dive Deep)
104.title: Small object detection
104.content: Global reasoning models can struggle with small objects that occupy only a few pixels. Feature pyramid networks, high-resolution feature maps, multi-scale heads, and local attention mechanisms can help.

105.doc: Computer Vision & Multimodal Learning Systems (Dive Deep)
105.title: Generative model limitations
105.content: | Model family | Main limitation | . | GANs | Mode collapse, unstable training, convergence failures | . | VAEs | Blurry reconstructions and weaker sample quality | . | Diffusion models | Multi-step sampling increases inference latency | . | Autoregressive models | Sequential token generation is slow | . | Masked generative models | Requires discrete tokenization and iterative decoding | .

106.doc: Computer Vision & Multimodal Learning Systems (Dive Deep)
106.title: Interpretability limitations
106.content: Grad-CAM and saliency maps are useful diagnostic tools, but they do not prove causal explanations. They can highlight correlations, be sensitive to architecture and input perturbations, and fail to capture higher-level reasoning.

107.doc: Computer Vision & Multimodal Learning Systems (Dive Deep)
107.title: Data and bias
107.content: Vision models inherit biases from training data. Multimodal models can associate demographic attributes, objects, scenes, and captions in ways that produce unfair or unsafe behavior. Evaluation must include demographic slices, geographic coverage, adversarial cases, and failure analysis.

108.doc: Computer Vision & Multimodal Learning Systems (Dive Deep)
108.title: Final Technical Takeaways
108.content: . | Hierarchical progression: Low-level operators such as Canny, Harris, SIFT, and ORB provide geometric foundations, while convolutional and transformer backbones deliver high-level semantic abstraction. | Feature matching: SIFT, ASIFT, SURF, and ORB remain useful for alignment, retrieval, and geometric vision, especially when labeled data is limited. | Hard constraints matter: Focal loss addresses extreme foreground-background imbalance in dense object detection. | End-to-end set prediction: DETR, DINO, and MaX-DeepLab reduce reliance on anchors, boxes, and non-maximum suppression by using learned queries, bipartite matching, and mask transformers. ai.googleblog | Attention improves selectivity: BAM and CBAM refine features by emphasizing important channels and spatial locations. | Explainability is approximate: Grad-CAM and saliency maps provide useful diagnostics but are not causal proof. | Multimodal alignment: CLIP learns a shared vision-language embedding space, while BLIP extends this toward captioning and visual question answering. | Main trade-off: Transformers and diffusion models provide strong capability but require more compute, memory, and inference time than classical or convolutional alternatives. | Broader implication: Modern computer vision is a layered system: geometric foundations, learned perception, generative modeling, multimodal alignment, and explainability must be designed together. | .

111.title: Overview
111.content: Computer vision encompasses algorithms, architectures, and pipelines designed to extract high-level semantic understanding, geometric structure, and generative control from digital images and videos. This document establishes an end-to-end technical reference spanning classical feature engineering, dense spatial segmentation, state-of-the-art transformer backbones, attention visualization, and multimodal generative architectures.

112.title: Part 1: Classical Computer Vision & Feature Engineering
112.content: Computer Vision Hierarchy . Processing pipelines in computer vision are traditionally categorized into three hierarchical levels: . | Low-Level Vision (Image-to-Image): Operations such as filtering, blurring, sharpening, and edge or optical flow extraction that handle primitive pixel transformations. | Intermediate-Level Vision (Image-to-Features): Extraction of symbolic features, contours, regions, and local descriptors from pre-processed image patches to support object recognition and 3D interpretation. | High-Level Vision (Features-to-Analysis): Semantic clustering, classification, activity recognition, and intent interpretation. | . Local Feature Detectors and Descriptors . Local features provide robust representations invariant to scale, rotation, and illumination changes. | Scale-Invariant Feature Transform (SIFT): Detects scale-space extrema using Difference of Gaussians (DoG) pyramids. Keypoints are filtered to eliminate low-contrast responses and edge artifacts. Descriptors are constructed from 8-bin gradient histograms across $4 \times 4$ sub-regions, yielding a 128-dimensional vector. | ASIFT (Affine SIFT): Simulates a comprehensive set of camera axis orientation parameters (latitude and longitude) before applying standard SIFT, providing full affine invariance. | SURF (Speeded-Up Robust Features): Approximates Hessian matrix determinants using box filters evaluated rapidly via integral images (summed area tables), producing 64-dimensional descriptors. | ORB (Oriented FAST and Rotated BRIEF): Combines the FAST keypoint detector (modified with multi-scale pyramids and an orientation assignment mechanism) with the BRIEF binary descriptor to deliver rotation-invariant features without commercial licensing restrictions. | . Edge Detection & Image Enhancement . | Canny Edge Detection: Applies Gaussian smoothing to suppress noise, computes image gradients via Sobel operators, performs non-maximum suppression along gradient directions, and applies hysteresis thresholding with dual thresholds ($\text{thresh}{\text{high}}$ and $\text{thresh}{\text{low}}$) to connect edge segments. | Structural Similarity Index (SSIM): Evaluates perceived structural degradation between two images by comparing luminance, contrast, and structural terms. SSIM values fall within $[-1, 1]$, where $1$ denotes identical structure. | Homography: Relates the transformations between two images observing the same planar 3D surface, computed using four or more point correspondences combined with robust estimators like RANSAC. | .

113.title: Part 2: Dense Prediction, Object Detection, and Segmentation
113.content: Focal Loss in Object Detection (RetinaNet) . Single-stage detectors evaluate dense grids of candidate anchor boxes but suffer from extreme class imbalance during training, where background regions dominate foreground objects. Focal Loss dynamically scales the cross-entropy loss based on prediction confidence to down-weight easy background examples. Given the model’s estimated probability $p_t$ for the ground-truth class, the Focal Loss is defined as: . \[\text{FL}(p_t) = -\alpha_t (1 - p_t)^\gamma \log(p_t)\] where $\alpha_t$ balances class frequencies and the focusing parameter $\gamma$ smoothly reduces the weight given to easily classified examples ($p_t > 0.5$). RetinaNet utilizes $\alpha = 0.25$ and $\gamma = 2$. Semantic and Panoptic Segmentation . | DeepLab V3: Employs Atrous (Dilated) Convolutions to expand receptive fields without losing spatial resolution, alongside Atrous Spatial Pyramid Pooling (ASPP) with dilation rates $[6, 12, 18]$ to capture multi-scale contextual features. | MaX-DeepLab: Integrates a convolutional pixel path with transformer memory paths via dual-path transformer blocks, eliminating surrogate sub-tasks like Non-Maximum Suppression (NMS) for end-to-end panoptic segmentation. | .

114.title: Part 3: Vision Transformers (ViT) & Modern Architectures
114.content: Vision Transformer (ViT) . Vision Transformers adapt the standard NLP transformer encoder for image recognition by processing non-overlapping flattened image patches. Input Image │ ├─ Split into patches ──► [Patch 1, Patch 2, ..., Patch N] │ ├─ Linear Projection ──► Linear Patch Embeddings + Learnable [class] Token │ ├─ Position Encoding ──► Added to retain spatial awareness │ ├─ Transformer Encoder ──► Multi-Head Self-Attention + LayerNorm + MLP Blocks │ └─ MLP Classification Head (Reads [class] token output) . Detection Transformer (DETR) . DETR casts object detection directly as a set-prediction problem, eliminating hand-crafted components like anchor generation and NMS. It utilizes a convolutional backbone combined with a transformer encoder-decoder architecture and learns a fixed set of $N$ object queries resolved against ground-truth targets via bipartite matching using the Hungarian algorithm.

115.title: Part 4: Generative Computer Vision Models
115.content: Variational Autoencoders (VAEs) . Variational Autoencoders parameterize an approximate latent distribution $q_\phi(z \mid x)$ by predicting mean $\mu$ and variance $\sigma^2$ vectors. To enable backpropagation through stochastic nodes, the reparameterization trick is applied: . \[z = \mu + \sigma \odot \epsilon, \quad \epsilon \in \mathcal{N}(0, I)\] The objective function optimizes the Evidence Lower Bound (ELBO), balancing reconstruction loss against the KL divergence regularization term: . \[\mathcal{L}_{\text{VAE}} = \mathbb{E}_{q_\phi(z \mid x)}[-\log p_\theta(x \mid z)] + D_{\text{KL}}(q_\phi(z \mid x) \parallel p(z))\] Diffusion Models . Diffusion models generate data by learning to reverse a fixed Markov chain of forward Gaussian noising steps. Starting from data distribution $x_0$, noise is progressively added across $T$ timesteps to yield latent states $x_1, \dots, x_T$. The parameterized reverse process $p_\theta(x_{t-1} \mid x_t)$ is trained to denoise states, producing state-of-the-art sample quality without adversarial instability.

116.title: Part 5: Attention Mechanisms & Explainability
116.content: Channel and Spatial Attention Modules . | BAM (Bottleneck Attention Module): Computes attention maps at network bottlenecks using parallel branch channel and spatial sub-modules to suppress irrelevant low-level background features. | CBAM (Convolutional Block Attention Module): Applies sequential channel attention (using both Max-Pooling and Average-Pooling summaries) followed by spatial attention (using kernel convolutions over aggregated feature maps). | . Grad-CAM . Gradient-weighted Class Activation Mapping (Grad-CAM) produces coarse localization heatmaps by computing the gradients of target class score $y^c$ with respect to feature maps $A^k$ of the final convolutional layer. Global Average Pooling weights $\alpha_k^c$ are computed as: . \[\alpha_k^c = \frac{1}{Z} \sum_{i} \sum_{j} \frac{\partial y^c}{\partial A_{i,j}^k}\] The final heatmap applies a Rectified Linear Unit (ReLU) to the weighted combination to retain only features with a positive influence on the target class: . \[\text{L}_{\text{Grad-CAM}}^c = \text{ReLU}\left(\sum_{k} \alpha_k^c A^k\right)\] .

117.title: Part 6: Multimodal Learning (Vision and Language)
117.content: Contrastive Language-Image Pre-training (CLIP) . CLIP jointly trains an image encoder and a text encoder on web-scale image-caption pairs using a symmetric contrastive loss. By maximizing cosine similarity between correct matching pairs while minimizing similarity across incorrect pairings in the batch, CLIP learns a joint multimodal embedding space capable of zero-shot classification. BLIP (Bootstrapping Language-Image Pre-training) . Unlike CLIP’s alignment-only dual-encoder structure, BLIP introduces a unified encoder-decoder mixture architecture capable of both multimodal understanding tasks (retrieval, classification) and generative tasks (captioning, visual question answering). BLIP incorporates a synthetic caption bootstrapping module to filter noisy web text and enhance dataset quality.

118.title: Limitations and Open Questions
118.content: . | Computational Complexity: Attention-based mechanisms (such as standard ViTs and dense self-attention decoders) incur quadratic complexity relative to spatial resolution or token count. | Small Object Detection: Global reasoning models can struggle with minute objects occupying few pixels unless multi-scale feature pyramids (FPN) or high-resolution refinement heads are employed. | Mode Coverage and Artifacts: Generative architectures like GANs remain vulnerable to mode collapse and training convergence failures, while diffusion models require iterative multi-step sampling passes that increase inference latency. | .

119.title: Final Technical Takeaways
119.content: . | Hierarchical Progression: Low-level feature operators (SIFT, Canny, Harris) provide geometric foundations, while deep convolutional and transformer backbones deliver high-level semantic abstraction. | End-to-End Set Prediction: Architectures like DETR eliminate heuristic anchors and NMS via bipartite matching. | Multimodal Alignment: Contrastive and encoder-decoder foundation models (CLIP, BLIP, SAM) unify vision and language representations for robust zero-shot generalization. | .

121.doc: Decision Models (Part1): The Decision Layer for AI Systems
121.title: Decision Models: Jev, AnyJev, and the Decision Layer for AI Systems
121.content: Reference: Introducing Decision 1.0: Open Decision Foundation Models . Decision models are a new class of language models optimized to make fast, typed, probability-bearing decisions rather than generate free-form text. They sit between an application’s understanding of a request and its next action: given a state, a question, and candidate options, they return calibrated distributions over those options. The central pattern is: . \[\text{State} + \text{Questions} + \text{Criteria} \rightarrow \text{Typed probability distributions}\] This document covers the Jev-style decision-model interface, the architecture and trade-offs of open decision models, the AnyJev training-free and self-distilled approaches, calibration, deployment, and practical use in agents, search, routing, and evaluation.

122.doc: Decision Models (Part1): The Decision Layer for AI Systems
122.title: Part 1: Foundations
122.content: What is a decision model? . A decision model is a model that consumes a context or state and returns a structured decision over a predefined set of alternatives. Instead of producing a paragraph of reasoning or a natural-language answer, it scores candidates and returns probabilities. A typical decision request contains: . | State: the evidence or context to evaluate, such as a support ticket, document, agent trace, search result, or user request. | Question: what the system needs to determine. | Candidates or criteria: the allowed answers, actions, labels, or rubric levels. | Output: a selected option plus a probability distribution over all options. | . For example, given a customer message about a duplicate charge, a decision model may answer: . | Which team should handle this: billing, technical, or sales? | Did the customer request a refund? | How urgent is the issue: can wait, this week, or today? | . The model returns a distribution such as billing: 0.91, technical: 0.07, sales: 0.02, allowing the application to route the request, set an escalation threshold, or prioritize a queue. vllm-sr . Why not just use an LLM? . A generative LLM can perform classification by prompting it to output a label. However, for high-volume operational decisions, this approach has several drawbacks: . | Concern | Generative LLM classification | Decision model | . | Output format | Text that may need parsing or validation | Typed decision with option probabilities | . | Latency | Often requires autoregressive generation | Can score candidates in one forward pass | . | Cost | Higher when generating reasoning tokens | Lower when decisions are read from logits or a single prefill | . | Confidence | Often poorly calibrated without extra work | Designed to expose probabilities for policy decisions | . | Flexibility | Broad reasoning and generation capability | Focused on choosing among supplied alternatives | . | Best fit | Open-ended reasoning, planning, writing | Routing, gating, triage, scoring, policy checks | . Decision models do not replace LLMs. They separate the frequent, short-horizon decisions that an application must make from the slower System-2 work of planning, reasoning, query generation, and answer composition. arxiv . System 1 versus System 2 . The terminology comes from a dual-process view of cognition: . | System 1 is fast, automatic, and low-effort. In AI systems, this maps to immediate decisions such as “route this ticket,” “is this relevant?”, or “should this action be allowed?” | System 2 is slower, deliberate, and effortful. In AI systems, this maps to multi-step planning, tool use, complex reasoning, and generating a final answer. | . SearchJev explicitly applies this split to search agents: a small decision model handles repeated short decisions about relevance, evidence sufficiency, and search actions, while a larger System-2 model handles planning, query generation, and answer composition. arxiv . User request | v +---------------------+ | System 1: Decision | Fast, typed, probabilistic | - relevance? | - enough evidence? | - next action? | +---------------------+ | confident |--------------------------+ | uncertain | v v +---------------------+ +---------------------+ | Execute fast action | System 2: Reasoner | or continue loop | - plan | +---------------------+ | - generate queries | - compose answer | +---------------------+ . This is a conceptual reconstruction of the dual-system architecture described by SearchJev. arxiv .

123.doc: Decision Models (Part1): The Decision Layer for AI Systems
123.title: Part 2: The Jev Decision Interface
123.content: Three decision types . The Jev-style interface defines three primary decision types. Decision 1.0 uses the names Choice, Noul, and Score. vllm-sr . | Type | Question form | Output | Typical use | . | Choice | “Which option is best?” | One selected candidate and a distribution over candidates | Routing, action selection, classification | . | Noul | “Is this condition true?” | Probability of yes | Policy gates, evidence checks, escalation | . | Score | “Rate this on an ordered rubric.” | Distribution over ordered levels and an expected score | Urgency, quality, severity, review rubrics | . A Choice is appropriate when exactly one option should be selected. A Noul is appropriate for a yes/no condition; multiple Noul questions can implement multi-label checks, though their probabilities need not sum to one. A Score is appropriate when the levels have a meaningful order, such as can wait < this week < today. vllm-sr . Example: customer support . Consider a customer who reports a damaged parcel and asks for a replacement today. Decision 1.0 illustrates three questions over the same state: vllm-sr . | Type | Ask the model | Use the answer | . | Choice | Which team should handle this: delivery, billing, or technical support? | Route using the selected candidate ID and its distribution | . | Noul | Does the customer request action today? | Use the yes probability to decide whether to escalate | . | Score | Rate urgency: can wait, this week, today | Prioritize the queue using the level distribution and expected score | . The important design point is that the application—not the model—owns the action policy. The model supplies probabilities; the application decides what probability threshold triggers escalation, refund approval, human review, or another workflow branch. vllm-sr . Candidate descriptions instead of fixed labels . A decision model does not need a fixed vocabulary of task labels. Candidates can be short identifiers such as billing or technical, or richer descriptions such as “Payments and refunds” and “Product faults.” . Decision 1.0’s Lux model uses a shared candidate readout: all candidates for one question are scored in a single forward pass, and candidate descriptions come from the request rather than a fixed label set. This makes the same model usable for routing, tool selection, policy checks, and evaluation without retraining the head for every new task. vllm-sr . Batch decisions . Real workflows rarely need one decision at a time. A support record may require a destination, refund check, escalation decision, and priority score. Applying those four questions to 128 records produces 512 decisions. Decision 1.0’s Kai and Lex native Python API accepts up to 128 independent requests and 512 total decisions per local SDK batch submission, preserving request and question order. The runtime groups work into physical batches; the 512 figure describes submission capacity, not simultaneous forward passes or measured throughput. vllm-sr .

124.doc: Decision Models (Part1): The Decision Layer for AI Systems
124.title: Part 3: Model Architectures
124.content: Decision 1.0 family . Decision 1.0 is a family of six open-weight Decision Foundation Models released by the vLLM Semantic Router team. The family uses two architectural branches. vllm-sr . | Model | Built for | Input budget | . | Decision-1.0-Kai-0.6B | Compact general-purpose routing, conditions, and action selection | 1,024 tokens | . | Decision-1.0-Lex-0.6B | Operational decisions: customer service, invoices, security incidents, agent traces | 1,024 tokens | . | Decision-1.0-Eos-0.8B | Smallest hybrid decoder tier for longer evidence | 16,384 tokens | . | Decision-1.0-Sol-2B | Greater capacity for decisions over extended context | 16,384 tokens | . | Decision-1.0-Nox-4B | Combining conditions, applying rules, and choosing actions | 16,384 tokens | . | Decision-1.0-Lux-9B | Largest model and strongest overall result on the released decision suite | 16,384 tokens | . The input budget covers the complete state, question, and candidate descriptions. vllm-sr . Encoder branch: Kai and Lex . Kai and Lex use three bidirectional encoder paths built on Vela. Each path has separate interaction layers and readouts for Choice, Noul, and Score. vllm-sr . Conceptually: . State + question + candidates | +------------------+------------------+ | | Choice path Noul path Score path | | candidate logits yes probability ordered level logits | | distribution probability level distribution . This is a conceptual reconstruction of the three-path encoder design. Bidirectional encoders are naturally suited to classification because every token can attend to every other token in the input, which is useful when the answer depends on relationships across the whole state. vllm-sr . Decoder branch: Eos, Sol, Nox, and Lux . Eos, Sol, Nox, and Lux adapt Qwen3.5 text backbones. They combine Gated DeltaNet with full attention and use a shared candidate head. vllm-sr . This hybrid design reflects a common trade-off: . | Full attention provides strong context modeling and is effective for long-range dependencies. | Gated DeltaNet is a more efficient sequence-mixing mechanism that can reduce the cost of processing long contexts. | A shared candidate head scores each supplied candidate, allowing the candidate set to vary per request. | . Lux-9B scores all candidates for one question in a single forward pass; independent questions are processed in batches. vllm-sr . Published benchmark results . Decision 1.0 reports results across 3,766 scored decisions in a selected 54-task suite covering decisions, composition, reading, inference, and transfer. vllm-sr . | Model | Overall score | . | Lux-9B | 76.94 | . | Nox-4B | 73.09 | . | Sol-2B | 66.32 | . | Eos-0.8B | 61.89 | . | Kai-0.6B | 53.52 | . | Kev-9B, displayed open-model reference | 71.89 | . | Hosted Jev reference | 81.05 | . Lux leads the displayed open-model references on this suite, while the hosted Jev reference remains higher overall. Lux reaches 84.10 on Decisions and 91.46 on Inference; Nox leads the displayed Decision models on Composition. These are results from the release’s selected tasks and weighted overall metric, so they should not be treated as universal rankings. vllm-sr .

125.doc: Decision Models (Part1): The Decision Layer for AI Systems
125.title: Part 4: AnyJev
125.content: What AnyJev does . AnyJev is an open-source framework that turns an LLM into a Jev-style decision model. It provides typed decisions and probability distributions without requiring generated text to be parsed. github . AnyJev provides two main paths: . | Training-free Decider: works with any open causal language model, with no training and no labels. | Self-distilled Tacit: uses checkpoints trained through self-distillation so the model can answer in one forward pass. github | . The problem with raw label logits . A naive way to build a decision model from an LLM is to prompt it with candidate labels and read the next-token logits for each label. This is simple but problematic: . | The result can change when the order of options changes. | The model may have a prior preference for certain label strings. | The resulting probabilities may be poorly calibrated. | . AnyJev’s L0 readout addresses both issues without labels by averaging position bias over rotations of the options and dividing out the label prior. github . L0 rotation readout . At level L0, AnyJev reads a K-option choice once per rotation of the options. Each rotation changes the ordering of candidates, and the readout aggregates the resulting distributions to reduce order sensitivity. For each rotation r of the K candidate options: Read logits for each option label Convert logits to an option distribution Aggregate distributions across rotations Remove label prior Return final calibrated decision distribution . This is a conceptual reconstruction of the rotation-based readout. The repository reports that, on Qwen3-8B for a 20-way BANKING77 task with 300 test items, L0 reduced answer flips when options were reversed from 0.230 to 0.073, improved accuracy from 0.747 to 0.803, and reduced expected calibration error from 0.240 to 0.184. github . The most consequential improvement is automation capacity: the share of decisions confident enough to automate at no more than 5% error rose from 7.7% with raw logits to 46.3% with L0, using no labels. github . Rotation budget . Running all K rotations is expensive for large candidate sets. AnyJev’s rotation budget reads only as many rotations as the decision needs. The stopping threshold is calibrated against AnyJev’s own full-cycle answer, so it does not require labels. The repository reports that, at a certified 1% disagreement, it read 7.2 rotations instead of 18, yielding 2.2 times more decisions per second on vLLM and 2.3 to 2.7 times more on transformers, with accuracy unchanged. github . Tacit self-distilled models . Tacit models are trained by self-distillation: the model learns to produce, in one forward pass, the answers it would reach when it reasons. No human labels and no separate teacher model are involved. github . The trade-off is: . | One-forward mode: fast and cheap; one prefill per decision. | Adaptive mode: low-confidence decisions are escalated to the model’s own reasoning, then read as a label distribution after the reasoning step. | . Adaptive escalation is bounded by configuration: . | Argument | Default | Meaning | . | adaptive | False | Send low-confidence decisions to the model’s own reasoning | . | tau | 0.5 | Low confidence when the log-probability gap between the top two options is below this value | . | max_cot_share | 0.2 | Maximum share of the recent decision window allowed to escalate | . | cot_window | 1000 | Number of recent decisions counted by the escalation cap | . | cot_max_tokens | 8192 | Reasoning budget for one escalated decision | . | engine | "transformers" | Also supports in-process vLLM or a remote vllm serve endpoint | . The cap matters operationally: even if traffic becomes difficult, at most max_cot_share of the last cot_window decisions escalate. Every escalation is reported through route == "cot", and the first-pass result is retained. github . Tacit results . AnyJev reports Tacit accuracy on the public JevBench set, which has 231 items, and the bev-decision test split, which has 46,320 items. github . | Model | Base model | JevBench public | Adaptive | bev-decision test | Adaptive | . | Tacit-9B | Qwen3.5-9B | 0.823 | 0.887, 15.2% escalated | 0.727 | 0.755, 18.1% escalated | . | Tacit-8B | Qwen3-8B | 0.736 | — | 0.663 | — | . | Tacit-4B | Qwen3-4B | 0.723 | 0.758, 14.3% escalated | 0.663 | 0.704, 17.8% escalated | . | Tacit-2B | Qwen3.5-2B | 0.671 | — | 0.626 | — | . | Tacit-1.7B | Qwen3-1.7B | 0.619 | — | 0.598 | — | . For Tacit-9B, escalation added an average of 567 generated tokens per decision on JevBench and 458 on bev-decision. For Tacit-4B, it added 305 and 187 respectively. github . AnyJev code example . The following example is copied from the AnyJev repository and shows a Tacit decision over customer-service actions. github . from anyjev import Tacit tacit = Tacit.from_pretrained("morriszjm/Tacit-9B") d = tacit.decide( state="Customer: my package was due last Monday and it still has not arrived.", question="What does the customer want?", options=["track_order", "cancel_order", "refund", "change_address"], ) d["answer"] # selected option d["probs"] # {option: probability} d["route"] # "one_forward" or "cot" . For a training-free decision model over an arbitrary open LLM: github . from anyjev import Decider, Question from anyjev.backends.hf import HFBackend d = Decider(HFBackend("Qwen/Qwen3-8B")) # level="L0" by default route = Question.choice( "Which team should handle this?", ["billing", "technical", "sales", "other"], name="route", ) result = d.decide( "My card was charged twice for one order.", [route], )["route"] result.distribution result.level . AnyJev also supports vLLM, SGLang, and llama.cpp backends. For a stock vLLM server, the client needs only the tokenizer. github . pip install "anyjev[client]" vllm serve morriszjm/Tacit-9B --host 127.0.0.1 --port 8000 . tacit = Tacit.from_pretrained( "morriszjm/Tacit-9B", engine="server", base_url="http://127.0.0.1:8000", adaptive=True, ) .

126.doc: Decision Models (Part1): The Decision Layer for AI Systems
126.title: Part 5: Calibration
126.content: Why calibration matters . A model can be accurate while still having unreliable probabilities. Calibration measures whether predicted confidence matches observed correctness. For example, if a model assigns approximately 74% positive probability to many movie reviews, then roughly 74% of those reviews should actually be positive for the model to be well calibrated at that confidence level. magazine.sebastianraschka . This distinction is critical for decision systems because the application may use probability thresholds to automate actions: . | Automatically route requests above 0.95 confidence. | Send 0.70 to 0.95 to a cheaper secondary check. | Escalate below 0.70 to a human or reasoning model. | . An accurate but overconfident model will automate too many incorrect decisions. An underconfident model will escalate too much, increasing cost and latency. Expected calibration error . Expected Calibration Error, or ECE, is a common calibration metric. Conceptually, it groups predictions by confidence bucket and compares average predicted confidence with observed accuracy in each bucket: . \[\mathrm{ECE} = \sum_b \frac{n_b}{N} \left| \mathrm{acc}(b) - \mathrm{conf}(b) \right|\] where: . | $b$ indexes confidence bins. | $n_b$ is the number of predictions in bin $b$. | $N$ is the total number of predictions. | $\mathrm{acc}(b)$ is observed accuracy in the bin. | $\mathrm{conf}(b)$ is average predicted confidence in the bin. | . Lower ECE indicates better calibration. AnyJev reports ECE reduction from 0.240 with raw logits to 0.184 with L0 on its Qwen3-8B BANKING77 evaluation. github . Temperature scaling . Temperature scaling is a common post-hoc calibration method. It divides logits by a learned positive temperature $T$ before softmax: . $ p_i = \frac{\exp(z_i / T)}{\sum_j \exp(z_j / T)} $ . where: . | $z_i$ is the logit for candidate $i$. | $T$ is learned on a held-out calibration set. | $T > 1$ generally reduces confidence. | $0 < T < 1$ generally increases confidence. | . Temperature scaling preserves the ordering of logits, so it changes confidence without changing the argmax decision. This general calibration background is added for clarity; it is not a claim about the internal training method of every decision model. magazine.sebastianraschka . Calibration in decision models . Decision models are designed around calibrated confidence. Jev’s documentation describes its probabilities as well calibrated, and the JEV-as-a-Judge paper uses the model’s confidence directly to decide whether to accept a verdict or escalate it to a reasoning judge. magazine.sebastianraschka . However, calibration is dataset- and distribution-dependent. A model calibrated on support-ticket routing may not be calibrated on medical triage, code review, or adversarial text. Production systems should validate thresholds on representative local data before relying on confidence-based automation. arxiv .

127.doc: Decision Models (Part1): The Decision Layer for AI Systems
127.title: Part 6: Decision Cascades
127.content: Accept or escalate . A decision cascade uses a fast decision model as the first stage and escalates uncertain or high-stakes cases to a slower reasoning system. Input state | v +----------------------+ | Decision model | Returns probabilities| +----------------------+ | confidence >= threshold |--------------------------------+ | v v Accept decision Escalate to System 2 - reasoning LLM - human reviewer - tool-using agent . This architecture is valuable when most decisions are easy but a minority require deeper reasoning. The fast model handles the bulk of traffic; the expensive path handles only uncertain cases. JEV-as-a-Judge results . The JEV-as-a-Judge paper studies evaluation with JEV as a decision-only judge that returns label probabilities instead of text. Its confidence determines whether to accept the verdict or escalate to a reasoning judge. arxiv . Key reported findings: . | Against 16 generative and reward-model judges, with blinded human adjudication, JEV came within three points of GPT-6 wherever a verdict could be read from the text. | It did so at 0.36% of GPT-6’s fee and with a 0.15-second median latency. | It fell behind where the verdict had to be derived, such as math, code, and logic. | With a threshold frozen in advance, accepting confident verdicts and escalating the rest was 0.9 points more accurate than GPT-6 on 1,610 held-out pairs, at 41% of GPT-6’s fee. | In a pre-specified live test on two new workloads, the cascade matched GPT-6’s accuracy exactly. | Confidence routing weakened on style-adversarial pairs and reference-free prose. arxiv | . The practical lesson is that a decision model is strongest when the judgment can be read from the supplied evidence. It is weaker when the correct answer requires deriving a new result through multi-step reasoning.

128.doc: Decision Models (Part1): The Decision Layer for AI Systems
128.title: Part 7: Search and Agent Applications
128.content: SearchJev . SearchJev is a fast, calibrated System-1 model for search agents. It separates search decisions from System-2 reasoning and generation. arxiv . Given a search state and a decision schema, SearchJev directly scores legal options without autoregressive output generation. It uses Soft-Label Learning for Calibrated Decisions, or SLCD, to learn decision probabilities from uncertain supervision and calibrate confidence. arxiv . SearchDecision-Bench unifies six types of search decisions for training and evaluation. The paper reports: . | SearchJev improves decision quality over same-size Qwen3.5 autoregressive models. | It achieves 5.2 to 5.3 times faster decisions. | It reduces average expected calibration error by 41% to 74%. | In dual-system agents on BrowseComp-Plus, active search time improves by 3.7 to 4.7 times. | Answer accuracy improves from 45% to up to 54%. arxiv | . Search-agent decision examples . Typical System-1 decisions in a search agent include: . | Decision | Candidate options | Use of result | . | Relevance | Relevant, not relevant | Filter or retain a document | . | Evidence sufficiency | Sufficient, insufficient | Stop searching or continue | . | Next action | Search, read, refine query, answer | Control the agent loop | . | Query quality | Good, needs refinement | Decide whether to regenerate a query | . These examples illustrate the decision types described by SearchJev; the exact benchmark schema contains six decision types, and the paper should be consulted for the complete task definitions. arxiv . Agent policy and routing . In an agent system, decision models can gate actions before execution: . Agent observes state | v Decision model | +-- safe_action probability high --> execute tool | +-- uncertain or unsafe -----------> ask planner / human | +-- policy violation --------------> block action . The decision layer is especially useful for: . | Selecting a tool or backend. | Checking whether an action is allowed by policy. | Deciding whether retrieved evidence supports an answer. | Triage of incidents, tickets, invoices, or agent traces. | Scoring completed agent runs against a rubric. vllm-sr | .

129.doc: Decision Models (Part1): The Decision Layer for AI Systems
129.title: Part 8: Building and Fine-Tuning
129.content: When to fine-tune . A general decision model is attractive when tasks change frequently or labeled data is scarce. A specialized classifier can still be better when: . | The task is narrow and stable. | Latency requirements are extreme. | The label set is fixed. | Large volumes of high-quality labeled data exist. | The cost of maintaining a custom model is acceptable. | . Sebastian Raschka’s analysis frames the trade-off clearly: Jev-like models are more general than task-specific classifiers, while specialized classifiers can be better, faster, and cheaper for a narrow, well-defined problem. magazine.sebastianraschka . SFT workflow . Supervised fine-tuning, or SFT, adapts a decision model to domain-specific states, questions, candidates, and preferred decisions. The Liquid4All cookbook provides SFT notebooks for decision models using both Unsloth and TRL. vllm-sr . A typical workflow is: . 1. Define decision schema - state fields - questions - candidate sets - score rubrics 2. Collect or synthesize examples - state - question - correct option or score level 3. Format for SFT - preserve candidate order policy - include candidate descriptions - retain task instructions 4. Fine-tune - train model and decision head - use validation split for calibration 5. Evaluate - accuracy - calibration error - escalation rate - latency and cost 6. Deploy - serve with vLLM, llama.cpp, or managed endpoint - monitor drift and threshold performance . This workflow is a general engineering reconstruction; the exact data format and training hyperparameters depend on the chosen framework and base model. Unsloth and TRL . Unsloth provides documentation and tooling for training your own decision model, and the Liquid4All cookbook includes notebooks for SFT with both Unsloth and TRL. vllm-sr . | Tool | Role | . | Unsloth | Efficient fine-tuning library and decision-model training guide | . | TRL | Transformer Reinforcement Learning library for training workflows | . | Hugging Face | Model and dataset hosting | . | vLLM | High-throughput serving | . | llama.cpp | Local CPU/GPU inference for supported model formats | . These are infrastructure options; selecting one does not by itself guarantee calibration or accuracy. Evaluation on task-specific held-out data remains necessary.

130.doc: Decision Models (Part1): The Decision Layer for AI Systems
130.title: Part 9: Deployment
130.content: Local inference . Decision 1.0 provides weights and local inference code in its model repositories. An HTTP endpoint must be deployed separately if the application uses the System One-compatible HTTP interface. vllm-sr . AnyJev supports several execution modes: . | Mode | Description | . | transformers | In-process Hugging Face Transformers execution | . | vllm | vLLM running in the same process | . | server | Client to a separately running vllm serve endpoint | . | HTTP gateway | AnyJev endpoint in front of an upstream model server | . The AnyJev HTTP gateway listens on 127.0.0.1 and has no authentication of its own, so it should not be exposed directly to untrusted networks without adding authentication and transport security. github . System One request format . Decision 1.0 uses the upstream System One request format: state, model, and named questions. The official TypeSafe Python SDK or an equivalent HTTP request can be used with a SystemOne-compatible deployment. vllm-sr . Install the SDK: . pip install typesafe-sdk . The following Python example is published in the Lux model card and reproduced from the Decision 1.0 announcement. vllm-sr . from typesafe_sdk import Choice, Noul, TypeSafeClient with TypeSafeClient( api_key="YOUR_ENDPOINT_API_KEY", base_url="https://your-decision-endpoint.example", model="Decision-1.0-Lux-9B", ) as client: result = client.system_one( state="Customer reports a duplicate charge and asks for a refund.", questions={ "route": Choice( instructions="Which team should handle this request?", criteria={ "billing": "Payments and refunds", "technical": "Product faults", }, ), "refund_requested": Noul( instructions="Did the customer request a refund?" ), }, ) print(result.choices["route"].choice) print(result.nouls["refund_requested"].noul) . The equivalent HTTP request is: vllm-sr . curl -X POST 'https://your-decision-endpoint.example/v1/systemone' \ -H 'Authorization: Bearer YOUR_ENDPOINT_API_KEY' \ -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \ --data-raw '{ "model": "Decision-1.0-Lux-9B", "state": "Customer reports a duplicate charge and asks for a refund.", "questions": { "route": { "type": "choice", "instructions": "Which team should handle this request?", "criteria": { "billing": "Payments and refunds", "technical": "Product faults" } }, "refund_requested": { "type": "noul", "instructions": "Did the customer request a refund?" } } }' . Deployment checklist . | Define explicit candidate descriptions rather than relying only on short labels. | Set action thresholds from local validation data, not intuition. | Log the full probability distribution, not only the selected option. | Monitor calibration, escalation rate, latency, cost, and drift. | Bound reasoning escalation with a token budget and a share cap. | Keep a human or System-2 path for high-impact or low-confidence decisions. | Test candidate-order sensitivity, especially when using raw logits. | Validate behavior under adversarial, out-of-distribution, and reference-free inputs. github | .

131.doc: Decision Models (Part1): The Decision Layer for AI Systems
131.title: Part 10: Comparisons and Trade-Offs
131.content: Decision model versus classifier versus LLM . | Dimension | Task-specific classifier | Decision model | Generative LLM | . | Candidate set | Usually fixed at training time | Supplied at inference time | Can be specified in the prompt | . | Output | Label or score | Typed distribution over candidates | Free-form text | . | Training need | Usually requires task labels | Can be zero-shot, training-free, or fine-tuned | Can be prompted without training | . | Latency | Usually lowest | Low, especially with one-pass readout | Higher when generating text | . | Cost | Low at scale | Low to moderate | Highest for reasoning-heavy paths | . | Generality | Narrow | Broad across decision tasks | Broadest | . | Reasoning depth | Limited | Limited unless escalated | Strongest | . | Calibration | Requires evaluation and post-processing | Core design goal | Often requires additional calibration work | . This comparison combines source claims with general engineering context. The source material specifically emphasizes that Jev-like models occupy a middle ground: more general than a custom classifier, faster and cheaper than using a large generative model for every decision. magazine.sebastianraschka . One-pass readout versus reasoning escalation . | Approach | Latency | Cost | Accuracy potential | When to use | . | Raw logits | Very low | Very low | Sensitive to order and label bias | Prototyping only | . | L0 rotations | Low to moderate | Low | Better order robustness and calibration | Training-free decisions | . | Tacit one-forward | Very low | Low | Strong when model is well trained | High-volume operational decisions | . | Adaptive reasoning escalation | Variable | Higher | Better on uncertain cases | High-stakes or ambiguous decisions | . | Full System-2 reasoning | Highest | Highest | Strongest for derivation-heavy tasks | Planning, math, code, complex logic | . AnyJev’s adaptive mode operationalizes this trade-off by sending only a capped share of low-confidence decisions to reasoning. github .

132.doc: Decision Models (Part1): The Decision Layer for AI Systems
132.title: Part 11: Limitations and Open Questions
132.content: Known limitations . | Derived answers are harder. JEV-as-a-Judge found that decision-only judging falls behind where the verdict must be derived, such as math, code, and logic. arxiv | Adversarial and reference-free evaluation are difficult. Confidence routing weakened on style-adversarial pairs and reference-free prose. arxiv | Calibration is not universal. A model calibrated on one distribution may be miscalibrated on another; local threshold validation is necessary. arxiv | Candidate order can matter. Raw label logits can flip answers when options are reordered; AnyJev’s L0 reduces but does not inherently eliminate the need for careful evaluation. github | Escalation costs tokens. AnyJev reports hundreds of additional generated tokens per escalated decision for Tacit-9B and Tacit-4B. github | Benchmark scores are suite-dependent. Decision 1.0’s results use a selected 54-task suite and a weighted overall metric; they should not be generalized as universal superiority. vllm-sr | Open questions remain. AnyJev’s roadmap lists label-free early exit, agent-loop evaluation, additional log-prob backends, and span readout beyond 26 options as areas still under development. github | . Evaluation gaps . Production adoption should evaluate more than headline accuracy: . | Accuracy by decision type and candidate-set size. | ECE and reliability diagrams. | Automation rate at a fixed error budget. | Escalation rate and reasoning-token cost. | Sensitivity to candidate order and paraphrasing. | Out-of-distribution performance. | Latency distributions, including median and p95. | Failure impact by action severity. | .

134.content: . | Central mechanism: Decision models map a state, question, and candidate set to typed probability distributions instead of generating free-form answers. vllm-sr | Main architectural insight: Separate frequent System-1 decisions from slower System-2 reasoning; use the fast path for routing, gating, and scoring, and escalate uncertainty. arxiv | Important specifications: Decision 1.0 includes six open models from 0.6B to 9B parameters, with input budgets of 1,024 or 16,384 tokens; Lux-9B reports an overall score of 76.94 on the release’s 54-task suite. vllm-sr | Key calibration result: AnyJev’s label-free L0 readout raised the share of Qwen3-8B BANKING77 decisions automatable at no more than 5% error from 7.7% to 46.3%. github | Most important trade-off: One-pass decision readouts minimize latency and cost, while reasoning escalation improves difficult cases at materially higher token cost. github | Main limitation: Decision models are strongest when the answer can be read from supplied evidence; derivation-heavy tasks such as math, code, and logic still benefit from System-2 reasoning. arxiv | Engineering implication: Treat the decision layer as a programmable control plane: define candidates and rubrics explicitly, use calibrated probabilities for policy, and reserve expensive reasoning for genuinely uncertain or high-impact cases. vllm-sr | .
