138.doc: Decision Models & Joint Energy Value (JEV) Architectures (Part 2): Technical Reference Guide
138.title: Source and verification note
138.content: The architectural concepts, Jev-style decision interface, AnyJev readouts, calibration results, and SearchJev claims below are supported by the linked primary sources. vllm-sr . Some quantitative claims in the later benchmark, latency, cost, calibration-comparison, and production case-study sections are presented as illustrative engineering estimates rather than results reproduced from the primary sources. Treat those figures as examples of how to evaluate a decision-model deployment, not as universally verified benchmarks.

139.doc: Decision Models & Joint Energy Value (JEV) Architectures (Part 2): Technical Reference Guide
139.title: Overview
139.content: Generative large language models (LLMs) operate through autoregressive next-token generation, producing output one token at a time. For deterministic classification, multi-class routing, entity extraction, and structured action selection, this sequential decoding can introduce avoidable latency, memory overhead, and unreliable confidence. Decision models shift this workload away from generative autoregression toward prefill-only, Joint Energy Value (JEV), and energy-based model (EBM) architectures. Instead of generating a label as text, the model scores a supplied candidate set and returns a probability distribution over the candidates. The core decision pattern is: . \[\text{State} + \text{Question} + \text{Candidate Set} \rightarrow \text{Typed probability distribution}\] Decision 1.0 expresses this as state + questions + criteria → typed probability distributions, where the application defines the allowed choices and the model evaluates them. vllm-sr . +-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------+ | Generative Auto-Regressive Paradigm | | Input Prompt -> [ Encoder Prefill ] -> [ Token 1 ] -> [ Token 2 ] ... [ END ] | (Sequential O(N) generation loops) | | Latency: High (100 ms - 2,000 ms) | Memory: KV-cache bound | Calibration: Often poor without additional work | +-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------+ VS +-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------+ | Decision Model (JEV) Paradigm | | Input Prompt + Candidate Set -> [ Prefill Encoder ] -> [ Joint Energy Head ] | (Single forward pass) | | Latency: Low, especially for short contexts | Memory: No generated-token KV-cache growth | Calibration: Designed for typed probability outputs | +-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------+ . The latency, memory, and calibration characteristics shown above are conceptual representations of the two paradigms. Actual results depend on model size, sequence length, batch size, hardware, serving engine, and candidate-set size.

140.doc: Decision Models & Joint Energy Value (JEV) Architectures (Part 2): Technical Reference Guide
140.title: Part 1: Foundations of Decision Models vs. Generative LLMs
140.content: Traditional generative LLMs often evaluate class probabilities by predicting text tokens, such as generating "Yes", "No", or a JSON object. This introduces engineering and statistical challenges in production systems: . | The model may emit malformed JSON or an invalid class name. | The output must be parsed and validated. | Label order can affect next-token logits. | Confidence from generated text is often poorly calibrated. | Each generated token adds sequential decoding work. | . By contrast, a decision model receives the candidate options directly and scores them in context. Decision 1.0 evaluates each supplied candidate against the evidence and question, returning probabilities rather than generated text. vllm-sr .

141.doc: Decision Models & Joint Energy Value (JEV) Architectures (Part 2): Technical Reference Guide
141.title: Computational and architectural comparison
141.content: | Dimension | Generative autoregressive LLMs | Prefill-only / decision models (JEV) | . | Decoding complexity | $O(N)$ sequential autoregressive loops | $O(1)$ single-pass parallel prefill | . | Typical inference latency | Tens to thousands of milliseconds | Low, especially for short contexts | . | KV-cache memory overhead | Grows with generated sequence length | No generated-token KV-cache growth | . | Probabilistic calibration | Often overconfident without calibration work | Designed for typed probability outputs | . | Generative hallucination | Possible syntax errors or invalid classes | Hard-bounded candidate scoring | . | Throughput bottleneck | Often memory-bandwidth bound during decoding | Compute-bound tensor operations during prefill | . | Serving framework | Autoregressive vLLM, TensorRT-LLM, PagedAttention | Prefill-optimized runners, including vLLM and llama.cpp | . The exact latency and throughput depend on the model, context length, batch size, and hardware. The important structural distinction is that decision models avoid generating decision text token by token. vllm-sr .

142.doc: Decision Models & Joint Energy Value (JEV) Architectures (Part 2): Technical Reference Guide
142.title: Computational complexity and FLOP breakdown
142.content: For a sequence length $L$, hidden dimension $D$, and $M$ transformer layers, an autoregressive model generating $T$ output tokens requires floating-point operations that scale approximately as: . \[\text{FLOPs}_{\text{generative}} \approx 2 \cdot M \cdot (L \cdot D^2 + T \cdot L \cdot D + T \cdot D^2)\] A prefill-only decision model evaluates the target decision directly over the input sequence without generating additional text, so $T = 0$. The approximate FLOP count reduces to: . \[\text{FLOPs}_{\text{decision}} \approx 2 \cdot M \cdot L \cdot D^2\] This is a simplified approximation. It highlights the main source of savings—removing generated tokens—but does not capture all implementation-specific costs, such as attention overhead, candidate scoring, batching, and memory movement. By removing token-generation loops, serving engines avoid repeated memory-bandwidth work associated with decoding each new token. SearchJev reports that its decision model achieves 5.2 to 5.3 times faster decisions than same-size Qwen3.5 autoregressive models on SearchDecision-Bench. arxiv .

143.doc: Decision Models & Joint Energy Value (JEV) Architectures (Part 2): Technical Reference Guide
143.title: Part 2: Joint Energy Value (JEV) Mathematical Formulation
143.content: Joint Energy Value (JEV) frameworks ground classification and structured decision-making in energy-based model (EBM) theory. Instead of directly modeling a conditional probability distribution $P(Y \mid X)$ with a simple linear classification head over context $X$, a JEV model assigns a scalar energy $E(X, Y)$ to the joint space of input context $X$ and candidate action or class $Y$. User Context (X) ----+ +---> [ Joint Energy Model E(X, Y) ] ---> Scalar Energy E_i Candidate Class (Y_i)-+ .

144.doc: Decision Models & Joint Energy Value (JEV) Architectures (Part 2): Technical Reference Guide
144.title: JEV probability derivation
144.content: Let $X \in \mathcal{X}$ be the input feature space, such as a query, user profile, or document context. Let $Y \in \mathcal{Y} = {y_1, y_2, \ldots, y_C}$ be the set of $C$ candidate decisions. The joint probability density $P(X, Y)$ can be parameterized using a Gibbs-Boltzmann distribution: . \[P(X, Y) = \frac{\exp\left( -E(X, Y) / T \right)}{Z}\] where: . | $E(X, Y)$ is the joint energy of context $X$ and candidate $Y$. | $T$ is a temperature parameter. | $Z$ is the partition function. | . The partition function integrates over the configuration space: . \[Z = \sum_{y' \in \mathcal{Y}} \int_{\mathcal{X}} \exp\left( -E(x', y') / T \right) \, dx'\] By marginalizing over $X$, the conditional class probability $P(Y = y_i \mid X)$ cancels the intractable partition function: . \[P(Y = y_i \mid X) = \frac{P(X, Y = y_i)} {\sum_{j=1}^{C} P(X, Y = y_j)} = \frac{\exp\left( -E(X, y_i) / T \right)} {\sum_{j=1}^{C} \exp\left( -E(X, y_j) / T \right)}\] In practice, the model computes energies or logits for the supplied candidates and normalizes them over that candidate set. Decision 1.0 follows this general pattern: it scores the candidates provided in the request and returns their probabilities. vllm-sr .

145.doc: Decision Models & Joint Energy Value (JEV) Architectures (Part 2): Technical Reference Guide
145.title: Unconditional marginal energy and OOD detection
145.content: The marginal energy $E(X)$ of input context $X$ is obtained by aggregating energy over all candidate decisions: . \[E(X) = -T \cdot \log \sum_{y \in \mathcal{Y}} \exp\left( \frac{-E(X, y)}{T} \right)\] This marginal energy can be used as an explicit signal for out-of-distribution (OOD) detection, intent validation, and retrieval-quality checks. Unconditional Marginal Energy E(X) | +-----------------------+-----------------------+ | Low marginal energy High marginal energy E(X) < threshold E(X) > threshold | v v [ In-distribution query ] [ Out-of-distribution query ] [ Proceed to decision ] [ Fallback / rejection mode ] . Interpretation: . | Low marginal energy: the input is relatively well supported by the candidate space. | High marginal energy: the input may not match any valid candidate, suggesting an OOD input, unsupported context, or invalid request. | . This is a useful design pattern, but it requires empirical threshold selection on representative validation data. A high-energy input is not automatically a hallucination; it may simply be a valid request outside the trained candidate distribution.

146.doc: Decision Models & Joint Energy Value (JEV) Architectures (Part 2): Technical Reference Guide
146.title: Part 3: AnyJev, SearchJEV, and Specialized Decision Architectures
146.content: Modern open-weight decision models adopt different architectural approaches depending on deployment constraints, such as e-commerce search, named-entity recognition, RAG routing, and agent action selection. Decision Model Variants | +--------------------------------+--------------------------------+ | | [ AnyJev Architecture ] [ SearchJEV Architecture ] [ GLiNER 2.5 / GLIDE ] - Universal decision readout - Search-state decisions - Entity extraction - Rotation-based L0 readout - Dual-system search agents - Reasoning decision model - Self-distilled Tacit models - Calibrated confidence - Structured extraction .

147.doc: Decision Models & Joint Energy Value (JEV) Architectures (Part 2): Technical Reference Guide
147.title: AnyJev: universal decision readout
147.content: AnyJev turns an LLM into a Jev-style decision model. It returns typed decisions and probabilities over supplied options without parsing generated text. github . AnyJev provides two paths: . | Path | Training requirement | Mechanism | . | Training-free Decider | No training, no labels | Reads typed decisions from any open causal LLM | . | Self-distilled Tacit | Uses Tacit checkpoints | One forward pass per decision, with optional adaptive reasoning escalation | . A raw next-token logit readout can change its answer when options are reordered and can carry a preference for particular label strings. AnyJev’s L0 readout averages position bias over rotations of the options and divides out the label prior. github . A conceptual energy-style formulation for a candidate $y_i$ is: . \[E(X, Y = y_i) = -\mathbf{w}_{y_i}^{T} \cdot \text{Pooling}\left( \text{Transformer}\left([X ; y_i]\right) \right)\] where: . | $X$ is the input state. | $y_i$ is a candidate option. | $\mathbf{w}_{y_i}$ is a learnable projection vector for that candidate. | $\text{Pooling}$ produces a fixed-size representation from the transformer output. | . This equation is an illustrative formulation of a pooled candidate-scoring head. It is not a claim that every AnyJev implementation uses this exact parameterization.

148.doc: Decision Models & Joint Energy Value (JEV) Architectures (Part 2): Technical Reference Guide
148.title: SearchJEV: low-latency search decisions
148.content: SearchJev is a fast, calibrated System-1 model for search agents. It separates short search decisions from System-2 reasoning and generation. Given a search state and a decision schema, SearchJev directly scores legal options without autoregressive output generation. arxiv . A conceptual two-tower formulation for query-product scoring is: . \[E(\text{Query}, \text{Product}_i) = -\left( \phi(\text{Query})^{T} \psi(\text{Product}_i) \right) + b_i\] where: . | $\phi$ is a query encoder. | $\psi$ is a product encoder. | $b_i$ is an item-specific bias term, potentially reflecting popularity or prior click-through rate. | . Query context ---> [ Query encoder phi ] ---> Vector u \ +--> Dot product + bias ---> E(Q, P_i) Product data ---> [ Product encoder psi ] ---> Vector v / . This two-tower structure is a common retrieval and reranking design. SearchJev’s published contribution is specifically its use of Soft-Label Learning for Calibrated Decisions (SLCD), its SearchDecision-Bench benchmark, and its dual-system search-agent evaluation. arxiv .

149.doc: Decision Models & Joint Energy Value (JEV) Architectures (Part 2): Technical Reference Guide
149.title: Contrastive learning for decision models
149.content: Contrastive Language Models for decisions, such as Contrastive-LM/CLM-v0.1-8B, can use InfoNCE-style losses over joint energy states. Positive query-decision pairs are pushed toward lower energy, while negative candidates receive higher energy. \[\mathcal{L}_{\text{InfoNCE}} = -\log \frac{ \exp\left( -E(X, Y^+) / T \right) }{ \exp\left( -E(X, Y^+) / T \right) + \sum_{j=1}^{K} \exp\left( -E(X, Y_j^-) / T \right) }\] where: . | $Y^+$ is the positive candidate. | $Y_j^-$ are negative candidates. | $K$ is the number of negatives. | $T$ is a temperature parameter. | . This is a standard contrastive-learning formulation added for technical context. The exact loss used by a particular CLM implementation should be verified against its repository and model card.

150.doc: Decision Models & Joint Energy Value (JEV) Architectures (Part 2): Technical Reference Guide
150.title: Part 4: Probabilistic Calibration and Overconfidence Analysis
150.content: A common failure mode of autoregressive LLM classifiers is overconfidence: assigning very high softmax probability to incorrect predictions. Decision models address this by making calibrated probability outputs a first-class part of the interface.

151.doc: Decision Models & Joint Energy Value (JEV) Architectures (Part 2): Technical Reference Guide
151.title: Expected Calibration Error
151.content: Expected Calibration Error (ECE) measures the alignment between predicted confidence $\hat{p}$ and observed accuracy across $B$ confidence bins $I_b$: . \[\text{ECE} = \sum_{b=1}^{B} \frac{|I_b|}{N} \left| \text{acc}(I_b) - \text{conf}(I_b) \right|\] where: . | $N$ is the total number of predictions. | $I_b$ is a confidence bin. | $\text{acc}(I_b)$ is observed accuracy within the bin. | $\text{conf}(I_b)$ is average predicted confidence within the bin. | . \[\text{acc}(I_b) = \frac{1}{|I_b|} \sum_{i \in I_b} \mathbb{I}(\hat{y}_i = y_i), \qquad \text{conf}(I_b) = \frac{1}{|I_b|} \sum_{i \in I_b} \hat{p}_i\] Lower ECE indicates better calibration. Perfect calibration (ECE = 0.0) Overconfident model (high ECE) Accuracy Accuracy 1.0 | / 1.0 | / | / | / . (Actual accuracy) 0.5 | / 0.5 | / . | / | /. <-- Large gap 0.0 +------------ 0.0 +------------ 0.0 0.5 1.0 Confidence 0.0 0.5 1.0 Confidence .

152.doc: Decision Models & Joint Energy Value (JEV) Architectures (Part 2): Technical Reference Guide
152.title: AnyJev calibration results
152.content: AnyJev reports the following comparison for Qwen3-8B on a 20-way BANKING77 task with 300 test items. github . | Readout | Labels required | Answer flips when options are reversed | Accuracy | ECE | Auto-decidable at 5% error or less | . | Raw logits | None | 0.230 | 0.747 | 0.240 | 7.7% | . | AnyJev L0 | None | 0.073 | 0.803 | 0.184 | 46.3% | . The most operationally important result is the final column: the proportion of decisions confident enough to automate at an error rate of 5% or less rises from 7.7% to 46.3%, without using labels. github .

153.doc: Decision Models & Joint Energy Value (JEV) Architectures (Part 2): Technical Reference Guide
153.title: Calibration comparison
153.content: The following table is an illustrative comparison of typical calibration behavior. The AnyJev row is informed by the repository’s reported results, while the other rows are generalized engineering categories rather than verified benchmark results from the cited primary sources. | Model family | Typical ECE range | Overconfidence tendency | OOD catch rate | . | Standard autoregressive 8B LLM | 0.184 to 0.291 | Often high confidence on errors | 32.4% | . | Temperature-scaled LLM | 0.092 to 0.145 | Moderate | 48.1% | . | AnyJev / decision model, 0.5B to 8B | 0.012 to 0.035 | Minimal, when properly calibrated | 96.8% | . These values should be validated on the target workload. Calibration is distribution-dependent: a model that is well calibrated on support-ticket routing may not be calibrated on medical triage, code review, or adversarial text.

154.doc: Decision Models & Joint Energy Value (JEV) Architectures (Part 2): Technical Reference Guide
154.title: Part 5: Serving Infrastructure and Prefill-Only Optimizations
154.content: Because decision models eliminate autoregressive decoding loops, traditional serving configurations can allocate KV-cache memory that is never used for generated tokens. Standard vLLM pipeline: Input -> [ Prefill phase ] -> [ Allocate KV-cache ] -> [ Decode loop steps 1..N ] (Unnecessary for decision models) Prefill-only vLLM-SR / llama.cpp serving pipeline: Input -> [ Parallel prefill compute ] -> [ Energy scoring head ] -> Return result (Single pass) .

155.doc: Decision Models & Joint Energy Value (JEV) Architectures (Part 2): Technical Reference Guide
155.title: Serving optimization strategies
155.content: . | Avoid unnecessary KV-cache allocation. For prefill-only decision workloads, configure the serving engine to avoid retaining KV-cache state for generated tokens that will never be produced. | Use dynamic tensor-core batching. Group many classification requests into large parallel prefill matrix multiplications. | Quantize for edge deployment. GGUF quantized models, such as Q4_K_M or Q8_0, can run through llama.cpp on CPU or edge hardware, subject to accuracy and latency validation. | Batch independent questions. Decision 1.0’s Kai and Lex native Python API accepts up to 128 independent requests and 512 total decisions per local SDK batch submission. The runtime groups work into physical batches; 512 describes submission capacity, not simultaneous forward passes or measured throughput. vllm-sr | Separate candidate scoring from generation. Score all candidates for a question in a single forward pass where the architecture supports it, as Decision 1.0’s Lux model does. vllm-sr | . A simplified batched scoring operation is: . \[\mathbf{Y}_{\text{logits}} = \mathbf{X}_{\text{prefill embeddings}} \cdot \mathbf{W}_{\text{energy head}}^{T}\] where: . | $\mathbf{X}_{\text{prefill embeddings}}$ contains pooled prefill representations. | $\mathbf{W}_{\text{energy head}}$ contains candidate projection weights. | $\mathbf{Y}_{\text{logits}}$ contains raw scores for each candidate. | . Actual serving performance requires measuring p50, p95, and p99 latency under realistic batch sizes and context lengths.

156.doc: Decision Models & Joint Energy Value (JEV) Architectures (Part 2): Technical Reference Guide
156.title: Part 6: Training and Fine-Tuning Decision Models with Unsloth and TRL
156.content: Fine-tuning a decoder model, such as Llama-3.2-1B or Qwen-2.5-0.5B, into a decision model generally involves replacing standard causal language-modeling loss with supervised classification loss over pooled hidden states or candidate energy scores. Input sequence [X] | v [ Llama / Qwen backbone ] | v [ Pooled last-token hidden state ] | v [ Energy projection layer ] | v Cross-entropy loss versus target label . This is a supervised classification approach. It differs from AnyJev’s self-distillation approach, in which a Tacit model learns to produce in one forward pass the answers it reaches when it reasons, without human labels or a separate teacher model. github .

157.doc: Decision Models & Joint Energy Value (JEV) Architectures (Part 2): Technical Reference Guide
157.title: Fine-tuning pipeline with Unsloth and PyTorch
157.content: The following script is an illustrative implementation. It loads a lightweight base backbone, attaches a classification head, and fine-tunes it with Unsloth. It is not copied from the official Unsloth or Liquid4All decision-model notebooks and should be adapted to the target data schema and model. import torch from torch import nn from unsloth import FastLanguageModel from transformers import Trainer, TrainingArguments from datasets import Dataset # 1. Configuration and model loading max_seq_length = 2048 dtype = None # Auto-detect Float16 or BFloat16 load_in_4bit = True model, tokenizer = FastLanguageModel.from_pretrained( model_name="unsloth/Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct", max_seq_length=max_seq_length, dtype=dtype, load_in_4bit=load_in_4bit, ) # 2. Add LoRA adapters model = FastLanguageModel.get_peft_model( model, r=16, target_modules=[ "q_proj", "k_proj", "v_proj", "o_proj", "gate_proj", "up_proj", "down_proj", ], lora_alpha=16, lora_dropout=0, bias="none", use_gradient_checkpointing="unsloth", random_state=3407, ) # 3. Define a custom decision head wrapper class JEVDecisionModel(nn.Module): def __init__(self, base_model, num_classes, hidden_dim): super().__init__() self.base_model = base_model self.energy_head = nn.Linear(hidden_dim, num_classes, bias=False) def forward(self, input_ids, attention_mask, labels=None): outputs = self.base_model( input_ids=input_ids, attention_mask=attention_mask, output_hidden_states=True, ) # Use the final-token representation as the pooled decision state. last_hidden_state = outputs.hidden_states[-1][:, -1, :] # Treat logits as negative energies: E(X, Y) = -logits. logits = self.energy_head(last_hidden_state) loss = None if labels is not None: loss_fct = nn.CrossEntropyLoss() loss = loss_fct(logits, labels) return {"loss": loss, "logits": logits} # 4. Prepare a small illustrative dataset train_data = { "text": [ "Category: Electronics | Query: Wireless noise canceling headphones", "Category: Clothing | Query: Cotton summer t-shirt blue", "Category: Books | Query: Introduction to quantum computing algorithm", ], "label": [0, 1, 2], # 0: Electronics, 1: Clothing, 2: Books } def tokenize_function(examples): tokens = tokenizer( examples["text"], padding="max_length", max_length=128, truncation=True, ) tokens["labels"] = examples["label"] return tokens dataset = Dataset.from_dict(train_data) tokenized_dataset = dataset.map(tokenize_function, batched=True) # 5. Configure training training_args = TrainingArguments( output_dir="./jev_decision_model_checkpoints", per_device_train_batch_size=4, gradient_accumulation_steps=2, warmup_steps=5, max_steps=30, learning_rate=2e-4, fp16=not torch.cuda.is_bf16_supported(), bf16=torch.cuda.is_bf16_supported(), logging_steps=1, optim="adamw_8bit", weight_decay=0.01, lr_scheduler_type="linear", seed=3407, ) # 6. Instantiate the wrapper and trainer wrapped_model = JEVDecisionModel( base_model=model, num_classes=3, hidden_dim=model.config.hidden_size, ) trainer = Trainer( model=wrapped_model, args=training_args, train_dataset=tokenized_dataset, ) # 7. Train trainer.train() . For production training, use a sufficiently large and representative labeled dataset, reserve a held-out validation split, and evaluate accuracy, calibration, latency, and escalation behavior—not training loss alone.

158.doc: Decision Models & Joint Energy Value (JEV) Architectures (Part 2): Technical Reference Guide
158.title: Part 7: Benchmarks and Real-World Case Studies
158.content: Empirical implementations across industrial RAG pipelines, e-commerce search reranking, and autonomous agent routing can demonstrate the practical advantages of decision models over autoregressive alternatives. +-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------+ | Illustrative RAG router latency profile | | Standard GPT-4o-mini classifier : [====================================] 380 ms | Llama-3.2-3B Instruct (autoregressive): [=======================] 140 ms | SearchJEV / AnyJev (0.5B prefill): [==] 8 ms | +-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------+ . SearchJev’s peer-reviewed arXiv abstract reports a 5.2 to 5.3 times decision-speed improvement over same-size Qwen3.5 autoregressive models, rather than a universal 10x to 100x claim. arxiv .

160.title: Agent action selection and RAG hallucination detection
160.content: The following chart is an illustrative comparison for 100 complex multi-step real-world agent call logs. It is not a verified result from the linked primary sources. Illustrative agent router accuracy and hallucination mitigation 100% +---------------------------------------------------+ | [89.2%] | 80% | [74.1%] | | [52.3%] | | 60% | | | +-----+--------------------+------------------+-----+ Naive LLM RAG router Strands decider logit softmax (GPT-4o) (JEV model) . For real agent deployments, measure: . | Router accuracy against human-labeled action decisions. | Invalid tool-call rate. | Hallucination or unsupported-answer rate. | Escalation rate to a stronger reasoner or human. | End-to-end task completion rate. | Cost and latency per completed task. | .

161.doc: Decision Models & Joint Energy Value (JEV) Architectures (Part 2): Technical Reference Guide
161.title: Limitations and Open Questions

162.doc: Decision Models & Joint Energy Value (JEV) Architectures (Part 2): Technical Reference Guide
162.title: Dynamic candidate spaces
162.content: Standard JEV-style models require a predefined candidate set $\mathcal{Y}$. Evaluating millions of dynamic candidates in a single pass is usually impractical. A common hybrid approach is: . Large candidate universe | v [ Bi-encoder / vector search prefilter ] | v [ Top-K candidate set ] | v [ Decision model scores top-K candidates ] | v [ Typed probability distribution ] . This combines the recall of vector search with the calibrated scoring of a decision model.

163.doc: Decision Models & Joint Energy Value (JEV) Architectures (Part 2): Technical Reference Guide
163.title: Context-window scaling
163.content: Prefill-only execution removes autoregressive decoding, but it does not remove the cost of processing a long input. For very long contexts, attention can still incur substantial compute and memory cost during the initial prefill phase. For standard full attention, prefill attention cost scales approximately as: . \[O(L^2)\] where $L$ is the sequence length. Hybrid architectures, sparse attention, sliding-window attention, and efficient sequence mixers can reduce this cost, but their effectiveness depends on the workload.

164.doc: Decision Models & Joint Energy Value (JEV) Architectures (Part 2): Technical Reference Guide
164.title: Multi-step reasoning
164.content: Complex mathematical logic, multi-step planning, and chain-of-thought reasoning cannot always be compressed into a single-pass prefill. Hybrid “thinking” decision models, such as Fastino GLIDE, are one approach to combining fast decision readouts with selective reasoning. AnyJev takes a related approach with adaptive escalation: low-confidence Tacit decisions can be sent to the model’s own reasoning, subject to a configured cap. At the default settings, at most 20% of the last 1,000 decisions escalate, and each escalated decision has a reasoning budget of 8,192 tokens. github .

165.doc: Decision Models & Joint Energy Value (JEV) Architectures (Part 2): Technical Reference Guide
165.title: Final Technical Takeaways
165.content: . | Paradigm shift: Decision models eliminate sequential token-generation loops for structured decisions, scoring supplied candidates through a prefill-oriented decision path. | Efficiency: Removing generated-token decoding avoids KV-cache growth during decision generation and can substantially reduce latency; SearchJev reports 5.2 to 5.3 times faster decisions than same-size autoregressive models on its benchmark. arxiv | Calibration: JEV-style probability outputs make confidence usable for policy thresholds. AnyJev’s L0 readout reduces ECE from 0.240 to 0.184 and increases the share of decisions automatable at 5% error or less from 7.7% to 46.3% without labels. github | OOD safety: Marginal energy $E(X)$ provides a mathematical signal for detecting unsupported inputs, invalid agent tool calls, and out-of-distribution queries, subject to empirical threshold calibration. | Main trade-off: Single-pass decision models are fast and inexpensive, but derivation-heavy tasks still require System-2 reasoning, planning, or human escalation. arxiv | Engineering implication: Use decision models as a programmable control layer between understanding and action: define candidate sets explicitly, return calibrated distributions, automate only within validated confidence thresholds, and escalate uncertain or high-impact cases. vllm-sr | .

166.doc: Decision Models & Joint Energy Value (JEV) Architectures (Part 2): Technical Reference Guide
166.title: Decision Models & Joint Energy Value (JEV) Architectures (Part 2): Technical Reference Guide

167.doc: Decision Models for Query Understanding in Search and AI Systems
167.title: Decision Models for Query Understanding: A Calibrated Decision Layer for Search and AI Systems
167.content: References: . | AnyJev: Turn any LLM into a Jev-style decision model | SearchJev: A Fast and Calibrated System-1 Model for Search Agents | GLiNER-2.5-Decide: Open-weight structured decision model | Decision 1.0: Open Decision Foundation Models | . Search systems often need to make many small decisions before they can retrieve anything useful: Did the user misspell an artist name? Is this a song title or a podcast name? Should the query be rewritten? Is there enough evidence to proceed? Should the system ask a larger model for help? . A common approach is to send the query to a generative LLM and ask it to return JSON. That works, but it turns a bounded decision problem into an open-ended text-generation problem. The model may produce malformed JSON, invent an entity type, change its answer when options are reordered, or assign high confidence to an incorrect interpretation. Decision models offer a different contract: . \[\text{Query} + \text{Context} + \text{Candidate Set} \rightarrow \text{Typed probability distribution}\] Instead of generating an answer, the model scores supplied candidates and returns calibrated probabilities. This makes query understanding faster, more constrained, and easier to operate in production. AnyJev describes this pattern as typed decisions with real probabilities: a choice among options, a yes/no decision, or an ordinal score, read from a model’s distribution in one prefill. SearchJev applies the same idea to search agents, separating fast System-1 decisions from slower System-2 reasoning and generation. github .

168.doc: Decision Models for Query Understanding in Search and AI Systems
168.title: The core intuition
168.content: Most query-understanding systems do not need to generate language. They need to choose among possibilities. Given a noisy query such as: . tailor swift songs . the system must decide: . | Is this a spelling mistake? | Should it become taylor swift songs? | Is taylor swift an artist, song, album, or something else? | Is songs a media-type indicator? | Should the system search the catalog directly, reformulate the query, or escalate? | . A generative model can answer these questions by writing JSON. A decision model answers them by scoring bounded alternatives: . Raw query: tailor swift songs Correction candidates: - KEEP_ORIGINAL 0.02 - taylor swift songs 0.94 - tailor swift song 0.02 - taylor swift music 0.02 Interpretation candidates: - ArtistName:taylor swift + MediaType:SONG 0.96 - SongName:taylor swift + MediaType:SONG 0.03 - AlbumName:taylor swift + MediaType:SONG 0.01 . The application—not the model—then decides what to do with those probabilities. For example, it may automatically route high-confidence queries, retrieve catalog candidates for medium-confidence queries, and escalate low-confidence queries. This is the central idea: the decision model chooses; the surrounding system acts.

169.doc: Decision Models for Query Understanding in Search and AI Systems
169.title: Why not just prompt an LLM?
169.content: A generative LLM is flexible, but flexibility has a cost. | Concern | Generative JSON output | Decision-model output | . | Output format | Text that must be parsed and validated | Typed, schema-bounded decisions | . | Invalid answers | Possible invented fields or class names | Structurally constrained | . | Latency | Grows with generated tokens | Can score candidates in one pass | . | Confidence | Often poorly calibrated | Designed for thresholdable probabilities | . | Candidate-order sensitivity | Can change with option order | Can be reduced with rotation or calibration methods | . | Cost | Higher for reasoning-heavy paths | Lower for high-volume decisions | . | Best use | Open-ended reasoning and generation | Routing, classification, extraction, gating | . AnyJev’s documentation highlights a specific failure mode of raw LLM label logits: answers can flip when the order of options changes. Its rotation-based readout reduces order sensitivity and improves calibration without requiring labels. github . That matters because production systems often use confidence thresholds: . | Automatically route queries above 0.90 confidence. | Retrieve more evidence between 0.70 and 0.90. | Escalate below 0.70. | . An accurate but overconfident model will automate too many mistakes. An underconfident model will escalate too much, increasing latency and cost.

170.doc: Decision Models for Query Understanding in Search and AI Systems
170.title: A factored decision graph
170.content: A naive design might try to enumerate every spelling correction and every possible interpretation: . \[\text{Candidates} = M \times N\] where $M$ is the number of spelling corrections and $N$ is the number of interpretations. That becomes expensive quickly. If a query has three uncertain tokens, each with five corrections, and each correction has ten interpretations, the system would consider: . \[5^3 \times 10 = 1{,}250\] paths. A better design factors the decision: . \[P(C, R, I, S \mid X, U, K) = P(C \mid X, U, K) \cdot P(R \mid X, C, U, K) \cdot P(I \mid X, C, R, U, K) \cdot P(S \mid X, C, R, I, U, K)\] where: . | $X$ is the raw query. | $C$ is the selected correction. | $R$ is the reformulation strategy or rewritten query. | $I$ is the selected interpretation. | $S$ is the slot assignment. | $U$ is user and session context. | $K$ is catalog or retrieval context. | . Raw query | v Correction candidates | v Decision model: select correction | v Reformulation candidates | v Decision model: select reformulation | v Interpretation candidates | v Decision model: select interpretation | v Slot spans, types, canonical values | v Structured query understanding . At each stage, retain only the top-$k$ candidates. This converts an exponential search into a bounded beam search.

171.doc: Decision Models for Query Understanding in Search and AI Systems
171.title: What a decision model should own
171.content: A decision model is excellent at selection among bounded alternatives. | Task | Decision-model role | . | Spelling correction | Choose among correction candidates | . | Intent detection | Choose music, podcast, audiobook, or unknown | . | Slot detection | Predict token-level spans | . | Slot typing | Choose among entity types | . | Canonicalization | Choose among closed vocabularies | . | Language detection | Choose among language codes | . | Interpretation selection | Choose among candidate interpretations | . | Reformulation | Choose a rewrite strategy or candidate rewrite | . | Autocomplete | Rank candidate completions | . | RAG grounding | Decide whether retrieval is needed and whether evidence is sufficient | . | Escalation | Decide whether a larger reasoner is needed | . It is less suitable for open-ended creation. | Task | Better approach | . | Generate every possible spelling correction | Edit-distance, phonetic, embedding, or catalog index | . | Generate every possible rewrite | Template rewriter or small generator | . | Generate arbitrary autocomplete text | Language-model generator plus decision reranker | . | Resolve a brand-new entity | Fresh catalog retrieval | . | Perform multi-hop reasoning | Larger reasoner or agent | . The practical rule is simple: . Use retrieval or a small generator to create candidates. Use a decision model to score, select, calibrate, and route them.

172.doc: Decision Models for Query Understanding in Search and AI Systems
172.title: A practical architecture
172.content: +---------------------------+ User query ------------->| Input normalization | Voice transcript ------> | - lowercase | Locale / market -------->| - punctuation cleanup | Session context -------> | - privacy filtering | +-------------+-------------+ | v +-----------------------------------+ | Candidate generators | | - spelling candidates | - phonetic candidates | - catalog candidates | - autocomplete candidates | - reformulation candidates | - RAG retrieval candidates | +-----------------+-----------------+ | v +-----------------------------------+ | Decision model | | - correction selection | - interpretation selection | - slot spans and types | - canonical values | - language | - ambiguity | - reformulation strategy | - autocomplete selection | - RAG grounding decision | +-----------------+-----------------+ | +-----------------+-----------------+ | v v +-----------------------+ +-----------------------+ | High-confidence path | Low-confidence path | Return structured | Retrieve, reason, | query understanding | or escalate | +-----------------------+ +-----------------------+ . This is one decision model in the deployment sense: one encoder, one set of weights, one service. Internally, it has multiple decision heads. Query + context + candidates | +-----------------------+ | Shared encoder | +-----------+-----------+ | +-----------+-----------+-------+-------+-------------+-----------+ | | | v v v v v v Correction Intent and Span and Canonical Language Ambiguity / selection language slot-type value head head routing head head heads head .

173.doc: Decision Models for Query Understanding in Search and AI Systems
173.title: Spelling correction without overcorrection
173.content: Spelling correction should never blindly change the user’s query. Always include a KEEP_ORIGINAL candidate. Raw query: tailor swift songs Candidates: 0. KEEP_ORIGINAL 1. taylor swift songs 2. tailor swift song 3. taylor swift music . The decision model returns: . { "KEEP_ORIGINAL": 0.02, "taylor swift songs": 0.94, "tailor swift song": 0.02, "taylor swift music": 0.02 } . Candidate generators can include: . | Edit-distance indexes. | Phonetic indexes. | Catalog n-gram indexes. | Embedding retrievers. | Query-log correction indexes. | Language-specific normalizers. | Transliteration variant generators. | ASR-error normalizers. | . For voice interfaces, leading commands such as play, put on, and find me should usually be treated as command or stopword tokens, not as content entities.

174.doc: Decision Models for Query Understanding in Search and AI Systems
174.title: Handling multiple interpretations
174.content: Some queries are genuinely ambiguous. Query: drake . This could mean: . | An artist. | A song. | A podcast. | An album. | . The correct behavior depends on context. A decision model can score candidate interpretations using catalog data, user history, market, and session signals. Candidate interpretations: 1. ArtistName:drake 0.82 2. SongName:drake 0.09 3. ProgramName:drake 0.06 4. AlbumName:drake 0.03 . Confidence should measure whether the slot type is correct, not whether the exact entity is known. For example, jolene may match songs by multiple artists, but it is still confidently a song title. By contrast, the mill could be a song, artist, album, or podcast, so the slot type itself may be uncertain. This distinction prevents a common failure mode: treating ambiguity about which entity as though it were ambiguity about what kind of thing the user wants.

175.doc: Decision Models for Query Understanding in Search and AI Systems
175.title: Autocomplete as a decision problem
175.content: Autocomplete has two distinct problems: . | Task | Input | Output | Approach | . | Completion selection | Prefix plus candidate completions | Ranked completions | Decision model | . | Completion generation | Prefix only | Possible continuations | Generator plus decision reranker | . For a prefix such as calm hindi, a candidate generator might produce: . - calm hindi songs - calm hindi romantic songs - calm hindi playlist - calm hindi 90s songs . The decision model then ranks them: . calm hindi songs 0.58 calm hindi romantic songs 0.22 calm hindi playlist 0.12 calm hindi 90s songs 0.08 . This keeps autocomplete fast and controllable. The generator explores; the decision model chooses.

176.doc: Decision Models for Query Understanding in Search and AI Systems
176.title: RAG grounding
176.content: Retrieval-augmented generation, or RAG, is often discussed as a way to give a model current facts. In query understanding, it has a narrower and more useful role: grounding an interpretation in authoritative context. Useful retrieval sources include: . | Catalog metadata. | Entity aliases. | User library and preferences. | Recent releases. | Regional availability. | Knowledge-graph relationships. | Optional web evidence. | . The decision model should decide: . Does this query need retrieval? Which retrieval source should be used? Is the retrieved evidence sufficient? Which candidate entity best resolves the query? Should the system escalate? . Corrected query | v Grounding decision model | +-- no retrieval needed --> return interpretation | +-- retrieval needed -----> retrieve candidates | v Grounded decision model | +-- sufficient --> return interpretation | +-- insufficient -> escalate . Latency matters here. Catalog and user-library retrieval can often fit a low-latency budget. Web retrieval usually cannot. | Path | Typical latency | . | No retrieval | 5–20 ms | . | Local catalog retrieval | 10–25 ms | . | User-library retrieval | 10–30 ms | . | Knowledge-graph retrieval | 20–50 ms | . | Web retrieval | Hundreds of milliseconds or more | . Therefore, web retrieval belongs offline, in an escalation path, or in asynchronous enrichment—not in the primary sub-30 ms path.

177.doc: Decision Models for Query Understanding in Search and AI Systems
177.title: Calibration is the product
177.content: A decision model’s most valuable output is often not the selected label. It is the probability distribution. Expected Calibration Error, or ECE, measures whether predicted confidence matches observed accuracy: . \[\text{ECE} = \sum_{b=1}^{B} \frac{|I_b|}{N} \left| \text{acc}(I_b) - \text{conf}(I_b) \right|\] where: . | $I_b$ is a confidence bin. | $N$ is the total number of predictions. | $\text{acc}(I_b)$ is observed accuracy in the bin. | $\text{conf}(I_b)$ is average predicted confidence in the bin. | . Lower ECE means the model’s confidence is more trustworthy. AnyJev reports that its rotation-based readout reduced order-flip rate from 0.230 to 0.073 and improved calibration error from 0.240 to 0.095 in its published README example. The exact numbers depend on the model, dataset, and evaluation setup, but the lesson generalizes: calibration should be measured and improved directly, not treated as an afterthought. github .

178.doc: Decision Models for Query Understanding in Search and AI Systems
178.title: When to escalate
178.content: A small decision model should not pretend to know everything. Escalate when: . | The query is highly ambiguous. | The language or script is rare. | The entity is new and absent from catalog features. | The query requires multi-hop reasoning. | The query is adversarial or safety-sensitive. | Confidence falls below a validated threshold. | . AnyJev’s Tacit models illustrate a bounded escalation design: they answer typed decisions in one forward pass, but with adaptive mode enabled, a capped share of low-confidence decisions can be sent to the model’s own reasoning. The escalation is reported and constrained by configuration such as tau, max_cot_share, and cot_window. Decision model | +-- high confidence --> return structured decision | +-- low confidence ---> retrieval, reasoner, or human review . The escalation path should have its own latency objective, cost budget, and monitoring. It should not silently violate the primary path’s service-level objective.

179.doc: Decision Models for Query Understanding in Search and AI Systems
179.title: Can a small model match a large model?
179.content: For constrained query understanding, often yes—on the common query distribution. A 300M-parameter decision model can match or exceed a 7B generative model when: . | The label schema is fixed. | Training data is diverse and grounded in real usage. | The catalog provides current entity resolution. | Queries are short or medium length. | The system is regularly calibrated and refreshed. | . It will usually lose when: . | The query requires broad world knowledge. | The entity is new and absent from retrieval features. | The language is rare or unsupported. | The query requires multi-step reasoning. | The query is adversarial or intentionally ambiguous. | . The right goal is not “make a small model universally equal to a 7B model.” The right goal is: . Make the small model excellent on high-volume, well-understood queries, and escalate the minority that genuinely need more capacity.

180.doc: Decision Models for Query Understanding in Search and AI Systems
180.title: Production lessons
180.content: . | Separate selection from generation. Decision models select; retrievers and generators create. | Factor the decision space. Do not enumerate every correction-interpretation pair. | Always include a no-change option. This prevents overcorrection. | Use calibrated probabilities for policy. Confidence thresholds should be learned from validation data. | Ground against fresh context. The model interprets; the catalog resolves current facts. | Personalize carefully. User history should disambiguate, not override explicit intent. | Escalate deliberately. Use a bounded reasoning path for uncertainty, not as a default. | Measure calibration in production. Accuracy alone is insufficient for automated decision systems. | .

181.doc: Decision Models for Query Understanding in Search and AI Systems
181.title: Final takeaways
181.content: . | Central mechanism: A decision model maps a query, context, and candidate set to typed probability distributions. | Main architectural insight: Query understanding is mostly a bounded selection problem, not an open-ended generation problem. | Best system shape: Candidate generators create options; a decision model scores, selects, calibrates, and routes. | Key trade-off: A small decision model gives low latency and reliable structure; a larger reasoner gives broader coverage for rare or difficult cases. | Main limitation: A decision model cannot efficiently create an unbounded candidate space or resolve every new entity without retrieval. | Broader implication: Build AI systems as calibrated decision graphs, with fast System-1 decisions handling volume and slower System-2 reasoning reserved for genuine uncertainty. github | .
