250.title: Diving Deep into Large Language Models (LLMs)
250.content: Reference lecture by Andrej Karpathy: YouTube .

252.title: Introduction
252.content: Large Language Models (LLMs) such as ChatGPT present a deceptively simple interface: a single text box input yielding generated responses. Beneath this interface lies an extensive engineering and mathematical pipeline designed to build intuitive mental models of language processing. Understanding LLMs requires dissecting how these models are built from scratch, examining every sequential pipeline stage, and analyzing the cognitive and psychological implications of their architectural constraints.

253.title: Pretraining Data: Scraping & Curation
253.content: The first phase of creating an LLM is Pretraining, which centers on downloading, filtering, and curating vast amounts of raw text from the internet. +------------------+ +------------------+ +-------------------+ +------------------+ | Common Crawl | --> | URL Filtering | --> | Text Extraction | --> | Language Filter | (2.7B Webpages) | (Malware/Block) | (Strip HTML/CSS) | (e.g., >65% EN) | +------------------+ +------------------+ +-------------------+ +------------------+ | v +------------------+ +------------------+ +------------------+ | FineWeb Dataset | <-- | PII Removal | <-------------------------- | Deduplication | (44 TB Text) | (SSN/Addresses) | +------------------+ +------------------+ +------------------+ . Key Data Pipeline Stages . | Raw Web Scraping: The primary foundation for pretraining datasets is Common Crawl, an organization that has indexed over 2.7 billion webpages since 2007 by traversing hyperlinked internet networks starting from seed URLs. | URL Filtering: Eliminates domains present on blocklists, including spam, malware, adult content, marketing networks, and hate speech platforms. | Text Extraction: Converts raw HTML documents into plaintext by stripping markup tags, CSS scripts, and navigation UI metadata. | Language Filtering: Applies language classifiers to keep high-quality content matching target distributions (e.g., HuggingFace’s FineWeb dataset filters out pages containing less than 65% English text). | Deduplication & Quality Heuristics: Removes duplicated web content, boilerplate text, and low-quality machine-generated pages. | Personally Identifiable Information (PII) Removal: Detects and redacts sensitive individual data, such as Social Security numbers, telephone numbers, and street addresses. | . Despite the internet’s vast scope, aggressive curation reduces raw web data down to remarkably compact sizes. For example, the FineWeb dataset compresses down to approximately 44 terabytes of disk space—small enough to fit onto a single modern hard drive setup.

254.title: Tokenization
254.content: Neural networks cannot natively process raw string characters; they operate on one-dimensional sequences of discrete numeric tokens chosen from a finite vocabulary set. Raw Text: "Hello world" │ ▼ UTF-8 Encoding Binary/Bytes: [0x48, 0x65, 0x6c, 0x6c, 0x6f, 0x20, 0x77, 0x6f, 0x72, 0x6c, 0x64] (256 Symbol Vocab) │ ▼ Byte Pair Encoding (BPE) Token IDs: [15339, 1917] (Vocabulary Size: 100,277) . The Trade-off: Vocabulary Size vs. Sequence Length . | Raw Bit/Byte Representation: Representing text directly as UTF-8 bytes yields a tiny vocabulary size ($256$ possible symbols), but inflates sequence length, consuming context window capacity. | Byte Pair Encoding (BPE): BPE recursively merges common consecutive bytes or token pairs into new unique token IDs. This compresses sequence length while expanding vocabulary size. | Production Tokenizers: GPT-4 utilizes the cl100k_base tokenizer with a vocabulary size of 100,277 symbols. | . Tokenizer Characteristics . | Input String | Token Count | Token IDs | Notes | . | "Hello world" | 2 | [15339, 1917] | Includes space prefix in second token | . | "Helloworld" | 2 | [73, 20387] | Distinct IDs due to missing space | . | " Hello world" | 3 | [220, 15339, 1917] | Extra leading space creates explicit token 220 | .

255.title: Neural Network Input/Output
255.content: During pretraining, neural networks model the statistical relationships of tokens within context sequences. | Context Sampling: Random windows of token sequences are sampled from datasets (e.g., FineWeb’s 15-trillion token sequence). Context lengths range up to model-defined context limits ($N$). | Probability Distribution Output: Given a context window $[t_1, t_2, \dots, t_k]$, the network outputs a probability vector over the entire vocabulary $V$ (e.g., 100,277 values) estimating $P(t_{k+1} \mid t_1, \dots, t_k)$. | Loss Function & Gradient Updates: Predictions are compared against the ground-truth target token using Cross-Entropy Loss. Mathematical optimizations (backpropagation) adjust network weights to incrementally increase the target token’s probability. | .

256.title: Neural Network Internals
256.content: An LLM is a stateless mathematical function parameterized by billions or trillions of adjustable weights $W$. \[\text{Output Probabilities} = f(X; W)\] . | Parameters ($W$): Continuous numbers initialized randomly and tuned during training. | Statelessness: The network retains no biological memory or state updates across executions. Given identical inputs $X$ and fixed parameters $W$, internal mathematical operations execute identically. | Architecture: Modern models rely on the Transformer architecture, utilizing embedding tables, multi-head self-attention mechanisms, layer normalization, and multi-layer perceptrons (MLP). | .

257.title: Inference Dynamics
257.content: Inference is the autoregressive generation of output tokens from a fixed set of trained parameters: . | Provide an input token prefix sequence. | Calculate the output probability distribution $P(t_{k+1})$. | Sample a single token from the probability distribution using a stochastic sampling method (e.g., temperature sampling). | Append the sampled token to the context sequence and repeat the loop. | . Because inference relies on probabilistic coin-flipping over probability distributions, generations remain inherently stochastic and generative rather than deterministic text retrieval.

258.title: Part 2: Base Model Training & Inference (GPT-2 & Llama 3)

259.title: GPT-2: Historical Blueprint
259.content: OpenAI’s GPT-2 (2019) represents the foundational blueprint of modern LLM architectures. Although small by modern standards, its pipeline mirrors current state-of-the-art systems. | Parameter | GPT-2 (2019) | Modern Base Models (e.g., Llama 3.1) | . | Parameters | 1.6 Billion | 8B to 405 Billion+ | . | Context Length | 1,024 Tokens | 128,000+ Tokens | . | Training Tokens | ~100 Billion | 15 Trillion+ | . | Training Cost | ~$40,000 (2019) | ~$100–$600 (Reproduced via llm.c) | . Training Step Update (1 Million Tokens Batch) ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │ Loss Value: 10.8 (Random) ---> 3.2 ---> 2.1 (Trained) │ └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │ ▼ [Step 20 Inference] --> "Since she is mine it's a part of..." (Gibberish) [Step 32,000 Final] --> Coherent English structure & syntax . Hardware & GPU Compute Scaling . Training requires distributed GPU clusters (e.g., 8x NVIDIA H100 GPU nodes renting at ~$3/GPU/hour). Enterprise training deployments aggregate tens of thousands of GPUs into dedicated data centers to maximize parallel matrix operations.

260.title: Llama 3.1 Base Model Inference
260.content: Base models (such as Meta’s Llama 3.1 405B) are raw token simulators trained to complete internet text rather than act as helpful conversational assistants. Characteristics of Base Models . | Gradients Held Fixed: During inference, parameter weights are frozen. | Autocomplete Behavior: Prompting a base model with "What is 2+2?" will not yield an answer like "2+2 is 4". Instead, it completes the text based on web page patterns: ```text Input: What is 2+2? Output: What is 3+3? What is 4+4? (Simulating a math worksheet) | . 3. **Lossy Compression Metaphor**: A 405B parameter model acts like a lossy compression zip file of the 15-trillion token pretraining corpus. It retains a generalized representation of web knowledge rather than verbatim entries. 4. **Verbatim Regurgitation**: High-quality documents sampled multiple times during pretraining (such as Wikipedia entries) can be recited almost word-for-word from memory. 5. **Knowledge Cutoffs**: Queries regarding events occurring after dataset collection cutoffs result in plausible hallucinations grounded in pre-cutoff knowledge distributions. --- ## Base Model Prompting Techniques Despite lacking conversational tuning, base models can perform complex tasks when prompted using structured context priming: ### Few-Shot Prompting (In-Context Learning) ```text English: Teacher | Korean: Sim English: Apple | Korean: Saegwa English: Dog | Korean: Gae English: House | Korean: Jib English: Water | Korean: . Result: The model detects the pattern and outputs Mul. Assistant Persona Simulation via Structured Dialogue . A conversational transcript between a helpful AI assistant and a human. Human: Recommend top 5 landmarks in Paris. Assistant: 1. Eiffel Tower 2. Louvre Museum 3. Arc de Triomphe... Human: Why is the sky blue? Assistant: . Result: Priming the prompt as a synthetic transcript forces the base model to simulate the assistant persona cleanly.

262.title: Pretraining to Post-Training
262.content: Post-training transforms an unaligned Base Model (an internet text completer) into an Assistant Model capable of answering questions, following instructions, and refusing unsafe requests. +-----------------------------------------------------------------------+ | PRETRAINING STAGE | Data: 15 Trillion Web Tokens | Duration: ~3 Months | GPUs: Thousands | +-----------------------------------------------------------------------+ │ ▼ [ Base Model Weights ] │ ▼ +-----------------------------------------------------------------------+ | POST-TRAINING STAGE | Data: Conversation Dialogue | Duration: ~3 Hours | Compute: Small | +-----------------------------------------------------------------------+ │ ▼ [ Assistant Model Weights ] .

263.title: Post-Training Data & Formatting
263.content: Post-training uses Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) over curated dataset dialogues containing thousands of human-annotated multi-turn conversations. Tokenizing Multi-Turn Dialogue . Conversations are converted into linear token sequences using structural formatting tokens (such as ChatML standards): . <|im_start|>user What is 2+2?<|im_end|> <|im_start|>assistant 2 + 2 equals 4.<|im_end|> <|im_start|>user What if it was multiplication?<|im_end|> <|im_start|>assistant . | Control Tokens: <|im_start|> and <|im_end|> are unique tokens added to the tokenizer vocabulary during post-training to demarcate structural turn boundaries. | .

264.title: Data Annotation Protocols & InstructGPT
264.content: First popularized by OpenAI’s InstructGPT (2022), initial SFT datasets relied on human annotators hired to write explicit prompt-response pairs following strict quality guidelines: . +-----------------------------------+ | Human Labeling Guidelines | - Be Helpful, Honest, Harmless | - Refuse Malicious Requests | +-----------------------------------+ │ ▼ +-----------------------+ +-----------------------+ | User Prompt Ideas | ---> Annotator ---> | Ideal Assistant Responses | (e.g., Code/Writing) | (SFT Target Output) | +-----------------------+ +-----------------------+ . Modern Synthetic Data Evolution . In modern pipelines, human annotators no longer write all dialog responses from scratch. Frameworks like UltraChat utilize strong LLMs to generate vast synthetic conversational datasets, which are then filtered and edited by human experts. Mental Model of an Assistant Model . When querying an assistant model, you are not communicating with a conscious entity. You are sampling from a statistical simulation trained to mimic an expert human annotator operating under corporate labeling guidelines.

266.title: Hallucinations
266.content: Hallucinations occur when an LLM outputs incorrect or fabricated facts with high confidence. [ User Query: "Who is Orson Kovats?" ] │ ▼ +-------------------------------------------+ | Statistical Pattern Matching Triggered | Training data format: "Who is X?" -> Bio | +-------------------------------------------+ │ ┌────────────────┴────────────────┐ ▼ ▼ [ Naive Model (Falcon 7B) ] [ Calibrated Model (Llama 3) ] Outputs plausible fake bio Internal uncertainty triggers ("1950s TV actor") refusal: "I don't have records..." . Root Cause . SFT datasets historically contained mostly confident answers to questions starting with “Who is…” or “What is…“. Consequently, models learned to imitate the confident style of an answer even when internal activations indicated uncertainty. Mitigation via Interrogation . | Interrogate base models empirically on factual text passages to locate boundary limits of their memorized parametric knowledge. | Construct fine-tuning datasets that pair out-of-boundary queries with explicit refusals: “I don’t have access to information about X.” | Connect internal uncertainty activations to explicit refusal outputs. | .

267.title: Tool Use & Memory Boundaries
267.content: To overcome parametric memory limits, models are trained to use external execution tools via specific token protocols. User Context: "How many Stanley Cups did Dominic Hasek win?" │ ▼ LLM Token Output: Dominic Hasek Stanley Cups │ ▼ (Inference engine pauses, calls search API, injects text) Injected Text: "Dominic Hasek won 2 Stanley Cups (1998, 2002)..." │ ▼ LLM Continues: "Dominic Hasek won the Stanley Cup twice." [Citation 1] . Memory Hierarchy . | Memory Type | Location | Properties | Metaphor | . | Parametric Memory | Fixed Parameter Weights ($W$) | Vague, probabilistic long-term storage | Reading a book 1 month ago | . | Working Memory | Context Window Tokens | Crisp, directly accessible active text | Having the open book right in front of you | .

268.title: Knowledge of Self
268.content: LLMs have no intrinsic awareness of their identity or architecture. Answers to queries like “What model are you?” are entirely dictated by: . | Hardcoded identity strings written into system prompts. | Fine-tuning dialogue examples provided during post-training. | .

269.title: Token-Level Computation Limits
269.content: LLMs execute a fixed amount of mathematical computation per output token. \[\text{FLOPs per Token} \approx 2 \times N_{\text{params}}\] Consequences . | Complex Tasks Need Tokens to Think: For complex logic, math, or code tasks, an LLM cannot compute the answer in a single token. Prompting techniques (such as “Think step-by-step”) force the model to generate intermediate reasoning tokens, allocating more total compute to the problem. | .

270.title: Tokenization Traps: Spelling & Character Manipulation
270.content: Because transformers process subword tokens rather than raw character arrays, they struggle with character-level operations. Word: "strawberry" Tokenizer Mapping: ["straw", "berry"] -> Token IDs: [8238, 16801] . | Spelling Failure: The model never sees the individual letters 's', 't', 'r', 'a', 'w', 'b', 'e', 'r', 'r', 'y'. Asking how many 'r's are in “strawberry” requires predicting character compositions hidden inside subword token embeddings. | .

271.title: Jagged Intelligence
271.content: LLM capability profiles differ significantly from human cognition: . | Superhuman Capabilities: Immediate memorization of vast documentation, multi-language translation across dozens of tongues, and instantaneous code syntax generation. | Subhuman Blind Spots: Vulnerability to simple character-counting errors, logic traps without reasoning tokens, and subtle hallucination failures. | .

273.title: Supervised Fine-Tuning vs. Reinforcement Learning
273.content: While SFT forces models to imitate human responses, Reinforcement Learning (RL) allows models to exceed human annotation ceilings by discovering optimal problem-solving pathways through self-play and automated verification. SFT (Imitation Learning) Reinforcement Learning (RL) ┌───────────────────────┐ ┌───────────────────────┐ │ Target: Copy Human │ │ Target: Maximize │ │ Labeler Examples │ │ Verifiable Reward │ └───────────────────────┘ └───────────────────────┘ Cap: Human Labeler Level Cap: Superhuman Discovery .

274.title: Reinforcement Learning in Verifiable Domains
274.content: RL thrives in domains with unambiguous, programmatically verifiable feedback metrics (such as mathematics, code execution, and formal games). [ Problem Prompt ] ---> [ Model Generates 10 Solutions ] │ ▼ Programmatic Verifier / Test Suite [ Check Results ] - Solution 3: PASS (Reward = +1.0) - Solution 7: FAIL (Reward = -1.0) │ ▼ Policy Gradient Update (PPO / GRPO) [ Reinforce Paths Like Solution 3 ] .

275.title: DeepSeek-R1 & Emergent Reasoning
275.content: DeepSeek-R1 demonstrates the power of applying RL directly to base/SFT models in reasoning domains without relying on human CoT annotations. Emergent Properties from Pure RL . | Spontaneous Thought Generation: Models naturally learn to allocate variable “thinking tokens” before committing to a final answer. | Self-Correction Patterns: The model learns internal verification behaviors (e.g., generating phrases like “Wait, let me re-check this calculation…” mid-generation). | Length Expansion: Average token usage per response increases autonomously to solve harder benchmark problems. | .

276.title: The AlphaGo Parallel
276.content: The trajectory of RL in language models mirrors DeepMind’s AlphaGo: . | Phase 1 (SFT Equivalent): AlphaGo initially trained on thousands of human expert Go games, capping performance near human levels. | Phase 2 (RL Equivalent): AlphaGo played millions of self-play games against cloned versions of itself. | Move 37 Moment: Free from human imitation constraints, AlphaGo discovered novel moves beyond traditional human Go strategy. Reasoning models trained with RL undergo an identical transformation. | .

277.title: RLHF: Non-Verifiable Domains
277.content: For subjective tasks lacking automated programmatic verifiers (such as writing essays or conversational responses), models rely on Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF). Step 1: Train Reward Model Step 2: PPO / DPO Optimization ┌─────────────────────────────┐ ┌─────────────────────────────┐ │ Prompt: "Write an essay..." │ │ Policy Model Generates │ │ - Generation A │ │ Response Candidates │ │ - Generation B │ └──────────────┬──────────────┘ │ │ │ │ Human Prefers: A > B │ ▼ │ │ [ Evaluated by Reward Model ] ▼ │ │ [ Reward Model (RM) Trained ] │ ▼ └─────────────────────────────┘ [ Update Policy Model Weights ] . | Reward Model (RM): A neural network trained on human pairwise preference evaluations (Option A vs Option B) to output a scalar quality score. | Optimization Algorithms: Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) or Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) adjust LLM parameters to maximize scores from the Reward Model while penalizing drift via KL-Divergence constraints. | .

279.title: Preview of Things to Come
279.content: MODERN LLM EVOLUTION Multimodal Tokens Autonomous Agents Test-Time Compute ┌─────────────────────┐ ┌─────────────────────┐ ┌─────────────────────┐ │ Native Processing: │ │ Tool Execution Loops│ │ Allocate Inference │ │ Audio, Images, │ -> │ over Multi-Hour │ -> │ Time dynamically │ │ Video Streams │ │ Workflows │ │ for hard problems │ └─────────────────────┘ └─────────────────────┘ └─────────────────────┘ . | Native Multimodality: Moving away from separate modality wrappers to process text, image, audio, and video tokens unified within a single Transformer architecture. | Agentic Workflows: Shifting from single-turn response generation to autonomous loops where models issue execution commands, inspect output, fix errors, and iterate toward long-term goals. | Test-Time Compute Scaling: Shifting compute investment from pretraining to runtime inference. Harder problems receive significantly larger compute budgets at runtime, allowing models to reflect and verify longer before responding. | .

280.title: Navigating the LLM Ecosystem
280.content: Track state-of-the-art developments across model performance and research publications using these core platforms: . | LMSYS Chatbot Arena (lmarena.ai): Crowdsourced, blind A/B testing platform providing Elo rankings for open and proprietary language models. | Hugging Face Open LLM Leaderboard: Standardized benchmark evaluation tracking open-weights models. | LM Studio & Ollama: Local desktop frameworks for executing quantized open-weights models locally on user hardware. | ArXiv & AI News Newsletters: Repositories for tracking research papers on architectural optimizations, training methods, and dataset curation. | .

281.title: Grand Summary: The 3-Stage LLM Lifecycle
281.content: Stage 1: Pretraining ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │ Raw Internet Data (15T+ Tokens) ---> Transformer Training (Thousands GPU│ │ Output: Base Model (Internet Token Simulator) │ └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │ ▼ Stage 2: Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │ Conversation Dialogues ---> Supervised Alignment Training │ │ Output: Assistant Model (Imitates Human Annotator Persona) │ └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │ ▼ Stage 3: Reinforcement Learning (RL / RLHF) ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │ Reward Models / Verifier Systems ---> Policy Optimization (GRPO / DPO) │ │ Output: Reasoning Agent (Self-Correcting, Superhuman Problem Solver) │ └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ .

283.title: LLM Inference Engineering and Self-Improving Agent Harnesses: From Kernels to Production Systems
283.content: Primary references: . | 100 Days of LLM Inference | AirLLM | RRSI: Regularized Recursive Self-Improvement of Agent Harnesses | . Large language model (LLM) inference is no longer only about running a model on a GPU. It is a full-stack engineering discipline spanning CUDA kernels, KV-cache management, quantization, batching, model parallelism, autoscaling, routing, observability, and cost control. This document covers three complementary areas: . | Inference engineering: how to make a single model instance fast, memory-efficient, and production-ready. | Memory-constrained inference: how AirLLM runs very large models on small GPUs by streaming model layers. | Agent-harness self-improvement: how RRSI improves the prompts, tools, memory, control flow, and context management around a frozen model. | . A source-coverage note: the Pinterest VLM serving, Anyscale Ray Serve, vLLM explainers, AWS Bedrock and SageMaker posts, Kaggle competition, KiroCrew, Archestra routing, Harvard course, Dream-RSI, autoresearch, tiny-llm, and MDPI paper links were not fully verified from their primary pages in this pass. They are included as a reading list, not as verified technical claims.

285.title: What inference engineering is
285.content: Inference engineering is the discipline of serving generative AI models in production faster, cheaper, and more reliably. The 100 Days of LLM Inference project frames it as three layers: runtime, infrastructure, and tooling. github . +-------------------------------------------------------------+ | Inference stack | +-------------------------------------------------------------+ | Tooling | - benchmarking, profiling, metrics, tracing, dashboards | +-------------------------------------------------------------+ | Infrastructure | - GPUs, containers, autoscaling, routing, queues, clouds | +-------------------------------------------------------------+ | Runtime | - tokenization, attention, KV cache, kernels, quantization | +-------------------------------------------------------------+ . The runtime layer determines how efficiently one model instance uses one GPU. The infrastructure layer determines how many requests a cluster can serve reliably. The tooling layer makes both debuggable. github .

286.title: Inference versus training
286.content: Training and inference have different objectives. | Dimension | Training | Inference | . | Goal | Learn model weights | Generate outputs from fixed weights | . | Compute pattern | Large forward and backward passes | Usually forward-only generation | . | Memory pressure | Gradients, optimizer state, activations | Weights, activations, and KV cache | . | Latency metric | Time to converge | Time to first token and time between tokens | . | Cost driver | GPU-hours and data throughput | Tokens, concurrency, cache reuse, and hardware utilization | . | Typical optimization | Data loading, parallelism, mixed precision | Batching, caching, quantization, decoding strategy | . A large language model (LLM) is a neural network trained to model sequences of tokens. During inference, it processes a prompt and generates output tokens one at a time in an autoregressive loop. github .

287.title: Key inference metrics
287.content: | Metric | Definition | Why it matters | . | TTFT | Time to first token | Perceived responsiveness | . | TBT | Time between tokens | Streaming smoothness | . | Throughput | Tokens or requests per second | Capacity and cost | . | Queue depth | Requests waiting to be served | Saturation signal | . | GPU utilization | Fraction of GPU capacity in use | Efficiency signal | . | KV-cache hit rate | Share of requests reusing cached context | Cost and latency optimization | . | Cost per token | Infrastructure cost divided by generated tokens | Unit economics | . The 100 Days project explicitly includes TTFT, TBT, queue depth, GPU utilization, KV-cache hit rates, and end-to-end latency breakdowns in its production-system curriculum. github .

289.title: The generation loop
289.content: A simplified autoregressive inference loop is: . Prompt tokens | v Prefill: process all prompt tokens | v Generate token 1 | v Append token to KV cache | v Generate token 2 | v Repeat until stop condition . Prefill processes the entire prompt in parallel. Decode generates one token at a time, reusing the key-value cache from prior tokens. This distinction is central to inference optimization. github .

290.title: KV cache
290.content: The KV cache stores the key and value projections produced by attention layers for previously processed tokens. Without it, every new token would require recomputing attention over the entire prompt and all previously generated tokens. Prompt: [t1 t2 t3 t4] KV cache after prefill: Layer 1: K1, V1 Layer 2: K2, V2 ... New token t5: Uses cached K/V from t1..t4 Adds K/V for t5 . KV-cache memory grows with: . | Number of layers. | Number of attention heads. | Head dimension. | Batch size. | Sequence length. | Precision. | . The 100 Days curriculum treats KV cache, prefix caching, cache-aware routing, and cache managers as first-class runtime topics. github .

291.title: Prefix caching
291.content: Prefix caching reuses the KV cache for a shared prompt prefix. Request A: [System prompt][User A message] Request B: [System prompt][User B message] Shared prefix: [System prompt] Optimization: Compute KV cache for system prompt once. Reuse it for both requests. This is especially valuable for: . | Shared system prompts. | Few-shot examples. | Repeated document contexts. | Multi-turn conversations. | Agent harnesses with stable instructions. | . The 100 Days project includes hash-based prefix-cache deduplication and cache-aware routing as practical projects. github .

292.title: PagedAttention and continuous batching
292.content: vLLM introduced two influential serving optimizations: . | PagedAttention: manages KV-cache memory in blocks, similar to virtual-memory paging. | Continuous batching: adds new requests to a running batch as prior requests finish, rather than waiting for an entire batch to complete. | . Traditional static batching: Request 1 ------> Request 2 ------> Request 3 ------> Wait for all requests to finish before admitting new ones. Continuous batching: Request 1 ------> Request 2 ----> new request joins Request 3 --> new request joins GPU remains busy as requests complete at different times. The 100 Days curriculum covers vLLM, PagedAttention, continuous batching, SGLang, TensorRT-LLM, and NVIDIA Dynamo as major runtime systems. github .

293.title: Quantization
293.content: Quantization reduces the numerical precision used to represent model weights, activations, or both. | Format | Typical benefit | Trade-off | . | FP16 or BF16 | High accuracy | Higher memory and bandwidth | . | FP8 | Good speed and memory balance | Hardware-dependent | . | INT8 | Strong memory reduction | Requires calibration and validation | . | INT4 | Large memory reduction | Greater quality risk | . | NVFP4 | Hardware-accelerated low precision | Hardware-dependent | . The 100 Days curriculum covers FP8, INT8, INT4, NVFP4, GPTQ, AWQ, and SmoothQuant. github . A simplified quantization-and-dequantization operation is: . \[\hat{w} = \text{dequantize}(\text{quantize}(w))\] The goal is to minimize quality loss while reducing memory footprint and improving throughput. Quantization should always be evaluated on task-specific quality metrics, not merely model perplexity.

294.title: Speculative decoding
294.content: Speculative decoding uses a smaller draft model to propose several tokens. The larger target model then verifies them in parallel. Draft model proposes: [t5, t6, t7] Target model verifies: t5 accepted t6 accepted t7 rejected Output: t5, t6 Then target model generates a replacement for t7 . If the draft model’s proposals are accepted, the system generates multiple tokens for approximately one target-model verification pass. The 100 Days project includes draft-target, Medusa, and EAGLE speculative decoding, plus acceptance-rate measurement by draft-model size. github .

295.title: Part 3: Scaling Across GPUs and Clusters

296.title: Model parallelism
296.content: When a model does not fit on one GPU, or when throughput requires more compute, use parallelism. | Type | What is split | Best for | . | Tensor parallelism | Individual matrix multiplications across GPUs | Large dense layers | . | Pipeline parallelism | Model layers across GPUs | Very deep models | . | Expert parallelism | Mixture-of-experts experts across GPUs | Sparse MoE models | . | Data parallelism | Requests across model replicas | High request throughput | . The 100 Days curriculum includes tensor, expert, pipeline, and data parallelism, plus simulations of splitting matrix multiplication across workers. github .

297.title: Disaggregated serving
297.content: Disaggregated serving separates prefill and decode into different pools of hardware. Requests | v +----------------+ | Prefill pool | Compute-heavy | +-------+--------+ | v +----------------+ | Decode pool | Memory-heavy | +----------------+ . Prefill is compute-heavy because it processes many prompt tokens in parallel. Decode is more memory-bandwidth-sensitive because it generates tokens sequentially. Splitting them allows each pool to be sized and scaled independently. github .

298.title: Autoscaling and routing
298.content: A production inference service must decide: . | How many replicas to run. | When to scale up or down. | How to route a request. | How to queue or reject excess traffic. | How to handle cold starts. | How to route across clouds or regions. | . Client request | v +------------------+ | Load balancer | +--------+---------+ | +-- cache-aware route --> replica with matching prefix cache | +-- least-connections --> least-loaded healthy replica | +-- geo-aware route ----> nearest healthy region | v +------------------+ | Inference replica| +------------------+ . The 100 Days curriculum covers concurrency, batching, cold starts, routing, load balancing, queueing, multi-cloud capacity management, zero-downtime deployment, and cost estimation. github .

299.title: Observability
299.content: A production inference service should emit metrics and traces for every request. Useful signals include: . | Request arrival rate. | Queue depth. | Batch size. | TTFT. | TBT. | Tokens generated. | GPU utilization. | GPU memory usage. | KV-cache hit rate. | Error rate. | Model version. | Routing decision. | Cost estimate. | . The 100 Days project includes Prometheus metrics, Grafana dashboards, OpenTelemetry tracing, Locust load testing, and Nsight Systems profiling. github .

301.title: The problem
301.content: Large models often cannot fit in GPU memory. A 70B-parameter model in full precision can require far more memory than a consumer GPU provides. AirLLM reduces inference memory usage by keeping only one transformer layer on the GPU at a time and streaming the remaining layers from disk. github . Traditional inference: All model layers resident in GPU memory. AirLLM inference: Load layer 1 -> compute -> free Load layer 2 -> compute -> free Load layer 3 -> compute -> free ... This trades latency and disk bandwidth for a dramatically smaller GPU-memory footprint.

302.title: Reported capabilities
302.content: AirLLM reports the following examples: github . | Model | Size | Reported GPU VRAM | . | Qwen3, Mistral, or Phi, approximately 8B | 8B | About 1–2 GB | . | Qwen3-30B or Mixtral MoE | 30–47B | About 1–3 GB | . | Qwen3.8-27B dense vision-language model | 27B | 3.33 GB | . | Qwen3.8-Flash-Next | About 180B | 5.95 GB | . | Qwen3-235B MoE | 235B | About 3 GB | . | Llama 3.x 70B, full precision | 70B | About 4 GB | . | Llama 3.1 405B | 405B | About 8 GB | . | DeepSeek-V3 | 671B | About 12 GB | . | Kimi K3 | 2.8T | 3.72 GB | . These figures are reported by the AirLLM repository under its specific hardware, precision, model format, and streaming configuration. They do not imply that these configurations are fast enough for interactive production serving. github .

303.title: Why it works
303.content: AirLLM’s central trick is that GPU memory need depends on the size of the currently active layer, not the total model size. github . For a model with $L$ layers, traditional inference keeps all layer weights resident: . \[M_{\text{traditional}} \approx \sum_{l=1}^{L} W_l\] AirLLM keeps only one layer resident at a time: . \[M_{\text{AirLLM}} \approx \max_l W_l\] where: . | $W_l$ is the memory required by layer $l$. | $M$ is GPU memory usage. | . The trade-off is that weights must be repeatedly read from disk or host memory, making the approach highly sensitive to storage bandwidth, caching, and prefetching.

304.title: Compression
304.content: AirLLM also supports 4-bit and 8-bit block-wise quantization-based compression. The repository states that this can speed inference by up to 3 times with almost negligible accuracy loss in its evaluated setting. github . The key distinction it draws is: . | Conventional quantization: often quantizes weights and activations to improve compute speed. | AirLLM compression: primarily reduces the model-loading size because the bottleneck is disk loading. github | .

305.title: Example inference code
305.content: The following example is adapted from the AirLLM repository’s quickstart. github . from airllm import AutoModel MAX_LENGTH = 128 model = AutoModel.from_pretrained("Qwen/Qwen3-32B") input_text = ["What is the capital of United States?"] input_tokens = model.tokenizer( input_text, return_tensors="pt", return_attention_mask=False, truncation=True, max_length=MAX_LENGTH, padding=False, ) generation_output = model.generate( input_tokens["input_ids"].to(model.device), max_new_tokens=20, use_cache=True, return_dict_in_generate=True, ) output = model.tokenizer.decode(generation_output.sequences[0]) print(output) .

306.title: Example training configuration
306.content: AirLLM also supports fine-tuning large models on small GPUs by streaming frozen base weights one layer at a time while keeping adapters resident. github . python air_llm/examples/train_qwen38_flash_next_lora.py \ --data my_data.jsonl \ --seq-len 512 \ --epochs 1 \ --save-adapter qwen38-flash-next-lora.pt . The repository reports that Qwen3.8-Flash-Next, a 125B model, can train under 6 GB VRAM, and Qwen3.8-27B can train in approximately 2 GB at sequence length 512. github .

307.title: When to use AirLLM-style inference
307.content: | Use case | Fit | . | Experimenting with a very large model on limited hardware | Strong fit | . | Offline batch inference where latency is not critical | Possible fit | . | Low-latency interactive production serving | Usually poor fit | . | High-throughput production API | Usually poor fit | . | Edge inference with abundant fast storage | Possible fit | . | Training or evaluating huge models on small GPUs | Strong fit | . AirLLM optimizes memory footprint, not necessarily end-to-end latency or throughput. Production systems usually prefer quantization, batching, parallelism, and KV-cache optimization when latency and throughput matter.

309.title: What is an agent harness?
309.content: An agent harness is everything around a frozen model that determines how it behaves in an agent system: . | System and task prompts. | Control flow. | Tools. | Memory. | Context management. | Skills. | Sub-agents. | Configuration. | Evaluation logic. | . RRSI defines an LLM agent’s capability as largely determined by this harness. github . +----------------------------------------------------+ | Agent harness | | Prompt + control flow + tools + memory + context | +-------------------------+--------------------------+ | v +------------------+ | Frozen LLM | +------------------+ . The model may remain fixed while the harness evolves.

310.title: Why harnesses matter
310.content: A powerful model can still perform poorly if its harness: . | Gives unclear instructions. | Provides the wrong tools. | Fails to manage context. | Loses important memory. | Uses poor control flow. | Repeats failed strategies. | Overfits to a narrow evaluation set. | . RRSI argues that evolving a harness against a fixed evolve set is effective but prone to overfitting: gains on training tasks may shrink or disappear out of distribution. github .

311.title: The RRSI approach
311.content: RRSI, or Regularized Recursive Self-Improvement, keeps the harness edit space open while regularizing the search trajectory through it. github . Current harness H_t | v +----------------------+ | Analyst | Analyze failures | +----------+-----------+ | v +----------------------+ | Proposer | Propose edits | +----------+-----------+ | v +----------------------+ | Critic | Screen for leakage | +----------+-----------+ | v +----------------------+ | Evaluator | Measure score, cost | +----------+-----------+ | v +----------------------+ | Selector | Accept, reject, prune| +----------+-----------+ | v Next harness H_t+1 . This is a conceptual reconstruction of the RRSI improvement loop. github .

312.title: What can be edited
312.content: RRSI allows edits to: github . | Prompts. | Control flow. | Configuration. | Context management. | Tools. | Skills. | Memory. | Sub-agents. | . The constraint is not on what the harness may contain, but on how the search moves through the space of possible harnesses. github .

313.title: Regularization mechanisms
313.content: RRSI uses several mechanisms to reduce overfitting and wasteful search. github . | Mechanism | Purpose | . | Annealed edit budget | Limits how many independent edits a candidate can bundle | . | Full edit-history conditioning | Prevents revisiting falsified hypotheses | . | Stall detection | Redirects search toward unused components | . | Critic screening | Blocks suite-specific leakage before evaluation | . | Noise-adjusted floor | Rejects gains within evaluation variance | . | Cost rule | Requires added inference tokens to be paid for by measured gain | . | Component pruning | Removes components that stop helping | . | Novelty tracking | Encourages exploration of unused component types | . The cost rule is particularly important for production systems: a harness change that improves quality slightly but dramatically increases token cost may not be a real improvement.

314.title: Git-worktree evaluation
314.content: Every candidate harness is drafted, screened, and evaluated in its own Git worktree on a branch derived from evolve/<domain>. Accepting a candidate fast-forwards the branch, so the incumbent harness is always a commit. github . evolve/domain | +-- candidate worktree A | +-- candidate worktree B | +-- evaluation | +-- accept winner | v evolve/domain advances . This provides auditable evidence: each edit records the component, hypothesis, measured score, cost change, and verdict. github .

315.title: RRSI results
315.content: RRSI reports results with Claude Opus 4.8 as the frozen policy model, measured against the unevolved harness $H_0$. github . | Domain | Benchmark | Role | Baseline | RRSI | Change | . | Coding | Terminal-Bench 2.1 | Evolve | 74.2 | 80.2 | +6.0 | . | Coding | SWE-bench Verified | OOD | 82.0 | 83.8 | +1.8 | . | Agentic workspace | Harvey LAB | Evolve | 89.4 | 90.5 | +1.1 | . | Agentic workspace | Harvey LAB | In-distribution held-out | 86.9 | 89.2 | +2.3 | . | Agentic workspace | JobBench | OOD | 36.0 | 40.7 | +4.7 | . | Agentic workspace | GDPval | OOD | 48.8 | 52.3 | +3.5 | . | Agentic workspace | APEX-Agents | OOD | 34.2 | 37.9 | +3.7 | . | Engineering design | EngDesign | Evolve | 50.0 | 54.9 | +4.9 | . | Engineering design | Frontier-Eng | OOD | 17.7 | 22.0 | +4.3 | . RRSI also reports that, with Gemini 3.5 Flash as the frozen policy, the coding instance improves from 64.6 to 78.7 on Terminal-Bench 2.1 and from 76.8 to 79.0 on SWE-bench Verified. github . These results are specific to RRSI’s benchmarks, evaluation windows, models, and harness configurations. They should not be interpreted as universal improvements for every agent system.

318.title: Model routing
318.content: A production system may route requests to different models based on: . | Task complexity. | Required latency. | Confidence. | Cost budget. | Language. | Modality. | Available capacity. | Cache affinity. | . Request | v Router | +-- simple task ---------> small model | +-- complex task --------> large model | +-- low confidence ------> reasoner | +-- high cache affinity -> cache-friendly replica . This is the same basic pattern used in decision cascades: use a fast path for most traffic and reserve expensive paths for uncertainty.

319.title: Capacity-aware fallback
319.content: Capacity-aware inference handles the case where a preferred instance type is unavailable or saturated. The system can fall back to another instance type while preserving availability. A useful routing policy is: . Preferred GPU pool available? | +-- yes --> route to preferred pool | +-- no ---> fallback pool | +-- quality acceptable --> serve | +-- quality unacceptable -> queue, downgrade, or reject . This is general distributed-systems context; the AWS capacity-aware inference link in the source list should be consulted directly for its exact product behavior.

320.title: Deployment checklist
320.content: . | Containerize the inference server. | Pin model and dependency versions. | Use health and readiness probes. | Configure autoscaling on queue depth, concurrency, and GPU utilization. | Set request timeouts and cancellation policies. | Track model version in every response and log. | Use blue-green or canary deployment for model updates. | Load-test before launch. | Monitor TTFT, TBT, throughput, error rate, cache hit rate, and cost. | Maintain a rollback path. | . The 100 Days project includes production Dockerfiles, NIM-compatible containers, autoscaling simulation, cold-start measurement, blue-green deployment, Prometheus metrics, Grafana dashboards, tracing, Locust load testing, and reusable benchmark harnesses. github .

322.title: Inference optimization techniques
322.content: | Technique | Primary benefit | Main cost | Best for | . | Continuous batching | Higher GPU utilization | More complex scheduling | High-concurrency serving | . | PagedAttention | Reduced KV-cache fragmentation | More complex memory management | Variable-length workloads | . | Prefix caching | Lower TTFT and cost for shared prefixes | Cache management complexity | Shared prompts and agents | . | Quantization | Lower memory and higher throughput | Potential quality loss | Memory- or cost-constrained serving | . | Speculative decoding | Lower decode latency | Extra draft-model compute | Latency-sensitive generation | . | Tensor parallelism | Larger models and faster compute | Communication overhead | Large dense models | . | Expert parallelism | Scales MoE models | Routing and load-balancing complexity | Sparse MoE models | . | Disaggregation | Independent prefill and decode scaling | More infrastructure complexity | Heterogeneous workloads | . | Layer streaming | Very low GPU memory footprint | Much higher latency | Memory-constrained experimentation | .

323.title: Small fast model versus large streaming model
323.content: | Dimension | Small optimized model | Large model with layer streaming | . | Latency | Low | Often high | . | Throughput | High | Usually low | . | GPU memory | Low to moderate | Very low | . | Disk or host bandwidth | Lower | High | . | Capability | Limited by model size | Potentially much higher | . | Production complexity | Lower | Higher | . | Best use | Interactive production serving | Research, offline jobs, constrained hardware | . AirLLM demonstrates that very large models can run on small GPUs, but its layer-streaming approach is primarily a memory optimization rather than a latency optimization. github .

325.title: Inference limitations
325.content: . | KV-cache memory can become the dominant constraint for long contexts. | Quantization can degrade quality, especially for sensitive tasks or low-bit formats. | Speculative decoding helps only when draft proposals are accepted often enough. | Parallelism introduces communication overhead and operational complexity. | Autoscaling cannot eliminate cold starts entirely. | Cost per token depends heavily on utilization, batching, cache reuse, and hardware generation. | .

326.title: Agent-harness limitations
326.content: . | Harness optimization can overfit an evolve set. | Evaluation noise can cause false improvements. | More tools, memory, and sub-agents can increase cost and failure modes. | A better harness does not fix a fundamentally weak base model. | Automatic self-improvement requires strong leakage controls and auditable evaluation. | . RRSI addresses some of these issues with critic screening, noise-adjusted floors, cost rules, pruning, and held-out evaluation, but these mechanisms do not eliminate the underlying risks. github .

327.title: Open questions
327.content: . | What is the optimal division of labor between a frozen model and an evolving harness? | How should agent systems trade quality gains against token cost and latency? | Can harness self-improvement generalize reliably across domains without task-specific guards? | How should cache-aware routing balance prefix reuse against load balancing? | When is layer streaming preferable to quantization or model distillation? | How should production systems evaluate long-term agent value rather than short-term benchmark pass rate? | .

328.title: Resources
328.content: . | 100 Days of LLM Inference — structured curriculum covering CUDA kernels, KV cache, vLLM, quantization, speculative decoding, parallelism, autoscaling, observability, and production deployment. | AirLLM — layer-streaming inference and training for very large models on small GPUs. | RRSI — regularized recursive self-improvement of agent harnesses. | RRSI paper — research paper behind the RRSI repository. | Pinterest VLM serving on NVIDIA Dynamo — recommended reading on production vision-language-model serving. | Anyscale: Production-ready distributed inference with Ray Serve — recommended reading on distributed inference orchestration. | AWS: Capacity-aware inference — recommended reading on instance fallback for managed endpoints. | tiny-llm — recommended reading for implementing LLM inference components from scratch. | ai-engineering-from-scratch — recommended reading for foundational AI engineering concepts. | .

329.title: Final Technical Takeaways
329.content: . | Central mechanism: LLM inference performance is determined by the interaction of model architecture, KV cache, batching, kernels, precision, hardware, and request routing. | Main runtime insight: Prefill and decode have different computational profiles; optimizing them separately through caching, batching, and disaggregation can materially improve serving efficiency. github | Important memory insight: AirLLM reduces GPU memory by keeping only one layer resident at a time, enabling very large models on small GPUs at the cost of higher latency and storage bandwidth. github | Important agent insight: An agent’s capability is shaped as much by its harness—prompts, tools, memory, context, and control flow—as by the frozen model itself. github | Key production trade-off: Quality, latency, throughput, memory, and cost cannot all be maximized simultaneously; choose the constraint that matters most for the workload. | Main limitation: Automatic self-improvement and aggressive inference optimization can overfit benchmarks or degrade quality unless supported by held-out evaluation, cost controls, and observability. github | Broader engineering implication: Treat inference as a full-stack systems problem: optimize the runtime, design the infrastructure, and instrument both. github | .

331.content: Primary references: . | 100 Days of Inference GitHub Repository •elizabetht/100-days-of-inference | Pinterest Engineering • Building Pinterest’s VLM Serving Stack on NVIDIA Dynamo | AirLLM GitHub Repository • Extreme Memory-Optimized Inference (lyogavin/airllm) | vLLM Explainer & Deep-Dive Engine Architecture (aleksagordic.com / mlworks) | Production-Ready Distributed Inference with Ray Serve (Anyscale Masterclass) | AWS Machine Learning Blog • Capacity-Aware Inference & Amazon SageMaker HyperPod Deployments | .

332.title: Overview
332.content: Large Language Model (LLM) and Vision-Language Model (VLM) inference has evolved from simple single-GPU Python scripts into highly distributed, low-latency infrastructure engineering systems. Serving billion-parameter models at scale requires overcoming strict memory bottlenecks, high arithmetic intensity imbalances, and fluctuating request workloads. This technical reference document synthesizes foundational inference concepts, memory optimization techniques, distributed serving engines, hardware economic divergences, and production-grade architectures. +-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------+ | Traditional vs. Optimized Inference | | Standard PyTorch ---> [ Unbounded KV-Cache ] ---> [ Sequential GPU Memory Stalls ]| vLLM / Dynamo ---> [ PagedAttention ] ---> [ Zero-Copy Memory Management ]| Ray Serve / Cloud ---> [ Distributed Workers ] ---> [ Elastic Autoscaling Pool ] | +-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------+ .

333.title: Part 1: Foundations of LLM Inference Engineering
333.content: LLM inference is fundamentally divided into two distinct computational phases: Prefill and Decoding. Understanding their hardware profiles is essential for building scalable serving architectures. The Two-Phase Inference Lifecycle . | Prefill Phase (Matrix-Multiply Bound): . | Processes the entire input prompt in parallel across GPU tensor cores. | Exhibits high arithmetic intensity and high computational throughput. | Allocates the initial Key-Value (KV) cache tensors for all prompt tokens. | . | Decoding Phase (Memory-Bandwidth Bound): . | Generates output tokens auto-regressively one token at a time ($O(N)$ sequential loops). | Exhibits low arithmetic intensity because weights and KV-cache blocks must be fetched from High Bandwidth Memory (HBM) to SRAM for every single generated token. | Bounded strictly by GPU memory bandwidth (e.g., NVIDIA H100/H200 HBM transfer rates) rather than floating-point performance (TFLOPS). | . | . Computational Complexity & KV-Cache Footprint . For a transformer model with hidden dimension $D$, $L$ layers, $H$ attention heads, and sequence length $S$, the KV cache memory required per sequence in FP16 precision is: . \[\text{Memory}_{\text{KV}} = 2 \cdot \text{Layers} \cdot \text{SeqLen} \cdot \text{HiddenDim} \cdot \text{BytesPerParam}\] Without intelligent memory virtualization, naive contiguous memory allocation leads to massive internal fragmentation, wasting up to $60\% - 80\%$ of allocated GPU VRAM due to pre-allocated maximum sequence lengths.

334.title: Part 2: Core Serving Engines & Memory Optimization
334.content: Modern inference engines like vLLM, AirLLM, and NVIDIA Dynamo implement architectural innovations to eliminate memory waste and maximize GPU utilization. PagedAttention & Memory Virtualization . Inspired by virtual memory paging in operating systems, PagedAttention partitions the KV cache of each sequence into fixed-size blocks (e.g., 16 tokens per block). Logical KV Cache (Contiguous to Model): [ Token 1 .. Token 16 ] -> [ Token 17 .. Token 32 ] -> [ Token 33 .. Token 48 ] Physical GPU VRAM Blocks (Non-Contiguous Paging): [ Block #42 ] <---> [ Block #105 ] <---> [ Block #12 ] . | Zero Internal Fragmentation: Blocks are allocated dynamically on-demand as tokens are generated. | Efficient Memory Sharing: Enables prefix sharing and beam search branching without duplicating underlying tensor data in VRAM. | . Extreme Low-Memory Inference (AirLLM) . For developers running massive models (e.g., 70B+ parameters) on consumer-grade hardware with limited VRAM (e.g., a single 24GB RTX 3090/4090), AirLLM bypasses standard memory limits by streaming model layers dynamically from system RAM to GPU VRAM layer-by-layer during execution: . \[\text{Latency}_{\text{AirLLM}} = \sum_{l=1}^{L} \left( \text{TransferTime}(\text{Layer}_l) + \text{ComputeTime}(\text{Layer}_l) \right)\] While sacrificing token generation speed (Tokens/sec), AirLLM enables local execution of frontier-scale models on standard desktop hardware.

335.title: Part 3: Distributed Serving Architectures & Ray Serve
335.content: Scaling inference across multiple nodes requires distributed orchestration frameworks like Ray Serve, which decouples HTTP routing, request batching, and model execution worker pools. Distributed Ray Serve Pipeline . Client Request ---> [ Ray Serve HTTP Ingress Gateway ] | +---------------------+---------------------+ | | v v v [ Worker Node 1 ] [ Worker Node 2 ] [ Worker Node 3 ] (vLLM Replica A) (vLLM Replica B) (vLLM Replica C) . Key Distributed Primitives . | Dynamic Autoscaling: Automatically spins up or scales down GPU replica pods based on incoming request queue depth and P99 latency SLAs. | Continuous Batching (In-Flight Batching): Dynamically inserts new incoming requests into ongoing decoding batches as completed sequences finish, eliminating idle GPU compute bubbles. | .

336.title: Part 4: Production-Ready VLM Stacks (Pinterest & NVIDIA Dynamo)
336.content: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) introduce multimodal tokenization overhead, combining image patch embeddings with text sequences. Pinterest VLM Serving Stack on NVIDIA Dynamo . Pinterest engineering constructed an optimized VLM serving stack leveraging NVIDIA Dynamo to handle high-throughput visual search and recommendation payloads: . | Vision Encoder Offloading: Image patches are pre-processed and encoded asynchronously on dedicated accelerator pipelines before entering the autoregressive transformer backbone. | Dynamic Tensor Parallelism: Automatically shards multi-modal projection layers across NVLink-connected GPUs to minimize inter-node communication latency during multimodal prefill phases. | .

337.title: Part 5: Hardware Economics & Infrastructure Divergence
337.content: The economics of AI infrastructure have experienced a fundamental divergence between training and inference clusters. Training vs. Inference Economic Matrix . | Dimension | Training Infrastructure | Inference Infrastructure | . | Primary Bottleneck | Inter-node network bandwidth (InfiniBand, NVLink) | HBM memory bandwidth & capacity | . | Utilization Profile | Sustained high compute utilization ($>85\%$ FLOPs) | Variable, bursty, batch-size dependent | . | Precision Format | FP8 / BF16 mixed-precision checkpoint updates | INT8 / FP8 / INT4 quantized execution | . | Cost Driver | Capital expenditure (CapEx) on massive GPU clusters | Operational expenditure (OpEx) & query cost | .

338.title: Part 6: AWS & Enterprise Production Deployments
338.content: Enterprise deployments on cloud providers (such as AWS Amazon SageMaker HyperPod and Amazon Bedrock) integrate automated failover and capacity-aware scaling. Capacity-Aware Inference & Automatic Instance Fallback . Production systems maintain strict service-level agreements (SLAs) by implementing Capacity-Aware Routing: . Incoming Request ---> [ Primary SageMaker Endpoint (H100) ] | [ Capacity Check / Health ] | +---------------+---------------+ | (Healthy) | (Degraded / OOM) v v [ Execute on Primary ] [ Automatic Fallback to Secondary (A10G) ] .

339.title: Limitations and Open Questions
339.content: . | KV Cache Memory Pressure under Infinite Context: Supporting $128\text{k}+$ token context windows consumes significant VRAM per concurrent stream, limiting maximum batch sizes. | Quantization Degradation: Aggressive quantization (e.g., INT4 / GPTQ / AWQ) can introduce subtle accuracy drift in complex reasoning and tool-calling agent tasks. | Multi-Modal Latency Imbalance: Vision encoder latency varies significantly based on image resolution, complicating predictable SLA enforcement in real-time VLM pipelines. | .

340.title: Final Technical Takeaways
340.content: . | Memory Bandwidth Dominance: Decoding is strictly memory-bandwidth bound; optimization relies on paged memory virtualization (PagedAttention) and aggressive quantization. | Prefill vs. Decode Separation: Modern serving engines decouple compute-bound prefill from memory-bound decoding to maximize hardware utilization. | Distributed Orchestration: Tools like Ray Serve and vLLM are essential for maintaining sub-second P99 latencies under bursty production workloads. | Economic Divergence: Inference infrastructure prioritizes cost-per-query, HBM bandwidth, and operational stability over massive inter-node training fabrics. | .
