442.content: | Dimension | Reasoning model | Contextual retrieval | Continual learning | . | Primary goal | Solve harder problems | Ground answers in external knowledge | Retain knowledge over time | . | Weight updates | Often yes, through RLVR or distillation | Usually no | Yes, periodically | . | Latency impact | Can be high | Moderate | Usually offline | . | Cost impact | Higher inference cost | Retrieval and reranking cost | Training and infrastructure cost | . | Failure mode | Wrong reasoning or reward hacking | Bad chunks or failed retrieval | Catastrophic forgetting | . | Best for | Math, code, planning, complex analysis | Private, changing, or large knowledge bases | Long-lived assistants and evolving domains | .

443.doc: Reasoning Models, Contextual Retrieval, and Continual Learning (Part 2)
443.title: Inference scaling versus post-training
443.content: | Approach | When weights change | Cost profile | Best use | . | Chain-of-thought prompting | No | More output tokens | Quick improvement without training | . | Self-consistency | No | Multiple samples per query | High-value tasks where latency is acceptable | . | Self-refinement | No | Multiple generation passes | Tasks where critique improves quality | . | RLVR / GRPO | Yes | Expensive training | Verifiable domains such as math and code | . | Distillation | Yes | Teacher-generation plus student training | Deploying smaller reasoning models | . Raschka’s course treats these as complementary paths: inference-time scaling improves a fixed model, while RLVR and distillation change the model itself. magazine.sebastianraschka .

444.doc: Reasoning Models, Contextual Retrieval, and Continual Learning (Part 2)
444.title: Part 7: Limitations and Open Questions

445.doc: Reasoning Models, Contextual Retrieval, and Continual Learning (Part 2)
445.title: Reasoning models
445.content: . | Verifiers can be wrong, incomplete, or gameable. | Reward hacking can produce responses that satisfy the verifier without solving the task. | More inference-time compute does not always improve accuracy. | Distillation is bounded by teacher quality and data diversity. | RL training can be unstable and memory-intensive. | . Raschka’s course explicitly examines reward hacking, KL terms, clipped policy ratios, and the limitations of simplified KL formulations. magazine.sebastianraschka .

446.doc: Reasoning Models, Contextual Retrieval, and Continual Learning (Part 2)
446.title: Contextual retrieval
446.content: . | LLM-generated chunk context adds preprocessing cost. | Poor chunk boundaries can still harm retrieval. | Reranking adds runtime latency. | More retrieved chunks can distract the generator. | Retrieval evaluation must be separated from response-generation evaluation. | . Anthropic found that passing 20 chunks was more effective than 5 or 10 in its experiments, but recommends experimenting per use case because additional context can also distract the model. anthropic .

447.doc: Reasoning Models, Contextual Retrieval, and Continual Learning (Part 2)
447.title: Continual learning
447.content: . | Continual parameter updates remain risky. | Synthetic self-generated data can reinforce model errors. | Memory expansion increases model size and infrastructure complexity. | Long-context consolidation must preserve both new and old knowledge. | Benchmarks may not reflect real production distribution shift. | . Google’s sleep framework addresses forgetting through parameter expansion, low-rank memory blocks, distillation, and pruning, but these mechanisms add substantial system complexity. research .

448.doc: Reasoning Models, Contextual Retrieval, and Continual Learning (Part 2)
448.title: Part 8: Practical Design Checklist
448.content: . | Start with a strong evaluation harness before changing the model. | Use verifiable rewards where the task has checkable correctness. | Use inference-time scaling when model weights must remain fixed. | Use distillation when a smaller, cheaper reasoning model is needed. | Use hybrid retrieval when both semantic similarity and exact matching matter. | Add chunk-specific context before embedding and indexing. | Use reranking when retrieval precision matters more than minimal latency. | Keep retrieval evaluation separate from response evaluation. | Use in-context learning for session-local adaptation. | Use continual learning only with strong forgetting, cost, and safety controls. | Monitor factual accuracy, retrieval failure rate, reasoning quality, latency, and cost. | .

449.doc: Reasoning Models, Contextual Retrieval, and Continual Learning (Part 2)
449.title: Resources
449.content: . | Build Your Own Reasoning Model — eight-video, 11-hour course covering evaluation, inference-time scaling, GRPO-based RLVR, and distillation in Python and PyTorch. | Introducing Contextual Retrieval — Anthropic’s method for contextual embeddings, contextual BM25, and reranking. | The sleep framework — Google Research’s continual-learning framework using wake and sleep phases. | Headroom — further reading on retrieval and context management. | Why Spotify is not using Bayesian A/B testing — further reading on experimentation methodology. | KronLSTM — further reading on recurrent sequence-model architectures. | Gemma 4 Developer Agent Paper competition — further reading on agent benchmarking. | .

450.doc: Reasoning Models, Contextual Retrieval, and Continual Learning (Part 2)
450.title: Final Technical Takeaways
450.content: . | Central mechanism: Reasoning models improve problem-solving through verifiable rewards, inference-time scaling, and distillation; retrieval systems ground responses in external knowledge; continual learning systems retain new knowledge over time. | Main architectural insight: Separate the model engine from the agent harness. The harness manages context, tools, memory, and control flow; the model performs reasoning and generation. magazine.sebastianraschka | Important retrieval insight: Embeddings and BM25 solve different retrieval failures. Adding chunk-specific context before embedding and indexing, then reranking, reduced Anthropic’s top-20 retrieval failure rate from 5.7% to 1.9%. anthropic | Important continual-learning insight: Alternate active interaction with offline consolidation so short-term context can become stable parametric memory without relying solely on a fixed context window. research | Key trade-off: More reasoning, more retrieved context, and more training can improve capability, but each increases latency, cost, complexity, or forgetting risk. | Main limitation: A stronger model does not automatically produce a better system. Verifiers, retrieval quality, context management, and evaluation discipline often determine real-world performance. magazine.sebastianraschka | Broader engineering implication: Build LLM systems as closed loops: reason, retrieve, act, measure, consolidate useful experience, and improve—while keeping forgetting, hallucination, and cost under explicit control. magazine.sebastianraschka | .

451.doc: Reasoning Models, Contextual Retrieval, and Continual Learning (Part 2)
451.title: Reasoning Models, Contextual Retrieval, and Continual Learning (Part 2)

452.doc: Reinforcement Learning, Bandits, and Recommender Systems
452.title: Reinforcement Learning, Bandits, and Recommender Systems
452.content: Primary references: . | Netflix: GenRec — Towards LLM-Native Recommendation | Google Research: Retrieve-for-Train | Google Research: The sleep framework for continual learning | .

453.doc: Reinforcement Learning, Bandits, and Recommender Systems
453.title: Overview
453.content: Recommender systems are not a single model. They are multi-stage decision systems that interpret user intent, retrieve candidates, enforce constraints, rank items, diversify results, and learn from feedback. This document covers: . | Recommender-system funnels. | Candidate generation and ranking. | Multi-objective learning. | Multi-armed and contextual bandits. | Position and selection bias. | Diversity and exploration. | Set-level retrieval. | LLM-native recommendation. | Continual learning. | .

454.doc: Reinforcement Learning, Bandits, and Recommender Systems
454.title: Part 1: Recommender-System Foundations

455.doc: Reinforcement Learning, Bandits, and Recommender Systems
455.title: Module 1: The Recommendation Problem
455.content: Given a user $u$, interaction history $H$, context $\tau$, and time $t$, a recommender produces a ranking $\pi$ over catalog items $C$: . \[(u,\tau,t,H) \rightarrow \pi\] where $\pi(i)$ is the position assigned to item $i$. The objective is expected long-term user utility, not merely immediate clicks or short-term engagement. Netflix describes this as a proxy for satisfaction and retention.

456.doc: Reinforcement Learning, Bandits, and Recommender Systems
456.title: Module 2: The Industrial Recommendation Funnel
456.content: User and query context | v +---------------------------+ | Intent understanding | - behavior | - preferences | - context | - explicit feedback | +-------------+-------------+ | v +---------------------------+ | Candidate generation | - collaborative filtering | - content-based filtering | - ANN retrieval | +-------------+-------------+ | v +---------------------------+ | Filtering and diversity | - business rules | - availability | - novelty | +-------------+-------------+ | v +---------------------------+ | Re-ranking and scoring | - engagement prediction | - multi-objective ranking | +-------------+-------------+ | v +---------------------------+ | Post-processing | - fairness | - freshness | - explanations | +-------------+-------------+ | v Final recommendations | v Feedback and learning .

457.doc: Reinforcement Learning, Bandits, and Recommender Systems
457.title: Module 3: Candidate Generation
457.content: Candidate generation retrieves hundreds or thousands of potentially relevant items from a catalog that may contain millions. | Method | Mechanism | Strength | . | Collaborative filtering | Learns from user-item interactions | Captures behavioral similarity | . | Content-based filtering | Matches item metadata and user profile | Works for cold-start items | . | Matrix factorization | Learns user and item latent factors | Compact personalized representation | . | ANN retrieval | Searches embedding space | Scales to large catalogs | . Approximate Nearest Neighbor, or ANN, search commonly uses Hierarchical Navigable Small World graphs, Product Quantization, or inverted-file indexes. These trade exact recall for lower latency and memory use.

458.doc: Reinforcement Learning, Bandits, and Recommender Systems
458.title: Module 4: Filtering and Diversification
458.content: After retrieval, the system applies business and policy constraints: . | Remove out-of-stock items. | Remove age-restricted or region-blocked content. | Enforce content-mix rules. | Add freshness boosts. | Prevent redundant recommendations. | Introduce exploration. | . Over-personalization can create echo chambers. Diversity constraints, such as Maximal Marginal Relevance, and bandit exploration help broaden exposure.

459.doc: Reinforcement Learning, Bandits, and Recommender Systems
459.title: Part 2: Ranking and Multi-Objective Learning

460.doc: Reinforcement Learning, Bandits, and Recommender Systems
460.title: Module 5: Re-Ranking
460.content: Re-ranking refines a candidate set of hundreds or thousands of items into a final list of roughly 10 to 50 items. Candidate items | v +---------------------------+ | Feature enrichment | - item metadata | - real-time context | - behavioral features | +-------------+-------------+ | v +---------------------------+ | Ranking model | - GBDT | - deep network | - transformer | +-------------+-------------+ | v Final ranked slate . Transformer-based rankers use self-attention to model mutual influence among items in a candidate list. Wide-and-Deep networks combine memorization components with generalized neural components. Deep Listwise Context Models, or DLCM, model list-level context during ranking.

461.doc: Reinforcement Learning, Bandits, and Recommender Systems
461.title: Module 6: Multi-Task Learning
461.content: Recommenders must balance competing objectives: . | Click-through rate, or CTR. | Conversion rate, or CVR. | Watch time. | Completion rate. | Saves or adds to list. | Long-term retention. | Revenue. | Satisfaction. | . Multi-gate Mixture-of-Experts, or MMoE, uses multiple expert sub-networks and task-specific gating networks. This helps balance conflicting objectives without forcing full negative transfer between tasks. Input features | +--> Expert 1 | +--> Expert 2 | +--> Expert 3 | v Task-specific gates | +--> CTR tower | +--> CVR tower | +--> Watch-time tower . | Ranking aspect | Technical implementation | Core objective | . | Hard parameter sharing | Shared hidden layers with task-specific heads | Baseline multi-task efficiency | . | MMoE | Expert sub-networks and per-task gates | Balance conflicting objectives | . | Deep Interest Transformer | Transformer blocks over behavior timelines | Capture multi-timescale user intent | .

462.doc: Reinforcement Learning, Bandits, and Recommender Systems
462.title: Module 7: Bayesian Personalized Ranking
462.content: Bayesian Personalized Ranking, or BPR, optimizes matrix-factorization models for implicit feedback using pairwise ranking loss. For a user $u$, preferred item $i$, and non-preferred item $j$: . \[\mathcal{L}_{BPR} = -\sum_{(u,i,j)} \log \sigma(\hat{x}_{ui} - \hat{x}_{uj})\] where: . | $\hat{x}_{ui}$ is the predicted score for preferred item $i$. | $\hat{x}_{uj}$ is the predicted score for non-preferred item $j$. | $\sigma$ is the sigmoid function. | . BPR optimizes ordering, not absolute rating prediction.

463.doc: Reinforcement Learning, Bandits, and Recommender Systems
463.title: Part 3: Reinforcement Learning and Bandits

464.doc: Reinforcement Learning, Bandits, and Recommender Systems
464.title: Module 8: Why Bandits Matter
464.content: Recommenders operate in a feedback loop. What the system shows affects what data it collects. If it only exploits known high-performing items, it may never discover better content. Multi-Armed Bandits, or MABs, balance: . | Exploration: trying new or cold-start items. | Exploitation: recommending historically high-reward items. | . User context | v +------------------+ | Bandit policy | +--------+---------+ | +--> Explore: try uncertain item | +--> Exploit: choose known high-reward item | v Reward: click, play, watch time | v Update value estimates .

465.doc: Reinforcement Learning, Bandits, and Recommender Systems
465.title: Module 9: Multi-Armed Bandits
465.content: Each video, product, article, or item is an arm. Selecting an arm yields a stochastic reward, such as a click, play, watch time, purchase, or conversion. | Algorithm | Mechanism | Strength | . | $\epsilon$-Greedy | Explore randomly with probability $\epsilon$ | Simple baseline | . | UCB | Choose arm with high reward estimate plus uncertainty bonus | Principled optimism | . | Thompson Sampling | Sample from posterior reward distributions | Strong empirical performance | . | Contextual bandit | Choose arm using user and context features | Personalized decisions | .

466.doc: Reinforcement Learning, Bandits, and Recommender Systems
466.title: Module 10: Contextual Bandits
466.content: A contextual bandit observes context $x_t$, selects action $a_t$, and receives reward $r_t$: . \[x_t \rightarrow a_t \rightarrow r_t\] Unlike full reinforcement learning, it does not model long-horizon state transitions. It optimizes immediate reward under a given context. User features + item features | v Contextual bandit | v Choose item | v Observe reward | v Update model .

467.doc: Reinforcement Learning, Bandits, and Recommender Systems
467.title: Module 11: LinUCB
467.content: LinUCB models expected reward as linear in context features. Disjoint LinUCB . Disjoint LinUCB treats each arm independently and learns arm-specific parameters: . \[E[\text{reward} \mid x_t, a] = \alpha_a^T x_t\] where: . | $x_t$ is the context vector. | $\alpha_a$ are arm-specific parameters. | . Use it when arms have completely distinct feature spaces. Hybrid LinUCB . Hybrid LinUCB combines global shared features with arm-specific parameters: . \[E[\text{reward} \mid x_t, a] = z_{t,a}^T\beta + x_{t,a}^T\alpha_a\] where: . | $z_{t,a}$ are shared features. | $\beta$ are shared parameters. | $x_{t,a}$ are arm-specific features. | $\alpha_a$ are arm-specific parameters. | . This shares statistical strength across related arms.

468.doc: Reinforcement Learning, Bandits, and Recommender Systems
468.title: Module 12: UCB and Thompson Sampling
468.content: Upper Confidence Bound . UCB selects the arm with the highest optimistic reward estimate: . \[a_t = \arg\max_a \left[ \hat{\mu}_a + c \sqrt{ \frac{\log t}{N_a} } \right]\] where: . | $\hat{\mu}_a$ is the estimated mean reward for arm $a$. | $N_a$ is the number of times arm $a$ was selected. | $c$ controls exploration. | . Thompson Sampling . Thompson Sampling samples a reward estimate from each arm’s posterior distribution and selects the arm with the highest sampled value. For each arm: Sample reward from posterior Choose arm with largest sampled reward Observe real reward Update posterior .

469.doc: Reinforcement Learning, Bandits, and Recommender Systems
469.title: Part 4: Bias, Debiasing, and Exploration

470.doc: Reinforcement Learning, Bandits, and Recommender Systems
470.title: Module 13: Position Bias
470.content: Position bias occurs because users disproportionately click top-ranked items due to attention and trust heuristics. Position 1: high observed CTR Position 2: lower observed CTR Position 3: lower observed CTR . A model trained directly on clicks may learn “being at position 1 causes clicks,” rather than “this item is relevant.” . Position-Aware Learning . Position-Aware Learning, or PAL, models position as an explicit feature or factor. It separates item relevance from examination probability. Inverse Propensity Weighting . Inverse Propensity Weighting, or IPW, reweights observed outcomes by the inverse probability that the item was shown: . \[\mathcal{L}_{IPW} = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^{N} \frac{c_i}{p_i} \ell(y_i, \hat{y}_i)\] where: . | $c_i$ is whether item $i$ was clicked. | $p_i$ is the propensity or probability that item $i$ was exposed. | $\ell$ is the loss. | . Items shown rarely receive larger weights, correcting exposure bias.

471.doc: Reinforcement Learning, Bandits, and Recommender Systems
471.title: Module 14: Selection Bias
471.content: Selection bias occurs because training data is skewed toward items previously exposed by the system. System shows popular items | v Users engage with shown items | v Model learns from exposed data | v System continues showing similar items . Mitigations include: . | Propensity-weighted offline debiasing. | Randomized exploration. | Bandit exploration. | Counterfactual evaluation. | Exposure-aware training. | .

472.doc: Reinforcement Learning, Bandits, and Recommender Systems
472.title: Module 15: Echo Chambers and Diversity
472.content: Over-personalization can narrow user perspectives. User clicks one topic | v System recommends similar topics | v User sees less diversity | v Feedback reinforces narrow interests . Mitigations: . | Maximal Marginal Relevance. | Category or creator diversity constraints. | Exploration through bandits. | Freshness boosts. | Slate-level objectives. | . Maximal Marginal Relevance . Maximal Marginal Relevance, or MMR, selects items that are relevant to the user but dissimilar from already selected items: . \[\text{MMR} = \arg\max_{i \in R \setminus S} \left[ \lambda \text{sim}(i,q) - (1-\lambda) \max_{j \in S} \text{sim}(i,j) \right]\] where: . | $R$ is the remaining candidate set. | $S$ is the already selected set. | $q$ is the query or user representation. | $\lambda$ balances relevance and diversity. | .

473.doc: Reinforcement Learning, Bandits, and Recommender Systems
473.title: Part 5: Set-Level Retrieval

474.doc: Reinforcement Learning, Bandits, and Recommender Systems
474.title: Module 16: Why Item-Level Ranking Is Insufficient
474.content: A good recommendation slate is not merely a list of individually relevant items. It should be diverse, complementary, coherent, and grounded. For example, a query such as “camping gear” should not return ten slight variations of a four-person tent. It should return complementary items: a tent, sleeping bag, portable stove, and headlamp. research . Query: camping gear Poor slate: - four-person tent A - four-person tent B - four-person tent C - four-person tent D Better slate: - tent - sleeping bag - portable stove - headlamp .

475.doc: Reinforcement Learning, Bandits, and Recommender Systems
475.title: Module 17: Query Fan-Out
475.content: Query fan-out breaks a single broad prompt into several related sub-queries to cover potential user interests. research . Broad query | v +---------------------------+ | Fan-out model | +-------------+-------------+ | v Sub-queries | +--> "camping tent" | +--> "sleeping bag" | +--> "portable stove" | +--> "headlamp" | v Retrieved result set .

476.doc: Reinforcement Learning, Bandits, and Recommender Systems
476.title: Module 18: Retrieve-for-Train
476.content: Google Research’s Retrieve-for-Train uses offline reinforcement learning to learn property-aligned query fan-outs, then distills that behavior into a lightweight diffusion retriever. research . Broad query | v +---------------------------+ | Fan-out language model | Trained once with RL | +-------------+-------------+ | v +---------------------------+ | Supervision synthesis | query -> target-set pairs | +-------------+-------------+ | v +---------------------------+ | Diffusion retriever | Single-pass fan-out | +-------------+-------------+ | v Set of target embeddings . The framework has three stages: research . | Stage | Purpose | Output | . | Fan-out language-model training | Learn property-aligned sub-queries with RL | Fan-out model | . | Supervision synthesis | Generate query-to-target-set pairs offline | Training data | . | Diffusive retriever training | Map query embeddings to target embeddings | Lightweight retriever | . The fan-out language models were 4B open-source models: Gemma3-4B and Qwen3-4B. Each generated exactly 10 sub-queries per prompt. The final diffusion retriever has 53.9M parameters and maps a query embedding to a complete set of target embeddings in one non-autoregressive pass. research .

477.doc: Reinforcement Learning, Bandits, and Recommender Systems
477.title: Module 19: Set-Level Rewards
477.content: Retrieve-for-Train optimizes properties that exist only at the set level. research . | Property | Meaning | Failure prevented | . | Groundedness | Sub-queries correspond to retrievable items | Nonsense strings exploiting embedding coordinates | . | Diversity | Sub-queries cover broad semantic breadth | Repetitive paraphrases | . | Alignment | Sub-queries remain related to the original prompt | Semantic drift | . Diversity is measured using the Vendi Score over the full set of sub-queries. research . These rewards act as mutual counter-anchors: . | Groundedness alone can reward degenerate strings. | Alignment alone can reward repetitive paraphrases. | Diversity forces useful exploration. research | .

478.doc: Reinforcement Learning, Bandits, and Recommender Systems
478.title: Module 20: Inference Efficiency
478.content: Directly deploying the RL-tuned language model preserves quality but inherits autoregressive latency constraints. The distilled diffusion model generates all target directions simultaneously in one non-autoregressive parallel pass. research . Google reports that Retrieve-for-Train outperformed single-query search, zero-shot expansion, and Best-of-N baselines, while achieving 12 to 20 times faster inference than autoregressive approaches. research .

479.doc: Reinforcement Learning, Bandits, and Recommender Systems
479.title: Part 6: LLM-Native Recommendation

480.doc: Reinforcement Learning, Bandits, and Recommender Systems
480.title: Module 21: GenRec
480.content: Netflix’s GenRec is an LLM-backed recommendation ranker. It post-trains an internal foundation LLM on Netflix-specific data and objectives, then adds a catalog-aware scoring head. User history + context + item metadata | v Verbalized context | v Foundation LLM backbone | v Catalog-aware scoring head | v In-catalog item scores | v Personalized ranking . At inference time, GenRec feeds verbalized context into the model and applies the catalog-aware scoring head. It does not decode assistant messages. The conversational format is primarily a training-time device to preserve language understanding.

481.doc: Reinforcement Learning, Bandits, and Recommender Systems
481.title: Module 22: Two-Phase Training
481.content: GenRec uses a two-phase framework. | Phase | Purpose | Update frequency | . | Phase 1 | Adapt an open-source LLM on proprietary corpora to create a domain-aware backbone | Relatively infrequent | . | Phase 2 | Post-train the backbone on ranking-specific data and objectives | More frequent | . Netflix members generate hundreds of billions of interaction events across surfaces, including views, plays, durations, thumbs up or down, add-to-list actions, and abandons. These logs are converted into single-turn or multi-turn conversations between a user and a recommender.

482.doc: Reinforcement Learning, Bandits, and Recommender Systems
482.title: Module 23: Context Engineering
482.content: Naively verbalizing every interaction would exceed the token budget. Netflix treats the context window as a new feature budget and applies context engineering. The approach is: . | Prioritize recent, high-signal history. | Compress or drop older history. | Structure prompts to maximize shared prefixes. | Enable better prefix caching. | Preserve ranking quality while reducing serving cost. | . Netflix reduced context tokens to roughly one-third of the original budget with negligible degradation in offline ranking metrics. Because serving cost is approximately proportional to context length, serving cost fell similarly.

483.doc: Reinforcement Learning, Bandits, and Recommender Systems
483.title: Module 24: Training Objectives
483.content: GenRec uses a multi-objective loss combining: . | A recommendation ranking objective. | Language-modeling objectives. | Alignment through reward-weighted training. | . The ranking objective uses cross-entropy over the catalog or candidate set. Positives are derived from high-value engagements, such as sufficiently long plays or strong explicit feedback, with thresholds and denoising logic. The language-modeling objective preserves general language understanding and keeps open the possibility of text-generation use cases such as recommendation explanations.

484.doc: Reinforcement Learning, Bandits, and Recommender Systems
484.title: Module 25: Reward-Weighted Alignment
484.content: Training only on raw interaction sequences can cause undesirable behavior, such as over-favoring binge-watching or over-focusing on one content type. GenRec weights the ranking loss using signals from separate reward models. \[\mathcal{L}_{weighted} = w_i \cdot \mathcal{L}_{ranking}^{(i)}\] where: . | $w_i$ is a scalar reward-derived weight for example $i$. | $\mathcal{L}_{ranking}^{(i)}$ is the ranking loss for that example. | . High-value engagements receive larger weights; low-value engagements are down-weighted. Netflix describes this as simpler and more cost-efficient than full reinforcement learning, while noting that RL-style methods such as GRPO produced additional gains but were deferred due to cost.

485.doc: Reinforcement Learning, Bandits, and Recommender Systems
485.title: Module 26: Catalog-Aware Scoring
485.content: GenRec’s architecture follows its foundation LLM: a decoder-only transformer trained with next-token-prediction-style objectives, augmented with a catalog-aware ranking head. The scoring head scores only in-catalog items. For very large catalogs, sampled softmax or candidate sets can make training and inference efficient. This constrains recommendations to the catalog while supporting efficient scoring over large candidate sets.

486.doc: Reinforcement Learning, Bandits, and Recommender Systems
486.title: Module 27: GenRec Results
486.content: Netflix reports: . | Evaluation | Result | . | Offline ranking | GenRec outperformed the production ranker despite fewer input signals and labeled examples | . | Data efficiency | About 40 times fewer Phase-2 labeled examples | . | Offline MRR | About +1.6% improvement | . | Online test | Statistically significant short-term and long-term gains | . | Traffic coverage | About 10% of Netflix traffic | . | Test duration | About 4 weeks | . These results apply to Netflix’s production baseline, traffic, catalog, and evaluation setup. They demonstrate the potential of LLM-backed rankers, not a universal guarantee that an LLM ranker will outperform every existing recommender.

487.doc: Reinforcement Learning, Bandits, and Recommender Systems
487.title: Part 7: Continual Learning

488.doc: Reinforcement Learning, Bandits, and Recommender Systems
488.title: Module 28: The Static-Model Problem
488.content: Most deployed LLMs are static after training. They have a knowledge cutoff and cannot naturally acquire long-term facts or adapt to new information after deployment. Two common approaches have limitations: . | Approach | Strength | Limitation | . | Continue parameter training | Can add new knowledge | Can cause catastrophic forgetting | . | In-context learning | Fast adaptation without weight updates | Knowledge disappears when context ends | . Catastrophic forgetting occurs when learning new tasks severely degrades performance on previously learned tasks. In-context learning retains information only within the current context window.

489.doc: Reinforcement Learning, Bandits, and Recommender Systems
489.title: Module 29: The Sleep Paradigm
489.content: Google Research’s sleep framework introduces a periodic lifecycle with two states: . | Active or wake phase: the model processes inputs and stores temporary information in short-term memory. | Sleep phase: the model pauses new input processing and consolidates short-term memory into long-term parameters. | . Active phase | v Short-term memory | v Sleep phase | +--> Memory consolidation | +--> Dreaming / self-improvement | v Updated long-term parametric memory . The framework operates within a fixed model architecture and human-defined training rules. During the offline sleep phase, the model unlocks preallocated Mixture-of-Experts memory blocks and updates weights using self-generated practice examples.

490.doc: Reinforcement Learning, Bandits, and Recommender Systems
490.title: Module 30: Memory Consolidation
490.content: Memory consolidation transfers fragile short-term context into stable long-term parameters. It uses: . | Parameter expansion through newly unlocked low-rank experts. | A continuum memory hierarchy. | Knowledge seeding through upward distillation. | On-policy distillation. | Learning to imitate using semantic and Levenshtein-distance rewards. | Synaptic pruning after consolidation. | . The goal is not to copy every short-term detail into parameters. Google describes it as structured, low-rank compression: identify compact directions that preserve on-policy behavior and semantically useful information.

491.doc: Reinforcement Learning, Bandits, and Recommender Systems
491.title: Module 31: Dreaming
491.content: The dreaming stage generates synthetic training examples, or “dreams,” and uses them for self-improvement. Short-term memory | v Random expert activation | v Generate synthetic samples | v Gradient-based sample selection | v Reinforcement-learning refinement | v Improved model capability . Random expert selection forces the model to mix knowledge from different domains. Gradient-based filtering prioritizes synthetic samples with the highest potential to improve overall capability.

492.doc: Reinforcement Learning, Bandits, and Recommender Systems
492.title: Module 32: Reported Results
492.content: Google reports the following results for its sleep framework: . | Evaluation | Reported result | . | Continual translation in unseen languages | Near-zero performance drop across multi-stage evaluation | . | Long-context understanding on BABILong | Near-perfect scaling up to 10M tokens | . | Factual knowledge incorporation on SQuAD | 48.9% | . | Continued pre-training evaluation | 46.2% | . | AIME 24/25 | 79.2% | . | HMMT 25 | 46.1% | . The framework is reported to outperform baselines including in-context learning, supervised fine-tuning, Cartridges, GPT-4, Titans, SEAL, GRPO, and on-policy self-distillation in the respective evaluations. These results are specific to Google’s benchmarks, models, and experimental setup.

493.doc: Reinforcement Learning, Bandits, and Recommender Systems
493.title: Part 8: Evaluation and Production

494.doc: Reinforcement Learning, Bandits, and Recommender Systems
494.title: Module 33: Offline Metrics
494.content: | Metric | Measures | . | Recall@K | Whether relevant items appear in top K | . | Precision@K | Whether top K results are relevant | . | MRR | Quality of first relevant result | . | NDCG@K | Ranked relevance quality | . | MAP | Mean average precision | . | Coverage | Breadth of catalog exposure | . | Diversity | Semantic or categorical variety | . | Calibration | Alignment of predicted engagement with outcomes | .

495.doc: Reinforcement Learning, Bandits, and Recommender Systems
495.title: Module 34: Online Metrics
495.content: | Metric | Measures | . | CTR | Immediate click engagement | . | CVR | Conversion behavior | . | Watch time | Consumption depth | . | Completion rate | Content satisfaction | . | Save or add-to-list rate | Strong preference signal | . | Retention | Long-term user value | . | Time to first play | Immediate relevance and latency | . | Abandonment rate | Poor relevance or inventory | .

496.doc: Reinforcement Learning, Bandits, and Recommender Systems
496.title: Module 35: Bias-Aware Evaluation
496.content: Evaluate metrics by: . | Position. | User cohort. | Item popularity. | Content age. | Language and market. | New versus established items. | Cold-start versus warm-start users. | . A model can improve aggregate CTR while harming long-tail discovery, fairness, or long-term retention.

497.doc: Reinforcement Learning, Bandits, and Recommender Systems
497.title: Module 36: Production Architecture
497.content: Client request | v +------------------+ | Feature store | User features | Item features | Context features | +--------+---------+ | v +------------------+ | Candidate layer | CF, ANN, content | +--------+---------+ | v +------------------+ | Filter layer | Business rules | +--------+---------+ | v +------------------+ | Ranker | Multi-objective | +--------+---------+ | v +------------------+ | Diversity layer | MMR, exploration | +--------+---------+ | v Final slate | v Feedback logs | v Training and bandit updates .

498.doc: Reinforcement Learning, Bandits, and Recommender Systems
498.title: Module 37: Production Checklist
498.content: . | Log exposure, position, and propensity. | Separate candidate generation from ranking. | Use ANN indexes for large catalogs. | Apply business and availability filters before ranking. | Use multi-task models for competing objectives. | Add exploration for cold-start items. | Measure diversity and long-term retention. | Correct for position and selection bias. | Use online experiments before launch. | Monitor calibration, coverage, latency, and cost. | .

499.doc: Reinforcement Learning, Bandits, and Recommender Systems
499.title: Part 9: Limitations and Open Questions

500.doc: Reinforcement Learning, Bandits, and Recommender Systems
500.title: Recommender limitations
500.content: . | Feedback loops amplify popularity and exposure bias. | Clicks and short-term engagement do not always reflect long-term value. | Cold-start items lack interaction history. | Multi-objective trade-offs are business-specific. | Personalization can reduce discovery and diversity. | .

501.doc: Reinforcement Learning, Bandits, and Recommender Systems
501.title: Bandit limitations
501.content: . | Bandits optimize immediate reward, not necessarily long-horizon utility. | Delayed rewards complicate learning. | Contextual bandits require accurate context features. | Exploration can harm short-term user experience. | Propensity estimates can be noisy or biased. | .

502.doc: Reinforcement Learning, Bandits, and Recommender Systems
502.title: Set-level retrieval limitations
502.content: . | Set-level rewards are harder to define than item-level relevance. | Diversity can reduce precision if applied too aggressively. | Offline RL depends on the quality of the reward function. | Distilled retrievers may lose some capability of the original RL policy. | . Google notes that groundedness alone can reward degenerate strings, while alignment alone can reward repetitive paraphrases; diversity is needed as a counter-anchor. research .

503.doc: Reinforcement Learning, Bandits, and Recommender Systems
503.title: LLM-based ranking limitations
503.content: . | LLMs can hallucinate out-of-catalog items. | Long context increases serving cost. | Raw interaction data can reinforce popularity bias. | Reward-weighted training requires careful reward design. | Offline gains do not guarantee long-term online improvements. | . Netflix notes that off-the-shelf LLMs can over-recommend popular content, hallucinate out-of-catalog items, ignore business constraints, and provide limited personalization.

504.doc: Reinforcement Learning, Bandits, and Recommender Systems
504.title: Continual-learning limitations
504.content: . | Continual parameter updates remain risky. | Synthetic self-generated data can reinforce model errors. | Memory expansion increases model size and infrastructure complexity. | Long-context consolidation must preserve both new and old knowledge. | Benchmarks may not reflect real production distribution shift. | . Google’s sleep framework addresses forgetting through parameter expansion, low-rank memory blocks, distillation, and pruning, but these mechanisms add substantial system complexity.

505.doc: Reinforcement Learning, Bandits, and Recommender Systems
505.title: Final Technical Takeaways
505.content: . | Central mechanism: A recommender is a multi-stage decision system: understand intent, retrieve candidates, filter, rank, diversify, serve, and learn. | Main architectural insight: Separate candidate generation from ranking; use fast retrieval for scale and high-precision rankers for final ordering. | Main learning insight: Bandits balance exploration and exploitation, while contextual bandits personalize decisions using user, item, and session features. | Main bias insight: Position and selection bias require explicit mitigation through propensity weighting, position-aware models, randomized exploration, and counterfactual evaluation. | Important set-level insight: Optimize the entire slate for diversity, coherence, and complementarity, not merely individual item relevance. research | Important LLM insight: LLM-backed rankers need catalog-aware scoring and context engineering to avoid hallucination and control serving cost. | Main continual-learning insight: Alternate active interaction with offline consolidation so short-term context can become stable parametric memory without relying solely on a fixed context window. | Main trade-off: Exploitation maximizes immediate reward; exploration improves long-term discovery but can reduce short-term engagement. | Broader engineering implication: Treat recommendation as a closed-loop decision system, where exposure policy, feedback collection, bias correction, and evaluation are as important as the ranking model. research | .

506.title: Recommender Systems: High-Level Guide
506.content: This document is an extensive technical guide to modern recommendation systems. It synthesizes the supplied materials on recommendation-system foundations, candidate generation, collaborative filtering, ranking, re-ranking, calibration, search, evaluation, moderation, graph neural networks, Transformers, cold start, bias, multi-armed bandits, multi-objective optimization, generative recommendation, and representative research papers. The central engineering problem is to select and order a small set of useful items from a very large catalog for a particular user, context, or query, while satisfying latency, quality, safety, diversity, business, and fairness constraints.

507.title: Contents
507.content: . | Recommendation-system foundations | Production funnel architecture | Data and feature representations | Candidate generation | Collaborative filtering and matrix factorization | Two-tower retrieval and approximate nearest neighbors | Ranking and learning to rank | Re-ranking and slate optimization | Calibration | Search and hybrid retrieval | Evaluation and loss functions | Bias, feedback loops, and fairness | Content moderation and integrity | Cold-start strategies | Popular neural architectures | Graph neural networks | Transformers and sequential recommendation | Multi-armed and contextual bandits | Multi-objective optimization | Generative recommendation and LLMs | Production challenges | Research-paper map | End-to-end reference architecture | Implementation blueprint | Final technical takeaways | .

508.title: Recommendation-system foundations
508.content: What is a recommendation system? . A recommendation system is a machine-learning system that estimates which items a user is likely to find useful, relevant, enjoyable, or valuable, and then presents a selected set of those items. An item may be: . | A movie, song, video, article, product, restaurant, job, advertisement, or social connection. | A search result or document. | A notification, explanation, image, or content collection. | A generated response or conversational suggestion. | . A recommendation request usually contains three conceptual components: . | Component | Meaning | Examples | . | User or query | The entity for which recommendations are generated | User ID, search query, device, location | . | Item or document | A candidate that may be recommended | Movie, product, video, restaurant | . | Representation | A numerical description used by models | Features, embeddings, graph vectors | . A system attempts to estimate a relevance or utility function: . \[\hat{r}(u, i, c) = f_\theta(u, i, c)\] where: . | $u$ is the user or user representation. | $i$ is the item. | $c$ is contextual information. | $f_\theta$ is a learned model. | $\hat{r}$ is a predicted relevance, engagement probability, utility, or score. | . Why recommendation systems are difficult . A production recommender must solve several problems simultaneously: . | The catalog may contain millions or billions of items. | Most user-item interactions are unobserved. | Feedback is often implicit rather than explicit. | Exposure is not random; users interact with what the system shows them. | Popular items receive more exposure and therefore more feedback. | New users and items have little or no history. | User preferences change over time. | Different objectives can conflict. | The system must often respond within a strict latency budget. | A recommendation can affect user behavior, creating feedback loops. | Safety, policy, legal, and fairness requirements may override engagement. | . Discovery, search, and recommendation . Search and recommendation are closely related but have different starting conditions. | Property | Search | Recommendation | . | Explicit intent | Usually provided by a query | Often inferred from behavior or context | . | User state | Query-centric | User-history and context-centric | . | Candidate set | Query-matching documents | Personalized catalog items | . | Main challenge | Interpret the query and retrieve relevant results | Infer preferences and balance relevance with discovery | . | Typical signals | Terms, semantic similarity, filters | History, embeddings, context, social graph, popularity | . Modern systems often combine both. Search activity can enrich a recommender, while recommendation models can personalize search results.

509.title: Production funnel architecture
509.content: The two-stage funnel . A common production architecture separates fast retrieval from expensive ranking: . OFFLINE SYSTEMS +-------------------+-------------------+-------------------+ | Events and Data | Feature Pipelines | Model Training | +-------------------+-------------------+-------------------+ | | v v v +-------------------+-------------------+-------------------+ | Item Embeddings | User Features | Models and | ANN Indices | Feature Store | Checkpoints | +-------------------+-------------------+-------------------+ | v ONLINE REQUEST PATH +-------------------+ | User / Query | +-------------------+ | v +-------------------+ | Candidate | Generation | +-------------------+ | v +-------------------+ | Ranking / Scoring | +-------------------+ | v +-------------------+ | Final List | +-------------------+ . The two stages have different optimization goals: . | Stage | Main goal | Typical model or method | . | Candidate generation | High recall at low latency | Matrix factorization, two-tower model, ANN, popularity retrieval | . | Ranking | High precision and utility | Logistic regression, GBDT, deep ranker, Transformer | . Candidate generation operates over a large catalog and must be efficient. Ranking receives a much smaller candidate set and can use richer features and more computationally expensive models. The four-stage funnel . Some production systems separate ranking into retrieval, filtering, scoring, and ordering: . +-------------------+ | Entire Catalog | +-------------------+ | v +-------------------+ | Retrieval | High Recall | +-------------------+ | v +-------------------+ | Filtering | Eligibility Rules | +-------------------+ | v +-------------------+ | Scoring | Personalized | +-------------------+ | v +-------------------+ | Ordering | Diversity, Policy | +-------------------+ | v +-------------------+ | User-Facing Slate | +-------------------+ . The four stages separate concerns: . | Retrieval finds a broad set of potentially relevant items. | Filtering removes items that cannot or should not be shown. | Scoring estimates relevance or expected utility. | Ordering constructs the final slate while considering diversity, novelty, freshness, policy, and business constraints. | . Multiple candidate generators . A production system often combines several candidate sources: . | Collaborative-filtering candidates. | Content-similarity candidates. | Trending and popular candidates. | Geographical candidates. | Social-graph candidates. | Search-derived candidates. | Recently viewed or continued items. | New-item exploration candidates. | Sponsored or business-priority candidates. | . These sources are merged into a common candidate pool. Their individual scores are not necessarily comparable, which is one reason a separate ranking model is used. Offline and online environments . The offline environment creates artifacts needed by online serving: . | Item and user embeddings. | ANN indices. | Feature-store values. | Trained model checkpoints. | Popularity statistics. | Calibration maps. | Policy and moderation classifiers. | Candidate-generator configurations. | . The online environment performs request-specific work: . | Resolve user and context. | Retrieve candidates. | Apply eligibility filters. | Fetch online features. | Score candidates. | Re-rank the slate. | Log exposure and outcomes. | .

510.title: Data and feature representations
510.content: Explicit and implicit feedback . Feedback can be explicit or implicit. | Feedback type | Examples | Strengths | Limitations | . | Explicit | Rating, like, dislike, save | Direct preference signal | Sparse and subject to rating behavior | . | Implicit | Click, view, purchase, dwell time | Abundant and naturally collected | Ambiguous; exposure affects observations | . | Negative feedback | Hide, skip, report, unsubscribe | Useful for filtering and preference modeling | Often sparse and not always comparable across users | . An impression without an interaction is not always a true negative. The user may not have noticed the item, may have lacked time, or may have preferred another visible item. Dense and sparse features . Dense features are continuous or numerical values: . | Age or normalized price. | Rating statistics. | Time since the last interaction. | Watch duration. | Device or network measurements. | . Sparse features are categorical identifiers or high-cardinality values: . | User ID. | Item ID. | Country. | Language. | Product category. | Artist ID. | Search terms. | . Sparse features are commonly mapped to trainable embeddings. Sparse ID | v Embedding Lookup Table | v Dense Vector | +--> Concatenate with numerical features | v Neural or ranking model . Univalent and multivalent features . A univalent feature has one value for an entity, such as a user’s primary language. A multivalent feature contains a set or sequence, such as genres associated with a movie or a user’s viewing history. A variable-length collection can be transformed into a fixed-width vector using pooling: . \[\mathbf{h}_{\text{pool}} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{j=1}^{n}\mathbf{e}_j\] where $\mathbf{e}_j$ is the embedding of the $j$-th element. Mean pooling is simple and scalable, but it discards order and may treat all events equally. More advanced systems use recency weighting, attention, RNNs, Transformers, or graph aggregation. Embeddings . An embedding is a learned numerical vector representing an entity or event. Embedding spaces can encode: . | Similarity between items. | Similarity between users. | User-item compatibility. | Semantic content. | Behavioral patterns. | Graph neighborhoods. | . Similarity may be measured using a dot product: . \[s(u, i) = \mathbf{u}^{\top}\mathbf{i}\] or cosine similarity: . \[\text{cos}(\mathbf{u}, \mathbf{i}) = \frac{\mathbf{u}^{\top}\mathbf{i}} {\lVert\mathbf{u}\rVert_2\lVert\mathbf{i}\rVert_2}\] Embedding quality depends on the training objective, negative-sampling strategy, data coverage, and serving-time consistency. Feature stores and training-serving consistency . A feature store can provide a common definition of features for both training and serving. This reduces training-serving skew, where the model sees one representation during training and another during production inference. Important consistency requirements include: . | Identical transformations. | Identical normalization parameters. | Correct event-time semantics. | No future information leaking into historical examples. | Consistent missing-value handling. | Versioned feature definitions. | .

511.title: Candidate generation
511.content: Candidate generation reduces a large catalog to a manageable set of items that can be scored in later stages. Content-based filtering . Content-based filtering recommends items based on item characteristics and the user’s inferred profile. Examples of item features include: . | Text descriptions. | Genres. | Tags. | Images. | Audio features. | Actors, artists, or creators. | Product attributes. | . A content-based system can construct a user profile by aggregating features from items the user interacted with: . \[\mathbf{u} = \text{aggregate}(\{\mathbf{i}_j : j \in H_u\})\] where $H_u$ is the user’s interaction history. Advantages . | Can recommend new items when content features are available. | Does not require other users’ interactions. | Can personalize niche interests. | Is relatively easy to explain through item attributes. | . Limitations . | It may over-specialize in existing interests. | It requires useful item metadata. | It may lack serendipity. | It often requires domain-specific feature engineering. | . Collaborative filtering . Collaborative filtering uses interactions among users and items rather than item content alone. The central assumption is that users with similar behavior may prefer similar items, and items consumed by similar users may be related. User-item interactions | v +------------------------+ | Discover user patterns | and item patterns | +------------------------+ | v +------------------------+ | Learn latent vectors | +------------------------+ | v +------------------------+ | Retrieve or score | unseen items | +------------------------+ . Collaborative filtering can discover relationships that are not obvious from item metadata, but it is vulnerable to sparse data and cold start. Matrix factorization . A user-item interaction matrix can be approximated using latent user and item factors: . \[R \approx U V^{\top}\] The predicted interaction can be written as: . \[\hat{r}_{ui} = \mu + b_u + b_i + \mathbf{p}_u^{\top}\mathbf{q}_i\] where: . | $\mu$ is the global bias. | $b_u$ and $b_i$ are user and item biases. | $\mathbf{p}_u$ is the user latent vector. | $\mathbf{q}_i$ is the item latent vector. | . The model may minimize squared error for explicit ratings or use a ranking loss for implicit feedback. Weighted alternating least squares . Weighted alternating least squares (WALS) is useful for large sparse interaction matrices. It alternates between solving for user factors while holding item factors fixed and solving for item factors while holding user factors fixed. A generic objective is: . \[\min_{U,V} \sum_{u,i} c_{ui}(p_{ui} - \mathbf{u}_u^{\top}\mathbf{v}_i)^2 + \lambda(\lVert U\rVert_F^2 + \lVert V\rVert_F^2)\] where $c_{ui}$ weights confidence in an observed or unobserved interaction. Negative sampling . Many recommender tasks have far more unobserved pairs than observed positive pairs. Negative sampling selects a manageable set of presumed negative examples. Common strategies include: . | Uniform random negatives. | Popularity-weighted negatives. | In-batch negatives. | Hard negatives from a retrieval model. | Time-aware negatives. | Exposure-aware negatives. | . Negative sampling changes the training distribution. Evaluation and serving should account for that difference.

512.title: Two-tower retrieval and approximate nearest neighbors
512.content: Two-tower architecture . A two-tower model independently encodes a user or query and an item: . +------------------+ +------------------+ | User features | Item features | +------------------+ +------------------+ | v v +------------------+ +------------------+ | User tower | Item tower | Neural encoder | Neural encoder | +------------------+ +------------------+ | v v +------------------+ +------------------+ | User embedding | Item embedding | +------------------+ +------------------+ \ / \ / v v Similarity function | v Retrieval score . The item tower can be run offline for the entire catalog. At request time, only the user tower and ANN lookup need to run. A typical loss encourages positive pairs to have high similarity and negatives to have lower similarity: . \[\mathcal{L}_{\text{InfoNCE}} = -\log \frac{\exp(s(u, i^+)/\tau)} {\exp(s(u, i^+)/\tau) + \sum_{j \in N}\exp(s(u, i_j^-)/\tau)}\] where $\tau$ is a temperature parameter. Approximate nearest-neighbor retrieval . Exact comparison of a query vector with every catalog vector is expensive. Approximate nearest-neighbor methods trade a small amount of recall for much lower latency. Common index families include: . | HNSW graphs. | Inverted-file indices. | Product quantization. | Tree-based indices. | Hybrid graph and quantization systems. | . Important ANN trade-offs include: . | Recall versus latency. | Memory versus compression. | Update speed versus query speed. | Index freshness versus rebuild cost. | . Candidate-generator evaluation . Candidate generation is usually evaluated using recall at a candidate-set size: . \[\text{Recall@K} = \frac{|\text{relevant items in top-}K|} {|\text{relevant items}|}\] High retrieval recall is necessary but not sufficient. A generator may retrieve relevant items but create a candidate set that is redundant, unsafe, stale, or difficult for later ranking to process.

513.title: Ranking and learning to rank
513.content: Scoring versus ranking . Scoring assigns an independent value to each candidate. Ranking orders candidates according to those scores or according to a list-level objective. A scoring model may estimate: . | Click probability. | Purchase probability. | Watch probability. | Expected watch time. | Conversion value. | Long-term satisfaction. | . A ranking model may then sort candidates, subject to additional constraints. Point-wise learning to rank . Point-wise methods treat each item independently as a regression or classification example. Examples include: . | Logistic regression. | Linear regression. | Gradient-boosted decision trees. | Neural networks. | . For binary engagement, binary cross-entropy is common: . \[\mathcal{L}_{\text{BCE}} = -\left[y\log\hat{p} + (1-y)\log(1-\hat{p})\right]\] Point-wise approaches are simple and scalable, but they do not directly model competition among items in the same slate. Pair-wise learning to rank . Pair-wise methods train on item pairs and attempt to place the preferred item above the less-preferred item. A pairwise logistic loss can be expressed as: . \[\mathcal{L}_{\text{pair}} = -\log \sigma(s(u, i^+) - s(u, i^-))\] Examples include RankNet, RankSVM, LambdaRank, and LambdaMART. Pair-wise approaches align more closely with ordering but may require many item pairs. List-wise learning to rank . List-wise methods optimize an entire candidate list or an approximation to a list-ranking metric. Examples include ListNet, ListMLE, SoftRank, and list-wise Lambda methods. They can better represent the final ranking objective but usually have higher computational and implementation complexity. Multi-stage ranking . Large platforms may use multiple ranking passes: . Candidate pool: 500 items | v First pass: lightweight model | v Top 150 items | v Second pass: richer model | v Top 50 items | v Final pass: deep model and constraints | v Top 25 items . The first pass prioritizes speed, while later passes use richer features and more expressive models. Objective-function design . The ranking objective determines what the system learns to optimize. Optimizing only one metric can create undesirable behavior: . | Objective | Possible failure mode | . | Click-through rate | Clickbait and shallow engagement | . | Watch time | Bias toward long content | . | Purchases | Reduced discovery or over-commercialization | . | Popularity | Feedback loops and reduced long-tail exposure | . | Short-term engagement | Lower long-term satisfaction | . Production rankers often combine several predicted outcomes and apply constraints or re-ranking after model scoring.

514.title: Re-ranking and slate optimization
514.content: Re-ranking operates after initial scoring and modifies the candidate order or removes candidates to satisfy additional goals. Common re-ranking objectives . | Diversity. | Freshness. | Novelty. | Serendipity. | Popularity control. | Seasonality. | Fairness. | Creator or seller coverage. | Safety and policy compliance. | Business constraints. | . Diversity . If the highest-scoring items are almost identical, the user may receive a repetitive slate. Diversity can be encouraged through: . | Category quotas. | Similarity penalties. | Maximum marginal relevance. | Multiple candidate generators. | Multiple rankers with different objectives. | Clustering and coverage constraints. | . A simple diversity-aware objective is: . \[\text{Utility}(S) = \sum_{i \in S} \text{relevance}(i) - \lambda \sum_{i,j \in S} \text{similarity}(i,j)\] where $S$ is the selected slate. Freshness and seasonality . Freshness can be modeled using a time-decay function: . \[w(t) = \exp(-\lambda \Delta t)\] where $\Delta t$ is the age of the item or event. Seasonality can be represented through: . | Day-of-week features. | Month or holiday indicators. | Historical performance during similar periods. | Time-aware models. | Event-specific rules. | . Popularity control . Popularity is useful for cold-start fallback and broad appeal, but excessive popularity weighting can suppress long-tail content. A re-ranker may normalize or penalize popularity so that relevant niche items receive exposure. Re-ranking as constrained selection . A practical formulation is: . \[\max_{S \subseteq C} U(S)\] subject to constraints such as: . | Size constraint: $|S| = K$. | At most $m$ items from one category. | At least one fresh item. | No policy-violating item. | Minimum creator or seller coverage. | .

515.title: Calibration
515.content: Calibration measures whether predicted probabilities match observed frequencies. If a model assigns a click probability of $0.7$ to a group of impressions, approximately 70% of that group should click for the model to be well calibrated. Calibration matters when probabilities are used for: . | Threshold decisions. | Risk-sensitive decisions. | Utility calculations. | Multi-objective combinations. | Budget allocation. | Downstream re-ranking. | . Platt scaling . Platt scaling fits a sigmoid mapping from a raw score $s$ to a probability: . \[P(y=1 \mid s) = \frac{1}{1 + \exp(As+B)}\] The parameters $A$ and $B$ are learned on a held-out calibration set. Isotonic regression . Isotonic regression learns a non-decreasing mapping without assuming a sigmoid shape. It can be more flexible but may overfit when calibration data is limited. Bayesian calibration . Bayesian binning methods estimate event probabilities within score bins while incorporating uncertainty and priors. They can be useful when data is limited or estimates need uncertainty handling. Calibration evaluation . Common diagnostics include: . | Reliability diagrams. | Expected calibration error. | Maximum calibration error. | Brier score. | Log loss. | . Calibration should be evaluated by important slices, such as device, geography, language, user activity, item popularity, and traffic source.

516.title: Search and hybrid retrieval
516.content: Information retrieval . Information retrieval concerns representing, storing, organizing, and accessing information from large collections. A search system receives a query $q$ and a document collection $D$ and attempts to return a ranked subset of useful documents. Lexical search . Lexical search relies on term overlap. TF-IDF assigns a weight to a term based on its local frequency and global rarity: . \[\text{tfidf}(t,d) = \text{tf}(t,d) \cdot \log\left(\frac{N}{\text{df}(t)}\right)\] BM25 improves term-based retrieval by incorporating term frequency saturation and document-length normalization. Strengths . | Fast lookup through inverted indices. | Strong performance for identifiers and exact terminology. | Good interpretability. | Mature ecosystem. | . Limitations . | Vocabulary mismatch. | Weak synonym and paraphrase handling. | Limited semantic understanding. | Difficulty with ambiguous intent. | . Semantic search . Semantic search encodes queries and documents into dense vectors and retrieves nearby vectors. It can handle: . | Synonyms. | Paraphrases. | Related concepts. | Cross-language or cross-modal relationships. | . Limitations include: . | Higher compute cost. | Larger storage requirements. | Harder explanations. | Potential overgeneralization. | Need for domain adaptation. | . Hybrid search . Hybrid search combines lexical and semantic retrieval: . User Query | +------------------+ | v v Lexical Retrieval Dense Retrieval | +--------+---------+ v Candidate Fusion | v Neural Reranking | v Final Results . Reciprocal Rank Fusion combines rankings without requiring directly comparable scores: . \[\text{RRF}(d) = \sum_{m=1}^{M}\frac{1}{k + r_m(d)}\] where $r_m(d)$ is the rank of document $d$ in system $m$. Index structures . | Index | Mapping | Main use | . | Forward index | Document to terms | Reconstruction, metadata, snippets | . | Inverted index | Term to documents | Lexical retrieval | . | Embedding index | Vector to nearby vectors | Semantic retrieval | . Modern search systems may maintain all three.

517.title: Evaluation and loss functions
517.content: Offline evaluation . Offline evaluation typically involves: . | Define historical examples. | Split data by time or user appropriately. | Train candidate models. | Evaluate on held-out interactions. | Compare metrics and slices. | Check leakage and bias. | Select candidates for online testing. | . Random splitting can produce overly optimistic results when future interactions leak into training or when users appear in both sets in unrealistic ways. Online evaluation . Online evaluation uses live traffic, typically through: . | A/B tests. | Interleaving. | Contextual bandits. | Holdout groups. | Gradual rollouts. | . Online metrics should include guardrails, not only the primary objective. Precision and recall . \[\text{Precision} = \frac{TP}{TP+FP}\] \[\text{Recall} = \frac{TP}{TP+FN}\] At a cutoff $K$: . \[\text{Precision@K} = \frac{\text{relevant items in top }K}{K}\] \[\text{Recall@K} = \frac{\text{relevant items in top }K}{\text{total relevant items}}\] Mean reciprocal rank . MRR emphasizes the position of the first relevant item: . \[\text{MRR} = \frac{1}{M}\sum_{j=1}^{M}\frac{1}{\text{rank}_j}\] It ignores later relevant items after the first one. Average precision and mean average precision . Average precision rewards relevant items appearing early and averages precision at relevant positions. Mean average precision averages AP across queries or users. NDCG . Discounted cumulative gain discounts lower-ranked items: . \[\text{DCG@K} = \sum_{r=1}^{K}\frac{2^{rel_r}-1}{\log_2(r+1)}\] NDCG normalizes DCG by the ideal DCG: . \[\text{NDCG@K} = \frac{\text{DCG@K}}{\text{IDCG@K}}\] NDCG is useful when relevance is graded and rank position matters. Business and engagement metrics . Possible metrics include: . | Click-through rate. | Conversion rate. | Session length. | Dwell time. | Completion rate. | Repeat visits. | Retention. | Revenue or margin. | Creator coverage. | Catalog coverage. | Diversity. | Complaint or report rate. | Unsubscribe or disable rate. | . No single metric captures recommendation quality. A metric should be selected according to the product objective and evaluated with guardrails. Common loss functions . | Task | Typical loss | . | Binary engagement | Binary cross-entropy | . | Rating prediction | Mean squared error or mean absolute error | . | Pairwise preference | Pairwise logistic or hinge loss | . | Representation learning | Contrastive or triplet loss | . | List ranking | List-wise ranking loss | . | Diversity | Diversity regularizer or slate objective | . | Fairness | Group or exposure constraint loss | .

518.title: Bias, feedback loops, and fairness
518.content: Position bias . Items shown higher in a list often receive more attention regardless of intrinsic relevance. This creates a confound between position and relevance. Possible mitigations include: . | Randomized exposure experiments. | Inverse propensity weighting. | Position-aware click models. | Interleaving. | Position features used carefully during training. | Counterfactual evaluation. | . Inverse propensity weighting uses: . \[w_i = \frac{1}{P(\text{exposure}_i)}\] Care is required because low-propensity examples receive high weights and can increase variance. Popularity bias . Popularity bias causes popular items to receive more exposure, interactions, and future recommendations. This can suppress niche content and create a self-reinforcing loop. Possible mitigations include: . | Popularity-aware sampling. | Logit adjustment. | Long-tail exploration. | Exposure constraints. | Diversity-aware re-ranking. | Separate evaluation by popularity bucket. | . Selection bias . The training data contains interactions only for items that were exposed. Unexposed items provide little or no direct feedback, so the model may mistake lack of interaction for lack of relevance. Selection bias can be studied through: . | Exposure logs. | Propensity estimation. | Randomized traffic. | IPS or doubly robust estimators. | Counterfactual evaluation. | . Duration bias . If watch time is optimized directly, longer videos may appear better simply because they have more time available to accumulate watch time. Possible mitigations include: . | Completion rate. | Relative watch-time quantiles within duration buckets. | Normalized watch time. | Multi-objective objectives. | Separate short-form and long-form modeling. | . Clickbait bias . Click optimization can reward sensational content that attracts clicks but produces poor satisfaction. Weighted objectives can incorporate watch quality, completion, reports, or long-term engagement. Single-interest bias . A system may overrepresent a user’s most frequent interest and neglect other interests. Mitigations include: . | Interest-aware user representations. | Diversity constraints. | Multiple interest vectors. | Calibrated probability distributions. | Exploration policies. | Topic or category coverage metrics. | . Fairness . Fairness can concern: . | Equal opportunity for creators or sellers. | Exposure across item groups. | User-group performance parity. | Content safety and accessibility. | Geographic or language coverage. | . Fairness should be evaluated alongside utility, because improving one dimension can affect another.

519.title: Content moderation and integrity
519.content: Engagement alone is not an acceptable recommendation objective when content can cause harm. A moderation-aware funnel can be structured as follows: . +-------------------+ | Content Ingestion | +-------------------+ | v +-------------------+ | Input Moderation | Classifiers | +-------------------+ | v +-------------------+ | Eligible Catalog | +-------------------+ | v +-------------------+ | Retrieval | +-------------------+ | v +-------------------+ | Ranking | +-------------------+ | v +-------------------+ | Final Safety | and Policy Checks | +-------------------+ | v +-------------------+ | User Presentation | +-------------------+ . Moderation may include: . | Automated classifiers. | Human review. | User reporting. | Appeals. | Age and region policies. | Copyright enforcement. | Hate-speech detection. | Child-safety protections. | Misinformation policies. | Spam and coordinated inauthentic behavior detection. | . Moderation can occur at multiple points: . | At content ingestion. | Before candidate retrieval. | After retrieval. | During ranking or re-ranking. | Immediately before presentation. | After user reports or post-publication review. | . A content item can be removed, down-ranked, age-gated, region-restricted, or routed for human review depending on policy.

520.title: Cold-start strategies
520.content: Cold start occurs when the system lacks enough interaction data to personalize effectively. Item cold start . New items can be represented using content features: . | Text embeddings. | Image or audio embeddings. | Metadata. | Category information. | Creator or seller attributes. | Knowledge-based rules. | . This makes content-based and hybrid systems useful for newly added items. User cold start . New users can be handled using: . | Popular items. | Geography or language-specific popularity. | Demographic or contextual priors. | Onboarding surveys. | Preference elicitation. | Active learning. | Session-level behavior. | Search queries. | . A practical transition is: . New User | v Popular and Contextual Candidates | v Onboarding or Early Interactions | v Session Representation | v Personalized Retrieval and Ranking . Community or marketplace cold start . A new marketplace has both new users and new items. Possible strategies include: . | Early-adopter programs. | Internal testing. | Employee dogfooding. | Beta releases. | Transfer from similar markets. | Rules and domain knowledge. | Targeted exploration. | . Feature hashing . Feature hashing maps high-cardinality identifiers into a fixed number of buckets. It reduces memory but introduces possible collisions. A signed hashing scheme or multiple hash functions can reduce systematic collision effects. Hashing is useful for managing dynamic categories, but collision analysis and monitoring are important.

521.title: Popular neural architectures
521.content: Wide and Deep . Wide and Deep combines: . | A wide component for memorization of explicit feature crosses. | A deep component for generalization through embeddings and nonlinear layers. | . Sparse Features | +----------------------+ | v v +--------------+ +--------------+ | Wide Model | Deep Model | Crosses | Embeddings | +--------------+ +--------------+ | +----------+-----------+ v Combined Prediction . The wide side can memorize specific interactions such as user-category combinations. The deep side can generalize to related but unseen combinations. Factorization machines . Factorization Machines model pairwise feature interactions using latent vectors: . \[\hat{y} = w_0 + \sum_i w_i x_i + \sum_{i=1}^{n}\sum_{j=i+1}^{n}\langle \mathbf{v}_i, \mathbf{v}_j\rangle x_i x_j\] They are effective for sparse, high-dimensional features and can incorporate user, item, and context variables. DeepFM . DeepFM combines a factorization-machine component with a deep neural network. The FM part captures pairwise interactions, while the deep part models higher-order nonlinear relationships. Neural Collaborative Filtering . NCF replaces the simple matrix-factorization inner product with a neural interaction function. User and item embeddings are combined and passed through an MLP. Deep and Cross Networks . DCN learns explicit feature crosses through a cross network rather than requiring manual cross-feature engineering. The deep component provides generalization. DLRM . Deep Learning Recommendation Models typically use embedding tables for sparse features, dense feature processing, feature interaction, and an MLP prediction tower. They are common in large-scale click and conversion prediction. When deep learning may not help . Deep models are not always better. Simpler models may win when: . | Data is sparse. | The dataset is small. | Features are homogeneous. | Latency constraints are strict. | Interpretability is essential. | A well-tuned linear or tree model already captures the available signal. | .

522.title: Graph neural networks
522.content: Graph representation . A recommendation graph may contain: . | User nodes. | Item nodes. | Creator or seller nodes. | Category nodes. | Query nodes. | Interaction edges. | Purchase, click, follow, or friendship edges. | . A user-item system is often represented as a bipartite graph. User A -------- Item 1 | | +---------- Item 2 User B -------- Item 2 | +---------- Item 3 . Message passing . A generic graph-convolution layer aggregates neighbor information: . \[\mathbf{h}_v^{(l+1)} = \phi\left( W_0^{(l)}\mathbf{h}_v^{(l)} + \text{AGG}_{u\in\mathcal{N}(v)} W_1^{(l)}\mathbf{h}_u^{(l)} \right)\] where $\mathcal{N}(v)$ is the neighborhood of node $v$. The process consists of: . | Compute messages. | Aggregate messages. | Transform the aggregate. | Update the node representation. | Repeat across layers. | . GCNs, GATs, and GraphSAGE . | Architecture | Main idea | RecSys value | . | GCN | Aggregate neighborhood features | Captures relational structure | . | GAT | Learn attention weights over neighbors | Focuses on important relationships | . | GraphSAGE | Sample and aggregate neighbors | Supports scalable and inductive learning | . | Edge-aware GNN | Uses edge attributes in message passing | Models interaction type and strength | . GraphSAGE is particularly useful for new nodes because it can generate representations from features and sampled neighborhoods rather than requiring a learned vector for every node. Graph losses . Possible objectives include: . | Node classification loss. | Link-prediction binary cross-entropy. | Pairwise ranking loss. | Triplet loss. | Graph reconstruction loss. | Regularization losses. | . For a positive user-item edge and a negative sampled edge: . \[\mathcal{L}_{\text{margin}} = \max\left(0, m - s(u,i^+) + s(u,i^-) \right)\] where $m$ is a margin. Graph recommender workflow . User-item events | v Construct graph | v Sample neighborhoods | v Run message passing | v Generate user/item embeddings | v Score unseen edges | v Retrieve and rank items . Industry patterns . Graph-based recommendation is useful for: . | Social friend and story ranking. | Item discovery. | Food and restaurant recommendations. | Related content. | Pinterest-style visual discovery. | Search and entity relationships. | . Graph models can improve relational understanding, but they also introduce costs related to graph storage, neighborhood sampling, freshness, and distributed training.

523.title: Transformers and sequential recommendation
523.content: Why sequences matter . A user’s recent actions may reveal short-term intent that differs from long-term preferences. Order, timing, and the relationship between events can therefore matter. Pooling treats events as an unordered collection. Sequential models can represent: . | Recency. | Repeated patterns. | Session intent. | Transition probabilities. | Long-range dependencies. | . Transformer self-attention . For queries $Q$, keys $K$, and values $V$, scaled dot-product attention is: . \[\text{Attention}(Q,K,V) = \text{softmax}\left(\frac{QK^{\top}}{\sqrt{d_k}}\right)V\] Self-attention allows an event to use information from other events in the sequence. Sequential recommendation pipeline . Ordered interaction history | v +--------------------------+ | Item and event embeddings| +--------------------------+ | v +--------------------------+ | Positional or temporal | information | +--------------------------+ | v +--------------------------+ | Transformer encoder | +--------------------------+ | v +--------------------------+ | User or session vector | +--------------------------+ | v +--------------------------+ | Candidate scoring | +--------------------------+ . RNNs and GRUs . RNNs and GRUs process event sequences recurrently. They can be effective for short sessions but have sequential computation and may struggle with long histories. Behavioral Sequence Transformer . A ranking model can condition on a user’s behavior sequence and a target item, predicting the probability of engagement. The target item can be marked or included alongside the historical sequence. Multimodal and multitask Transformers . Modern systems may combine: . | Text embeddings. | Image embeddings. | Audio embeddings. | Product or item metadata. | User history. | Search queries. | Multiple engagement labels. | . Multitask training can improve sparse objectives by sharing representations across clicks, saves, purchases, and other events.

524.title: Multi-armed and contextual bandits
524.content: Multi-armed bandit problem . A bandit chooses an action from a set of arms and observes a reward. The objective is to maximize cumulative reward while balancing exploration and exploitation. \[\max \mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{t=1}^{T} r_t\right]\] Regret compares the reward obtained with the reward that would have been obtained by always choosing the best action. Epsilon-greedy . With probability $\epsilon$, choose an exploratory action. With probability $1-\epsilon$, choose the action with the highest estimated reward. Upper confidence bound . UCB selects an action using both estimated reward and uncertainty: . \[\text{UCB}_i(t) = \hat{\mu}_i(t) + c\sqrt{\frac{\ln t}{n_i(t)} }\] where $n_i(t)$ is the number of times arm $i$ has been selected.
