Thompson sampling . Thompson sampling maintains a posterior distribution over each arm’s reward and samples from those posteriors to select actions. Contextual bandits . Contextual bandits condition the action choice on user and environment context: . \[a_t = \pi(x_t)\] where $x_t$ may include: . | User attributes. | Device. | Time. | Location. | Recent history. | Item context. | . Contextual bandits are useful when different users respond differently to the same candidate. Bandits in recommendation systems . Bandits can be used for: . | Exploration of long-tail items. | Personalization. | Testing variants. | Recommendation explanations. | Artwork selection. | Cuisine discovery. | Dynamic content selection. | Cold-start items. | . Off-policy evaluation . Historical logs are generated by an old policy, but the goal is to estimate a new policy. Inverse propensity scoring can estimate counterfactual reward when exposure probabilities are known or estimated: . \[\hat{V}_{\text{IPS}}(\pi) = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{t=1}^{N} \frac{\mathbb{1}[a_t = \pi(x_t)]r_t} {p(a_t\mid x_t)}\] High variance is a major challenge. Self-normalized and doubly robust estimators can reduce some problems. Bandits versus A/B testing . | Property | A/B testing | Bandit testing | . | Allocation | Usually fixed | Adapts over time | . | Interpretation | Straightforward | More complex | . | Exploration | Controlled by experiment design | Built into policy | . | Underperforming variants | Continue receiving assigned traffic | Can receive less traffic | . | Best use | Clear statistical comparison | Continuous adaptation and personalization | .

525.title: Multi-objective optimization
525.content: A recommender may need to optimize several objectives: . | Relevance. | Engagement. | Diversity. | Freshness. | Creator coverage. | Revenue. | Long-term retention. | Safety. | Fairness. | . These objectives can conflict. Multi-objective optimization seeks Pareto-optimal trade-offs: improving one objective further would worsen at least one other objective. A weighted model may be written as: . \[S(i) = \sum_{j=1}^{m} w_j s_j(i)\] where $s_j$ are objective-specific scores and $w_j$ are tunable weights. Constrained optimization . A primary metric can be optimized subject to guardrails: . \[\max_x m_1(x)\] subject to: . \[m_j(x) \ge c_j, \quad j=2,\dots,m\] or, for safety constraints: . \[\text{violation}(x) \le \epsilon\] MOO versus MAB . | Concept | Multi-objective optimization | Multi-armed bandit | . | Core problem | Balance conflicting objectives | Explore and exploit uncertain actions | . | Typical setting | Static or periodically tuned | Sequential and adaptive | . | Output | Pareto set or weighted policy | Action-selection policy | . | Example | Relevance versus diversity | Explore new items versus exploit known items | .

526.title: Generative recommendation and LLMs
526.content: The generative shift . Traditional recommenders score or rank known items. Generative recommenders model recommendation as conditional generation: . \[\hat{y} = \arg\max_{y} p(y \mid C)\] where $C$ includes user history, context, item metadata, queries, or retrieved information. The generated output may be: . | An item identifier. | A sequence of item identifiers. | A semantic item ID. | A natural-language explanation. | A conversational recommendation. | A multimodal recommendation artifact. | . Semantic IDs . Semantic IDs represent items as sequences of discrete codes derived from content embeddings, often through residual vector quantization. Item content | v Dense item embedding | v Residual quantization | v Semantic ID tokens | v Autoregressive recommendation model . A Semantic ID can be represented as: . \[\text{SID}(i) = (c_1,c_2,\dots,c_L)\] where each $c_l$ is selected from a learned codebook. Semantic IDs may improve generalization to new or long-tail items because related items can share code structure. Hybrid dense-generative systems . A practical architecture may combine dense retrieval with an LLM or generative ranker: . User context | +----------------------+ | v v Dense retrieval Context and metadata | +----------+-----------+ v Candidate set | v Generative ranker | v Explanation and slate . Retrieval provides grounding and scalability. Generative models provide contextual reasoning, explanation, and flexible interaction. Retrieval-augmented recommendation . A retrieval-augmented recommender retrieves relevant catalog, profile, or policy context before generating a recommendation or explanation. This can reduce hallucination and improve factual grounding, but it introduces: . | Additional latency. | Retrieval-quality dependence. | Context-window constraints. | Privacy and authorization requirements. | More complex evaluation. | . LLM use cases in recommendation . LLMs may support: . | Query understanding. | Catalog enrichment. | Item summarization. | Natural-language explanations. | Conversational preference elicitation. | Cold-start item representation. | Cross-domain transfer. | Semantic ID generation. | Agentic recommendation workflows. | . LLMs should not replace all specialized models automatically. A production design must consider latency, cost, controllability, privacy, and the need for exact catalog grounding.

527.title: Production challenges
527.content: Offline-online mismatch . A model can improve offline metrics but perform worse online because of: . | Distribution shift. | Exposure bias. | Metric misalignment. | Training-serving skew. | Feedback loops. | User adaptation. | Latency or timeout behavior. | Differences in candidate availability. | . Reproducibility . Reproducible training requires versioning: . | Code. | Data. | Features. | Dependencies. | Random seeds. | Model configurations. | Training environment. | Evaluation scripts. | . Model freshness . User preferences and item popularity change. Systems may use: . | Periodic retraining. | Incremental updates. | Online learning. | Streaming features. | Time-decay features. | Bandit exploration. | . Latency . Latency can be improved through: . | Smaller first-stage models. | ANN retrieval. | Caching. | Batching. | Parallel candidate generators. | Quantization. | Distillation. | Feature precomputation. | Asynchronous enrichment. | Efficient serving infrastructure. | . Feature and model failures . A new feature can reduce performance if it introduces noise, leakage, or a mismatch with the target objective. Feature changes should be tested offline and online, with slice analysis and rollback capability. Monitoring . Production monitoring should cover: . | Request latency. | Candidate counts. | Ranking distributions. | Feature missingness. | Model scores. | Calibration. | Engagement. | Long-term retention. | Safety violations. | Fairness slices. | Popularity and creator exposure. | Drift and data quality. | .

528.title: Research-paper map
528.content: The supplied paper collection covers several influential production and research directions. | Area | Representative work or system | Main idea | . | Candidate generation | YouTube recommendations | Separate retrieval and ranking neural networks | . | Feature interaction | Wide and Deep | Memorization plus generalization | . | Neural CF | NCF | Replace matrix-factorization interaction with an MLP | . | Sequential recommendation | Behavior Sequence Transformer | Model behavior history with self-attention | . | Generative retrieval | TIGER | Generate Semantic IDs for retrieval | . | Graph recommendation | PinSage | Scalable graph convolution for item embeddings | . | Large-scale graph recommendation | Pixie | Random walks over a very large object graph | . | Social recommendation | GraFRank and ELR | Model multimodal and edge-contextual relationships | . | Search and recommendation | Netflix systems | Combine ranking, search, evidence, and page generation | . | Marketplace recommendation | DoorDash | Combine relevance, diversity, location, and cold start | . | Real-time recommendation | Monolith | Real-time training and collisionless embedding tables | . | Multimodal product representation | ItemSage | Combine text and image information for item embeddings | . | Generative recommendation | PLUM and related work | Adapt language-model-style generation to recommendation | . Research reading strategy . Read papers according to the part of the system they address: . | Start with a two-stage production architecture. | Study embeddings and matrix factorization. | Study feature-interaction architectures. | Study sequential and graph models. | Study re-ranking, bias, and evaluation. | Study bandits and counterfactual evaluation. | Study semantic IDs and generative retrieval. | .

529.content: The following design combines the main ideas covered in the source collection. +------------------------------------------------------------------+ | | | v v v v v +------------------------------------------------------------------+ | Validation, Cleaning, Joining, Labeling, and Feature Generation | +------------------------------------------------------------------+ | | | v v v v v +------------------------------------------------------------------+ | Embeddings | Feature Store | Popularity | Moderation | Policies | +------------------------------------------------------------------+ | | | +----------+-------------+-----------+----------+ | v +------------------------------------------------------------------+ | Model Training: Retrieval, Ranking, Calibration, Bandits, MOO | +------------------------------------------------------------------+ | v +------------------------------------------------------------------+ | ANN Indices | Model Registry | Calibration Maps | Configurations | +------------------------------------------------------------------+ | v ONLINE REQUEST +------------------------------------------------------------------+ | User, Query, Device, Location, Session, Time, and Authorization | +------------------------------------------------------------------+ | v +------------------------------------------------------------------+ | Candidate Re-ranking, Diversity, Freshness, Fairness, MOO | +------------------------------------------------------------------+ | v +------------------------------------------------------------------+ | Final System contracts . Each stage should expose clear contracts: . | Stage | Input | Output | Main quality requirement | . | Candidate generation | User and context | Broad candidate set | High recall and low latency | . | Filtering | Candidates and policy context | Eligible candidates | Safety and correctness | . | Ranking | Candidates and features | Scored candidates | Predictive quality and calibration | . | Re-ranking | Scores and constraints | Ordered slate | Diversity, fairness, freshness | . | Serving | Slate and presentation context | User response | Latency and reliability | . | Logging | Exposure and outcomes | Training and evaluation data | Causal and audit quality | .

530.title: Implementation blueprint
530.content: Phase 1: Define the product objective . Write down: . | What users are trying to accomplish. | What an item means in the product. | What successful interaction means. | Which outcomes are short-term. | Which outcomes are long-term. | Which outcomes must be prevented. | Which stakeholders require coverage or fairness. | . Phase 2: Build a baseline . Start with simple baselines: . | Global popularity. | Segment popularity. | Recently popular items. | Item-to-item co-occurrence. | Logistic regression. | Matrix factorization. | Simple content similarity. | . A baseline provides a reference for complexity and failure analysis. Phase 3: Build the data pipeline . Implement: . | Event collection. | Catalog ingestion. | Identity resolution. | Time-aware joins. | Feature computation. | Negative sampling. | Training and validation splits. | Data-quality checks. | Versioned datasets. | . Phase 4: Add candidate generators . Use multiple generators: . | Collaborative filtering. | Content-based retrieval. | Two-tower ANN retrieval. | Popularity and trending. | Search-derived candidates. | Exploration candidates. | . Track candidate-source coverage and per-source recall. Phase 5: Add ranking . Begin with a simple calibrated model, then add complexity only when needed. Evaluate: . | Log loss. | AUC. | NDCG. | MRR. | Recall at candidate cutoffs. | Slice-level metrics. | Calibration. | . Phase 6: Add re-ranking and guardrails . Implement: . | Deduplication. | Diversity constraints. | Freshness. | Moderation. | Creator or seller coverage. | Geographic and age restrictions. | Fairness checks. | Business rules. | . Phase 7: Run online experiments . Use a controlled rollout with: . | Primary metrics. | Guardrail metrics. | User segmentation. | Minimum sample size. | Rollback conditions. | Monitoring dashboards. | Experiment documentation. | . Phase 8: Improve adaptivity . Consider: . | Contextual bandits. | Online features. | Incremental embeddings. | Sequence models. | Graph representations. | Multi-objective tuning. | Generative or conversational layers. | . Phase 9: Productionize . Add: . | Model registry. | Feature and schema versioning. | Shadow testing. | Canary deployment. | Latency budgets. | Fallback models. | Monitoring and alerting. | Audit logs. | Privacy controls. | Incident response. | .

531.title: Final technical takeaways
531.content: . | A production recommender is usually a funnel, not a single model. | Retrieval optimizes broad coverage and latency; ranking optimizes precision and utility. | Re-ranking is where diversity, freshness, fairness, moderation, and business constraints can be enforced explicitly. | Collaborative filtering discovers behavior-based relationships but is vulnerable to sparsity and cold start. | Content-based representations help new items but can over-specialize. | Two-tower models and ANN indices make large-scale retrieval practical. | Ranking objectives must be chosen carefully because optimizing clicks, watch time, or revenue alone can create harmful behavior. | Calibration matters whenever predicted probabilities drive downstream decisions. | Search and recommendation increasingly share lexical, semantic, and hybrid retrieval infrastructure. | Offline metrics are necessary but cannot replace online experimentation. | Logged interaction data is biased by exposure, position, popularity, and previous policies. | Counterfactual methods, randomized exposure, and contextual bandits help address feedback loops. | Cold-start handling requires content, context, exploration, onboarding, or knowledge-based strategies. | Wide and Deep, Factorization Machines, DeepFM, DCN, DLRM, and NCF represent different ways to model feature interactions. | Graph neural networks exploit relationships among users, items, and interactions. | Transformers model ordered behavior and long-range dependencies. | Multi-objective optimization is needed when relevance, diversity, safety, fairness, and business value conflict. | Generative recommendation reframes retrieval and ranking as conditional generation, often using semantic item identifiers. | LLMs can support query understanding, metadata enrichment, explanations, conversational preference elicitation, and generative retrieval, but production deployment still requires grounding, latency control, and evaluation. | The best practical system is usually the simplest architecture that meets the product’s quality, latency, safety, and operational requirements. | .

533.doc: Recommendation, Search, Retrieval, and Ranking in 2026
533.title: Recommendation, Search, Retrieval, and Ranking: Modern Architectures for Relevant AI Systems (in late 2026)
533.content: Primary references: . | Bypassing inference bottlenecks: Accelerating complex AI search with Retrieve-for-Train | Make Retrieval / Search More Relevant With An LLM | GenRec: Towards LLM-Native Recommendation at Netflix | . Modern search and recommendation systems are moving beyond a single embedding similarity score. Production systems increasingly combine structured query understanding, hard metadata filtering, semantic retrieval, learned ranking, catalog constraints, and personalization. This document covers three complementary patterns: . | Retrieve-for-Train: compile expensive retrieval reasoning into a lightweight, single-pass retriever. | Search-expert: convert natural-language queries into structured filters before semantic retrieval. | GenRec: use an LLM-backed ranker with catalog-aware scoring for large-scale recommendation. | . A note on source coverage: the ACM paper, several arXiv papers, LinkedIn engineering posts, Pinterest and Instacart posts, Spotify research, and Perplexity Photon links provided could not be fully verified from their primary pages in this pass. This document therefore focuses in depth on the three accessible primary sources above and treats the remaining links as a reading list rather than as verified technical claims.

534.doc: Recommendation, Search, Retrieval, and Ranking in 2026
534.title: Part 1: Foundations

535.doc: Recommendation, Search, Retrieval, and Ranking in 2026
535.title: Search versus recommendation
535.content: Search and recommendation solve related but different problems. | Dimension | Search | Recommendation | . | Primary input | Explicit user query | User history, context, and candidate inventory | . | Primary goal | Satisfy the stated intent | Maximize long-term user value | . | Typical output | Ranked results for a query | Personalized ranked slate | . | Hard constraints | Often explicit: price, color, availability | Often business or policy constraints | . | Main challenge | Interpreting intent correctly | Balancing relevance, diversity, and long-term satisfaction | . | Feedback signal | Clicks, conversions, reformulations | Plays, watch time, saves, skips, retention | . A search query such as “noise cancelling headphones any colour but black, under $300, with a 4 star rating” contains both semantic intent and hard constraints. A recommendation request may contain no explicit query at all, but must still respect catalog, business, and personalization constraints. sarthakai.substack .

536.doc: Recommendation, Search, Retrieval, and Ranking in 2026
536.title: The modern retrieval stack
536.content: A common production pattern is: . Natural-language query | v +---------------------------+ | Query understanding | - intent | - entities | - filters | - language | - reformulation | +-------------+-------------+ | v +---------------------------+ | Structured pre-filtering | - price | - color | - availability | - category | +-------------+-------------+ | v +---------------------------+ | Semantic retrieval | - vector search | - lexical search | - hybrid retrieval | +-------------+-------------+ | v +---------------------------+ | Ranking / reranking | - relevance | - personalization | - business constraints | - diversity | +-------------+-------------+ | v Ranked results . This pipeline separates concerns: . | Query understanding decides what the user means. | Filtering enforces non-negotiable constraints. | Retrieval finds semantically relevant candidates. | Ranking orders candidates using relevance, personalization, and business objectives. | . Search-expert frames this as structured pre-filtering followed by approximate nearest-neighbor vector search and a learning-to-rank reranker. sarthakai.substack .

537.doc: Recommendation, Search, Retrieval, and Ranking in 2026
537.title: Part 2: Query Understanding as Structured Extraction

538.doc: Recommendation, Search, Retrieval, and Ranking in 2026
538.title: The problem
538.content: Natural-language queries often contain implicit filters that a semantic retriever may treat as soft preferences rather than hard rules. For example: . noise cancelling headphones any colour but black, under $200 and over 4 stars . A pure vector-search system may return semantically similar headphones that are black, cost more than $200, or have a rating below 4 stars. The embeddings capture meaning, but they do not naturally enforce constraints. Search-expert addresses this by converting the query into structured fields before retrieval: . { "product": "headphones", "feature": "noise cancelling", "color": ["ne:black"], "price": "lt:200", "rating": "gte:4" } . The structured output uses explicit operators such as lt:, gte:, ne:, and between:100:200, so downstream systems can translate it into filters for Elasticsearch, SQL, ChromaDB, Pinecone, or another backend. sarthakai.substack .

539.doc: Recommendation, Search, Retrieval, and Ranking in 2026
539.title: Why structured extraction matters
539.content: Structured extraction enables a hybrid retrieval pipeline: . Natural-language query | v Structured extraction | v Hard metadata filters | v Vector search within filtered candidates | v Semantic ranking | v Ranked results . The hard filters ensure that a $400 product is not returned when the user asked for “under $200.” Vector search then ranks the surviving candidates by semantic relevance. sarthakai.substack .

540.doc: Recommendation, Search, Retrieval, and Ranking in 2026
540.title: Search-expert design
540.content: Search-expert is an 800M-parameter small language model, search-expert-json-0.8b, fine-tuned from Qwen3.5-0.8B using LoRA. It converts a natural-language search query into structured JSON. sarthakai.substack . | Property | Value | . | Base model | Qwen3.5-0.8B | . | Model size | 800M parameters | . | Fine-tuning method | LoRA | . | LoRA rank | 16 | . | LoRA alpha | 16 | . | Trainable parameters | 0.74% | . | Quantization | 4-bit NF4 | . | Approximate VRAM footprint | 1–2 GB | . | Training framework | Unsloth FastLanguageModel | . | Training data | 100,000 synthetic query-structured-output pairs | . | Domains | E-commerce, real estate, flights, hotels, jobs, cars, restaurants, movies, healthcare, courses | . | Reported key F1 | 0.913 | . | Reported parse rate | 98.2% | . The model is trained to output only fields explicitly present in the query, reducing hallucinated fields. A separate LoRA adapter is trained for each serialization format, such as JSON or YAML. sarthakai.substack .

541.doc: Recommendation, Search, Retrieval, and Ranking in 2026
541.title: Training configuration
541.content: The published training setup uses: sarthakai.substack . Effective batch size: 16 Per-device batch size: 8 Gradient accumulation: 2 Training steps: 300 Learning-rate schedule: Cosine Warmup steps: 100 Peak learning rate: 2e-4 Optimizer: AdamW 8-bit Maximum sequence length: 512 tokens Sequence packing: Enabled . LoRA adapters are injected into: . q_proj k_proj v_proj o_proj gate_proj up_proj down_proj . This is a practical demonstration that a small, domain-specialized model can perform constrained structured extraction reliably. The author explicitly argues that the task is bounded enough that a purpose-trained small model can outperform a general-purpose large model in cost, speed, and consistency. sarthakai.substack .

542.doc: Recommendation, Search, Retrieval, and Ranking in 2026
542.title: Constraint-satisfaction benchmark
542.content: Search-expert was evaluated on 25 complex, multi-constraint Amazon search queries. The evaluation measured whether the top six results satisfied the user’s hard constraints. sarthakai.substack . | Pipeline | Overall constraint satisfaction | Perfect@6 | . | Hybrid: search-expert plus filtered vector search | 1.00 | 1.00 | . | Amazon search | 0.76 | 0.42 | . | Pure vector search | 0.56 | 0.21 | . The hybrid pipeline achieved perfect price satisfaction, color exclusion, and color match across the evaluated queries. Pure vector search performed worst because embedding similarity treats constraints such as color and price as soft semantic signals rather than enforceable rules. sarthakai.substack . These results are specific to the author’s benchmark, query set, product pool, and retrieval configuration. They should not be generalized as universal superiority over any production search engine.

543.doc: Recommendation, Search, Retrieval, and Ranking in 2026
543.title: Text-to-SQL versus semantic search
543.content: Search-expert draws an important distinction: . | Approach | Strength | Limitation | . | Text-to-SQL | Exact lookup over structured data | Does not rank by semantic relevance | . | Pure vector search | Understands unstructured meaning | Treats hard constraints as soft signals | . | Hybrid retrieval | Enforces constraints, then ranks semantically | Requires query understanding and more infrastructure | . The production pattern is therefore: . structured extraction → hard metadata filters → vector search within filtered set → semantic ranking . Search is not merely “which rows match?” It is “which items are most relevant?” Relevance includes both structured constraints and unstructured meaning. sarthakai.substack .

544.doc: Recommendation, Search, Retrieval, and Ranking in 2026
544.title: Part 3: Retrieve-for-Train

545.doc: Recommendation, Search, Retrieval, and Ranking in 2026
545.title: The inference bottleneck
545.content: Complex AI search often requires query fan-out: breaking one broad prompt into several related sub-queries to retrieve a coherent set of results. For example, a query such as “camping gear” should not return ten slight variations of four-person tents. It should return a complementary slate: a tent, sleeping bag, portable stove, and headlamp. research . Google Research identifies two problems with using a general LLM for this at inference time: . | Paraphrastic collapse: the model generates near-synonymous queries instead of complementary facets. | Autoregressive latency: the model spends a large thinking budget generating intermediate reasoning tokens before producing search terms. research | . For example, given “Bohemian festival style,” a zero-shot LLM may generate: . - bohemian festival fashion - bohemian festival clothes . These are redundant paraphrases. A more useful fan-out might include distinct facets such as: . - fringe jackets - crochet dresses - suede boots . The second set covers complementary dimensions of the original intent. research .

546.doc: Recommendation, Search, Retrieval, and Ranking in 2026
546.title: Retrieve-for-Train idea
546.content: Retrieve-for-Train moves the expensive exploration offline. Instead of forcing an LLM to reason at inference time, it uses offline reinforcement learning once to learn reward-aligned query fan-outs, then distills that behavior into a lightweight retriever. research . Broad query | v +---------------------------+ | Fan-out language model | Trained once with RL | +-------------+-------------+ | v +---------------------------+ | Supervision synthesis | query -> target-set pairs | +-------------+-------------+ | v +---------------------------+ | Diffusion retriever | Single-pass fan-out | +-------------+-------------+ | v Set of target embeddings . This is a conceptual reconstruction of the three-step framework described by Google Research. research .

547.doc: Recommendation, Search, Retrieval, and Ranking in 2026
547.title: Three-stage pipeline
547.content: | Stage | Purpose | Output | . | Fan-out language model training | Learn property-aligned sub-queries with reinforcement learning | Fan-out language model | . | Supervision synthesis | Generate query-to-target-set pairs offline | Supervision data | . | Diffusive retriever training | Learn to map query embeddings to target embeddings | Lightweight diffusion retriever | . The fan-out language models used were 4B open-source models: Gemma3-4B and Qwen3-4B. Each generated exactly 10 sub-queries for every main search prompt. research . The final diffusion retriever has 53.9M parameters and maps a query embedding directly to a complete set of target embeddings in one non-autoregressive pass. research .

548.doc: Recommendation, Search, Retrieval, and Ranking in 2026
548.title: Set-level rewards
548.content: Traditional learning-to-rank evaluates items independently. Retrieve-for-Train optimizes properties that exist only at the set level. The composite reward balances: research . | Property | Meaning | Failure it prevents | . | Groundedness | Generated sub-queries correspond to retrievable database items | Nonsense strings that exploit embedding coordinates | . | Diversity | The sub-query set covers broad semantic breadth | Repetitive paraphrases | . | Alignment | Sub-queries remain related to the original prompt | Semantic drift | . Diversity is measured using the Vendi Score over the entire set of sub-queries. research . These rewards act as mutual counter-anchors: . | Groundedness alone can reward degenerate strings. | Alignment alone can reward repetitive paraphrases. | Diversity forces the model to explore distinct, useful directions. research | .

549.doc: Recommendation, Search, Retrieval, and Ranking in 2026
549.title: Training method
549.content: Google Research uses Soft-GRPO, combining group relative policy optimization with soft proximal policy optimization regularization. The fan-out language model is optimized against the composite reward. research . The important architectural insight is that reinforcement learning is used as a one-time objective transducer, not as an online inference engine. The expensive reward-driven exploration happens during training; the deployed retriever performs a fast single-pass mapping. research .

550.doc: Recommendation, Search, Retrieval, and Ranking in 2026
550.title: Results
550.content: Retrieve-for-Train was evaluated on: . | Open-ended abstract retrieval, where quality is measured by set-level properties such as diversity, alignment, and groundedness. | Weakly supervised compositional retrieval, where queries are paired with a weak reference set. research | . The evaluation used: . | A fashion dataset of user-curated outfits, evaluated with a CLIP-based retriever. | A proprietary industrial dataset of expert-generated music playlists, evaluated with MuLan. research | . Reported results: . | Outcome | Retrieve-for-Train result | . | Retrieval quality | Outperformed single-query search, zero-shot expansion, and Best-of-N baselines | . | Inference speed | 12 to 20 times faster than autoregressive approaches | . | Large-batch latency | Autoregressive fan-out approached 50 seconds; diffusion remained sub-second to a few seconds | . | Model size | Final diffusion retriever: 53.9M parameters | . | Fan-out models | Gemma3-4B and Qwen3-4B | . | Sub-queries per prompt | 10 | . These results are from Google Research’s described experiments and should be interpreted in the context of their datasets, embedding backbones, and retrieval tasks. research .

551.doc: Recommendation, Search, Retrieval, and Ranking in 2026
551.title: Why this matters
551.content: Retrieve-for-Train shows that expensive reasoning does not need to happen at inference time. A system can use a large model and reinforcement learning offline to discover good behavior, then compile that behavior into a much smaller, faster model. This is analogous to using a teacher model offline and deploying a student model online: . Large reasoner + reward model | offline training v Compact retriever | online inference v Fast, property-aligned retrieval .

552.doc: Recommendation, Search, Retrieval, and Ranking in 2026
552.title: Part 4: GenRec and LLM-Native Recommendation

553.doc: Recommendation, Search, Retrieval, and Ranking in 2026
553.title: The recommendation problem
553.content: Netflix’s GenRec addresses full-catalog ranking: given a user $u$, interaction history $H$, current context $\tau$, and time $t$, produce a ranking $\pi$ over catalog items $C$. netflixtechblog . Formally: . \[(u, \tau, t, H) \rightarrow \pi\] where $\pi(i)$ is the position assigned to item $i$. The objective is expected long-term member utility, not merely short-term engagement. netflixtechblog .

554.doc: Recommendation, Search, Retrieval, and Ranking in 2026
554.title: Why traditional recommenders become complex
554.content: Netflix describes its prior production stack as relying on thousands of hand-crafted features over users, items, and interactions, plus specialized architectures for sequence modeling, feature interactions, and multi-task objectives. Adding a new content type or surface can require substantial feature engineering, architecture change, infrastructure work, and experimentation. netflixtechblog . LLMs offer a different approach: represent user histories and item metadata as text, capture relationships in a shared semantic space, and steer behavior through natural-language prompts. netflixtechblog . However, off-the-shelf LLMs are not production recommenders. Netflix identifies four issues: . | Over-recommending globally popular content. | Hallucinating out-of-catalog items. | Ignoring business constraints. | Providing limited personalization. netflixtechblog | .

555.doc: Recommendation, Search, Retrieval, and Ranking in 2026
555.title: GenRec architecture
555.content: GenRec is an LLM-backed recommendation ranker. It post-trains an internal foundation LLM on Netflix-specific data and objectives, then adds a catalog-aware scoring head. netflixtechblog . User history + context + item metadata | v [ Verbalized context ] | v [ Foundation LLM backbone ] | v [ Catalog-aware scoring head ] | v In-catalog item scores | v Personalized ranking . At inference time, GenRec feeds verbalized context into the model and applies the catalog-aware scoring head. It does not decode assistant messages. The conversational format is primarily a training-time device to preserve language understanding. netflixtechblog .

556.doc: Recommendation, Search, Retrieval, and Ranking in 2026
556.title: Two-phase training
556.content: GenRec uses a two-phase framework. netflixtechblog . | Phase | Purpose | Update frequency | . | Phase 1 | Adapt an open-source LLM on proprietary corpora to create a domain-aware backbone | Relatively infrequent | . | Phase 2 | Post-train the backbone on ranking-specific data and objectives | More frequent | . Netflix members generate hundreds of billions of interaction events across surfaces, including views, plays, durations, thumbs up or down, add-to-list actions, and abandons. These logs are converted into single-turn or multi-turn conversations between a user and a recommender. netflixtechblog .

557.doc: Recommendation, Search, Retrieval, and Ranking in 2026
557.title: Context engineering
557.content: Naively verbalizing every interaction would exceed the token budget. Netflix treats the context window as a new feature budget and applies context engineering. netflixtechblog . The approach is: . | Prioritize recent, high-signal history. | Compress or drop older history. | Structure prompts to maximize shared prefixes. | Enable better prefix caching. | Preserve ranking quality while reducing serving cost. netflixtechblog | . In experiments, Netflix reduced context tokens to roughly one-third of the original budget with negligible degradation in offline ranking metrics. Because serving cost is approximately proportional to context length, serving cost fell similarly. netflixtechblog .

558.doc: Recommendation, Search, Retrieval, and Ranking in 2026
558.title: Training objectives
558.content: GenRec uses a multi-objective loss combining: netflixtechblog . | A recommendation ranking objective. | Language-modeling objectives. | Alignment through reward-weighted training. | . The ranking objective uses cross-entropy over the catalog or candidate set. Positives are derived from high-value engagements, such as sufficiently long plays or strong explicit feedback, with thresholds and denoising logic. netflixtechblog . The language-modeling objective preserves general language understanding and keeps open the possibility of text-generation use cases such as recommendation explanations. netflixtechblog .

559.doc: Recommendation, Search, Retrieval, and Ranking in 2026
559.title: Reward-weighted alignment
559.content: Training only on raw interaction sequences can cause undesirable behavior, such as over-favoring binge-watching or over-focusing on one content type. GenRec weights the ranking loss using signals from separate reward models. netflixtechblog . \[\mathcal{L}_{weighted} = w_i \cdot \mathcal{L}_{ranking}^{(i)}\] where: . | $w_i$ is a scalar reward-derived weight for example $i$. | $\mathcal{L}_{ranking}^{(i)}$ is the ranking loss for that example. | . High-value engagements receive larger weights; low-value engagements are down-weighted. Netflix describes this as simpler and more cost-efficient than full reinforcement learning, while noting that RL-style methods such as GRPO produced additional gains but were deferred due to cost. netflixtechblog .

560.doc: Recommendation, Search, Retrieval, and Ranking in 2026
560.title: Catalog-aware scoring
560.content: GenRec’s architecture follows its foundation LLM: a decoder-only transformer trained with next-token-prediction-style objectives, augmented with a catalog-aware ranking head. The scoring head scores only in-catalog items. netflixtechblog . For very large catalogs, sampled softmax or candidate sets can make training and inference efficient. This constrains recommendations to the catalog while supporting efficient scoring over large candidate sets. netflixtechblog .

561.doc: Recommendation, Search, Retrieval, and Ranking in 2026
561.title: Results
561.content: Netflix reports: netflixtechblog . | Evaluation | Result | . | Offline ranking | GenRec outperformed the production ranker despite fewer input signals and labeled examples | . | Data efficiency | About 40 times fewer Phase-2 labeled examples | . | Offline MRR | About +1.6% improvement | . | Online test | Statistically significant short-term and long-term gains | . | Traffic coverage | About 10% of Netflix traffic | . | Test duration | About 4 weeks | . These results apply to Netflix’s production baseline, traffic, catalog, and evaluation setup. They demonstrate the potential of LLM-backed rankers, not a universal guarantee that an LLM ranker will outperform every existing recommender. netflixtechblog .

562.doc: Recommendation, Search, Retrieval, and Ranking in 2026
562.title: The broader shift
562.content: Netflix frames GenRec as a shift from feature engineering to context engineering. netflixtechblog . | Traditional RecSys | LLM-native RecSys | . | Dense feature vectors | Verbalized textual context | . | Hand-crafted features | Context construction from logs and metadata | . | Task-specific architectures | Shared foundation backbone | . | Sparse IDs and custom objectives | Data, verbalization, objectives, and rewards | . | Classic RecSys infrastructure | LLM-style GPU infrastructure, batching, and caching | . The prompt becomes a new kind of feature vector. Modeling effort shifts from designing features to deciding which signals to include, how far back in time to go, and how to compress history within a token budget. netflixtechblog .

563.doc: Recommendation, Search, Retrieval, and Ranking in 2026
563.title: Part 5: Cross-Cutting Design Patterns

564.doc: Recommendation, Search, Retrieval, and Ranking in 2026
564.title: Pattern 1: Separate hard constraints from soft relevance
564.content: A semantic model should not be responsible for enforcing every business rule. User query | +-- hard constraints --> deterministic filters | +-- semantic intent ---> vector retrieval | +-- ranking signals ---> learned ranker . Search-expert demonstrates this clearly: structured extraction enables hard filtering before semantic ranking. sarthakai.substack .

565.doc: Recommendation, Search, Retrieval, and Ranking in 2026
565.title: Pattern 2: Move expensive reasoning offline
565.content: A large model can explore, plan, and optimize during training. The deployed model should be as small and fast as the quality bar allows. Retrieve-for-Train uses offline reinforcement learning to discover good fan-out behavior, then distills it into a 53.9M-parameter diffusion retriever. research .

566.doc: Recommendation, Search, Retrieval, and Ranking in 2026
566.title: Pattern 3: Use catalog-aware constraints
566.content: LLMs can hallucinate out-of-catalog items. Recommendation and search systems should constrain outputs to valid, available, and business-approved candidates. GenRec uses a catalog-aware scoring head that scores only in-catalog items. netflixtechblog .

567.doc: Recommendation, Search, Retrieval, and Ranking in 2026
567.title: Pattern 4: Treat context as a budget
567.content: Long histories improve potential signal but increase cost. Context engineering is the process of choosing, compressing, ordering, and prioritizing context within a token budget. Netflix reduced context tokens to about one-third of the original budget with negligible offline ranking degradation. netflixtechblog .

568.doc: Recommendation, Search, Retrieval, and Ranking in 2026
568.title: Pattern 5: Optimize sets, not just items
568.content: A good result slate is not merely a list of individually relevant items. It should be diverse, complementary, coherent, and grounded. Retrieve-for-Train optimizes set-level properties such as diversity, alignment, and groundedness using a composite reward. research .

569.doc: Recommendation, Search, Retrieval, and Ranking in 2026
569.title: Part 6: Architecture Comparison
569.content: | System | Primary task | Core mechanism | Key innovation | Main trade-off | . | Search-expert | Query understanding | Natural language to structured filters | Small fine-tuned model for constrained extraction | Requires high-quality domain-specific training data | . | Retrieve-for-Train | Set-valued retrieval | RL-trained fan-out distilled into diffusion retriever | Single-pass set-level retrieval | More complex training pipeline | . | GenRec | Recommendation ranking | LLM backbone plus catalog-aware scoring head | Verbalized context and reward-weighted ranking | Higher serving cost and context-management complexity | .

570.doc: Recommendation, Search, Retrieval, and Ranking in 2026
570.title: When to use each pattern
570.content: | Need | Recommended pattern | . | Enforce price, color, rating, or availability constraints | Structured extraction plus hard filtering | . | Improve semantic relevance after filtering | Vector or hybrid retrieval | . | Produce diverse, complementary result slates | Set-level retrieval and fan-out | . | Reduce inference-time reasoning cost | Offline RL plus distillation | . | Rank a large catalog with rich user history | LLM-backed ranker with catalog-aware scoring | . | Control recommendation cost | Context engineering and candidate-set scoring | . | Avoid out-of-catalog hallucination | Catalog-aware scoring head | .

571.doc: Recommendation, Search, Retrieval, and Ranking in 2026
571.title: Part 7: Evaluation

572.doc: Recommendation, Search, Retrieval, and Ranking in 2026
572.title: Retrieval and search metrics
572.content: | Metric | Measures | . | Recall@K | Whether relevant items appear in the top K | . | Precision@K | Whether top K results are relevant | . | MRR | Average reciprocal rank of the first relevant result | . | NDCG@K | Ranked relevance quality | . | Constraint satisfaction | Whether results satisfy explicit user constraints | . | Perfect@K | Whether every result in top K satisfies all applicable constraints | . | Diversity | Semantic breadth of the result set | . | Coverage | Whether the result set covers distinct facets | . Search-expert’s benchmark emphasizes constraint satisfaction and Perfect@6, which are useful when user queries contain non-negotiable filters. sarthakai.substack .

573.doc: Recommendation, Search, Retrieval, and Ranking in 2026
573.title: Recommendation metrics
573.content: | Metric | Measures | . | MRR | Quality of the first relevant recommendation | . | NDCG | Ranked relevance quality | . | Recall@K | Coverage of relevant items | . | Engagement rate | Immediate interaction | . | Long-term retention | Sustained user value | . | Catalog coverage | Breadth of recommended inventory | . | Business-mix compliance | Whether content-type or policy constraints are respected | . GenRec optimizes for expected long-term member utility rather than only short-term engagement. netflixtechblog .

574.doc: Recommendation, Search, Retrieval, and Ranking in 2026
574.title: Offline versus online evaluation
574.content: Offline metrics are necessary but insufficient. A model can improve offline ranking metrics while producing worse long-term user outcomes because of feedback loops, popularity bias, or exposure bias. GenRec was validated with both offline ranking metrics and a large-scale online A/B test covering about 10% of Netflix traffic for roughly four weeks. netflixtechblog .

577.title: Set-valued retrieval
577.content: . | Set-level rewards are harder to define than pointwise relevance. | Diversity objectives can conflict with alignment and groundedness. | Reward hacking is a real risk when optimizing against database geometry. | Diffusion-based retrieval requires appropriate embedding backbones and evaluation infrastructure. | . Google Research found that removing the diversity term allowed the fan-out model to collapse into degenerate strings that exploited vector coordinates. The Vendi Score acted as a counter-anchor. research .

578.title: LLM-native recommendation
578.content: . | LLM rankers can be expensive at scale. | Context length drives both quality and serving cost. | Raw interaction data can reinforce popularity bias or undesirable behavior. | Reward-weighted training is simpler than full RL but may not capture all long-term objectives. | Catalog constraints are essential to prevent out-of-catalog hallucination. | . Netflix explicitly notes that off-the-shelf LLMs often over-recommend popular content, hallucinate out-of-catalog items, ignore business constraints, and provide limited personalization. netflixtechblog .

579.title: Part 9: Practical Design Checklist
579.content: . | Extract hard constraints before semantic retrieval. | Use deterministic filters for price, availability, region, rating, and policy rules. | Use vector or hybrid retrieval for semantic relevance. | Use a reranker for final ordering. | Optimize result sets for diversity and complementarity, not only individual relevance. | Keep expensive reasoning offline when possible. | Distill complex behavior into a small, fast serving model. | Constrain recommendation outputs to the valid catalog. | Verbalize only high-signal context within a token budget. | Use reward weighting to align ranking with long-term value. | Evaluate constraint satisfaction, ranking quality, calibration, latency, cost, and online business metrics. | Run online experiments before replacing a mature production system. | .

Use structured extraction for constraints, retrieval for candidate generation, and ranking for final ordering. | Important efficiency insight: Expensive reasoning can be moved offline and distilled into a much smaller inference model; Retrieve-for-Train distills RL-trained fan-out behavior into a 53.9M-parameter diffusion retriever with a reported 12–20 times speedup. research | Important relevance insight: Vector similarity alone does not enforce hard constraints; structured pre-filtering plus semantic ranking can materially improve constraint satisfaction. sarthakai.substack | Important recommendation insight: LLMs can act as rankers, but they need catalog-aware scoring, business constraints, and carefully engineered context to avoid hallucination and popularity bias. netflixtechblog | Main trade-off: More context, more reasoning, and larger models can improve quality, but they increase latency, cost, and operational complexity. | Broader engineering implication: Treat the prompt, context, candidate set, and reward signal as first-class system components—not merely as implementation details around a model. | .

582.doc: Recommendation, Search, Retrieval, and Ranking in 2026
582.title: Recommendation, Search, Retrieval, and Ranking in 2026

584.title: Part 1: End-to-End System Foundations & Pipeline Architecture
584.content: Modern industrial recommendation engines process item catalogs ranging from millions to billions of candidates in real time. To serve personalized results under tight latency constraints (typically $< 100 \text{ ms}$), production architectures adopt a multi-stage funnel pattern. +-----------------------------------------------------------------------+ | Catalog (10^6 - 10^9 Items) | +-----------------------------------------------------------------------+ | v +-----------------------------------------------------------------------+ | Stage 1: Candidate Generation / Retrieval (Latency: 10-20 ms) | - High Recall, Low Complexity | - Algorithms: Collaborative Filtering, Two-Tower, ANN, Vector Search | -> Reduces pool to: ~10^2 - 10^3 Candidates | +-----------------------------------------------------------------------+ | v +-----------------------------------------------------------------------+ | Stage 2: Ranking / Scoring (Latency: 30-50 ms) | - High Precision, Complex Deep Learning Models | - Algorithms: Wide & Deep, DCN-v2, DLRM, Multi-Task Neural Nets | -> Output: Scored & Ranked List (~50 - 200 Candidates) | +-----------------------------------------------------------------------+ | v +-----------------------------------------------------------------------+ | Stage 3: Re-ranking & Business Logic (Latency: 5-10 ms) | - Constraints: Diversity, Freshness, Fair Distribution, Deduplication| - Multi-Objective Optimization (MOO), Multi-Armed Bandits (MAB) | -> Output: Top-K Filtered Set (~10 - 50 Items) | +-----------------------------------------------------------------------+ | v +-----------------------------------------------------------------------+ | Stage 4: Score Calibration & Page Generation (Latency: 5-10 ms) | - Probabilistic Alignment (Platt Scaling, Isotonic Regression) | - Layout Optimization, Slate Generation, Moderation Filters | -> Final User-Facing Slate / Feed | +-----------------------------------------------------------------------+ . Stage Responsibilities and Trade-Offs . | Funnel Stage | Input Pool | Output Pool | Primary Objective | Key Compute Bottleneck | Model Complexity | . | Candidate Generation | $10^6 - 10^9$ | $10^2 - 10^3$ | Maximize Recall | Vector Index Query / Sublinear Search | Low to Medium | . | Ranking | $10^2 - 10^3$ | $50 - 200$ | Maximize Precision / Engagement (CTR, Conversion) | Deep Neural Network Forward Pass / Cross-Features | High | . | Re-ranking | $50 - 200$ | $10 - 50$ | Optimize Diversity, Novelty, Business Constraints | Dynamic Rules & Multi-Objective Pareto Optimization | Medium | . | Calibration | $10 - 50$ | Top-K Slate | Align raw model scores with true click/conversion probabilities | Univariate function evaluation / Monotonic mapping | Low | .

585.title: Part 2: Candidate Generation & Retrieval Systems
585.content: The retrieval stage narrows down millions of items to hundreds of relevant candidates. Mathematical Notation & Formulation . Let $U$ be the set of users and $I$ be the set of items. The interaction matrix $R \in \mathbb{R}^{\vert{}U\vert{} \times \vert{}I\vert{}}$ contains observed interactions $r_{ui}$ (explicit ratings or implicit actions like clicks and views). Content-Based Filtering . Computes user profile representations $\mathbf{u} \in \mathbb{R}^d$ and item feature vectors $\mathbf{v}_i \in \mathbb{R}^d$ from metadata (text embeddings, genres, categories). Similarity is evaluated via cosine similarity: . \[\text{Sim}(u, i) = \frac{\mathbf{u} \cdot \mathbf{v}_i}{\Vert{}\mathbf{u}\Vert{}_2 \Vert{}\mathbf{v}_i\Vert{}_2}\] . | Advantages: Solves item cold-start for new items with rich metadata; highly interpretable. | Limitations: Overspecialization (“filter bubble”); cannot capture serendipitous preferences. | . Collaborative Filtering (CF) . Relies on historical user-item interactions without requiring explicit domain metadata. Matrix Factorization (MF) . Decomposes the interaction matrix $R$ into lower-rank user embeddings $P \in \mathbb{R}^{\vert{}U\vert{} \times k}$ and item embeddings $Q \in \mathbb{R}^{\vert{}I\vert{} \times k}$, where $k \ll \min(\vert{}U\vert{}, \vert{}I\vert{})$: . \[\hat{r}_{ui} = \mathbf{p}_u^T \mathbf{q}_i\] Objective function with L2 regularization: . \[\min_{P, Q} \sum_{(u, i) \in \mathcal{K}} \left( r_{ui} - \mathbf{p}_u^T \mathbf{q}_i \right)^2 + \lambda \left( \Vert{}\mathbf{p}_u\Vert{}_2^2 + \Vert{}\mathbf{q}_i\Vert{}_2^2 \right)\] Alternating Least Squares (ALS) for Implicit Feedback . For implicit datasets (clicks, watches, reads), preference $p_{ui}$ and confidence $c_{ui}$ are defined as: . \[p_{ui} = \begin{cases} 1 & r_{ui} > 0 \\ 0 & r_{ui} = 0 \end{cases}, \quad c_{ui} = 1 + \alpha r_{ui}\] The cost function is minimized by alternating between updating user vectors $\mathbf{p}_u$ and item vectors $\mathbf{q}_i$: . \[\mathbf{p}_u = \left( Q^T C^u Q + \lambda I \right)^{-1} Q^T C^u p_u\] Two-Tower Neural Retrieval Architectures . Two-Tower models use separate neural subnetworks to project user context and candidate metadata into a shared embedding space $\mathbb{R}^d$. User Context Features Candidate Item Features (User ID, Search Query, (Item ID, Category, Text, Recent History, Location) Image Vectors, Tags) | v v +-----------------------+ +-----------------------+ | User Tower (MLP) | Item Tower (MLP) | +-----------------------+ +-----------------------+ | v v User Vector u in R^d Item Vector v in R^d \ / \ / +--------------------> Dot Product <---------+ | v s(u, v) = u^T v (Cosine / Inner Product) . Loss Formulation: Sampled Softmax with In-Batch Negatives . For a batch of $B$ positive pairs ${(u_j, v_j)}_{j=1}^B$, the in-batch cross-entropy loss with logQ correction for item frequency sampling bias is: . \[\mathcal{L} = -\frac{1}{B} \sum_{j=1}^B \log \frac{\exp\left(s(u_j, v_j) - \log P(v_j)\right)}{\sum_{k=1}^B \exp\left(s(u_j, v_k) - \log P(v_k)\right)}\] Where $P(v_k)$ is the estimated sampling probability of candidate $v_k$.

586.title: Part 3: Deep Neural Network Ranking Architectures
586.content: The ranking stage scores candidate items using complex non-linear feature interactions. +------------------------+ | Output (CTR/pCTR) | +------------------------+ ^ | +--------------------+--------------------+ | +--------------------+ +--------------------+ | Explicit Cross | Deep MLP Layers | Network / Field | (Non-linear | Interactions | Transformations) | +--------------------+ +--------------------+ ^ ^ | +--------------------+--------------------+ | +--------------------------+ | Concatenated Dense | & Sparse Embeddings | +--------------------------+ . Architecture Comparison Matrix . | Architecture | Interaction Explicit/Implicit | Order of Feature Crosses | Sparse Embedding Handling | Best suited for | . | Wide & Deep | Combination (Explicit Wide + Implicit Deep) | 1st Order (Wide) + High-order (MLP) | Manual Cross-Product Transformations | CTR Prediction with Memorization + Generalization | . | Deep & Cross (DCN) | Explicit & Implicit | Arbitrary degree $L$ (bounded by cross layers) | Shared Embeddings | Automatic feature interactions without manual engineering | . | DCN-v2 | Explicit Matrix Cross + Implicit | Degree $L$ with Matrix-Vector multiplications | Low-rank tensor decomposition | Large-scale production CTR models | . | NCF (Neural CF) | Implicit | Arbitrary non-linear interaction via GMF + MLP | Sparse User & Item One-hot IDs | Matrix Factorization generalization | . | DeepFM | Explicit & Implicit | 1st, 2nd Order (FM) + High-order (MLP) | Dual sharing of embedding vectors between FM & Deep | Replacing manual feature engineering | . | AutoInt | Explicit Self-Attention | Multi-head attention interactions | Sparse categorical features | Interpretable multi-order feature interaction | . | DLRM | Explicit Pairwise Dot Product | 2nd Order explicit + High-order MLP | Large embedding tables with model parallel processing | E-commerce / Ad click systems | . Deep & Cross Network (DCN & DCN-v2) . DCN introduces explicit cross networks that apply feature crossing at each layer. DCN-v1 Cross Layer Formulation: . \[\mathbf{x}_{l+1} = \mathbf{x}_0 \mathbf{x}_l^T \mathbf{w}_l + \mathbf{b}_l + \mathbf{x}_l\] DCN-v2 Matrix Cross Layer Formulation: . \[\mathbf{x}_{l+1} = \mathbf{x}_0 \odot \left( W_l \mathbf{x}_l + \mathbf{b}_l \right) + \mathbf{x}_l\] Where $W_l \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times d}$ is parameter-wise factorized into low-rank matrices $U_l \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times r}$ and $V_l \in \mathbb{R}^{r \times d}$ ($r \ll d$) to reduce hardware memory footprints. Deep Learning Recommendation Model (DLRM) . DLRM computes explicit 2nd-order feature interactions by computing dot products between all embedding pairs, then concatenating the output with dense features processed by a Bottom MLP, passing the unified tensor to a Top MLP. +-----------------------+ | Top MLP | +-----------------------+ ^ | +--------------+--------------+ | [Dot Product Cross Interacts] [Bottom MLP Output (Dense)] ^ | [Sparse Embeddings (E1, E2, ...)] .

587.title: Part 4: Learning to Rank (LTR) & Scoring Mechanisms
587.content: Learning to Rank formulates recommendation scoring as an optimization problem across ordered item lists. LTR Approaches . +------------------+----------------------------------+------------------------------------+ | Paradigm | Input Data Unit | Loss Optimization Target | +------------------+----------------------------------+------------------------------------+ | Pointwise | Single Item (u, i) | Individual Item CTR / Binary CE | Pairwise | Item Pair (u, i, j) where i > j | Relative Preference Order / Margin | Listwise | Full Ranked List (u, i_1...i_k) | List-level Metrics (NDCG, MAP) | +------------------+----------------------------------+------------------------------------+ . Pairwise Ranking: RankNet & LambdaRank . RankNet . RankNet models the posterior probability that item $i$ is preferred over item $j$ using a sigmoid model on raw network scores $s_i = f(x_i)$ and $s_j = f(x_j)$: . \[P_{ij} = P(i \succ j) = \frac{1}{1 + \exp\left(-(s_i - s_j)\right)}\] The pairwise cross-entropy loss for target label $\bar{P}_{ij} \in {0, 1}$ is: . \[\mathcal{L}_{ij} = -\bar{P}_{ij} \log P_{ij} - (1 - \bar{P}_{ij}) \log (1 - P_{ij})\] LambdaRank . LambdaRank speeds up training by defining implicit gradients $\lambda_{ij}$ scaled by the change in target ranking metrics ($\Delta \text{NDCG}$): . \[\lambda_{ij} = \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}_{ij}}{\partial(s_i - s_j)} = \frac{-1}{1 + \exp(s_i - s_j)} \vert{}\Delta \text{NDCG}\vert{}\] Objective Functions & Loss Formulations . Bayesian Personalized Ranking (BPR) Loss . Designed for implicit feedback datasets where user $u$ interacted with $i$ ($i \in I_u^+$) and not $j$ ($j \notin I_u^+$): . \[\mathcal{L}_{\text{BPR}} = -\sum_{u \in U} \sum_{i \in I_u^+} \sum_{j \notin I_u^+} \log \sigma \left( \hat{x}_{ui} - \hat{x}_{uj} \right) + \lambda_{\Theta} \Vert{}\Theta\Vert{}^2\] .

588.title: Part 5: Multi-Objective Optimization (MOO) & Post-Processing
588.content: Real-world recommendation systems balance competing business metrics (e.g., Clicks, Watch Time, Likes, Shares, Conversions). Multi-Objective Formulations . \[\max_{\mathbf{x}} \mathbf{f}(\mathbf{x}) = \left[ f_{\text{click}}(\mathbf{x}), f_{\text{watch time}}(\mathbf{x}), f_{\text{share}}(\mathbf{x}) \right]^T\] Scalarization Methods . Combines objectives linearly using scalar weights $\mathbf{w}$: . \[S(u, i) = w_1 \cdot \hat{p}_{\text{click}} + w_2 \cdot \hat{y}_{\text{dwell time}} + w_3 \cdot \hat{p}_{\text{conversion}}\] Pareto Efficiency in Re-ranking . Item $i$ Pareto-dominates item $j$ if $f_k(i) \ge f_k(j)$ for all objectives $k$, and there exists at least one objective $m$ where $f_m(i) > f_m(j)$. The re-ranker selects items from the Pareto-optimal frontier. Re-ranking Dynamics . Ranked Candidates ---> [ Diversity Engine (DPP / Maximal Marginal Relevance) ] | v [ Freshness & Decay Filter ] | v [ Fairness & Popularity Regularizer ] | v Final Slate Output . Diversity via Maximal Marginal Relevance (MMR) . MMR greedily balances item relevance $S(u, i)$ against similarity to already selected candidates $R$: . \[\text{MMR} = \arg\max_{i \in C \setminus R} \left[ \lambda S(u, i) - (1 - \lambda) \max_{j \in R} \text{Sim}(i, j) \right]\] Freshness & Time Decay . Adjusts raw scoring using exponential time decay functions: . \[S_{\text{fresh}}(i, t) = S_{\text{raw}}(i) \cdot \exp\left( -\gamma (t - t_{\text{publish}})^k \right)\] Score Calibration . Raw outputs $s(x)$ from complex classification models often fail to represent true posterior probabilities. Calibration maps raw scores to accurate probabilities $P(y=1 \mid s)$. | Method | Mathematical Formulation | Pros | Cons | . | Platt Scaling | $P(y=1 \mid s) = \frac{1}{1 + \exp(A \cdot s + B)}$ | Simple, parametric, fast optimization | Assumes sigmoid shape; poor fit for non-sigmoidal error distributions | . | Isotonic Regression | $\min \sum \left( y_i - \hat{y}_i \right)^2 \quad \text{s.t.} \quad \hat{y}_i \le \hat{y}_j \text{ if } s_i \le s_j$ | Non-parametric, flexible monotonic curve fitting | Susceptible to overfitting on small validation datasets | . | Bayesian Binning (BBQ) | $P(y=1 \mid s) = \sum_{m} P(y=1 \mid s, M_m) P(M_m \mid D)$ | Robust uncertainty handling, prevents overfitting | High compute complexity; hyperparameter sensitive | .

589.title: Part 6: Graph Neural Networks & Sequential Transformers in RecSys
589.content: Graph models and sequential Transformers capture complex graph structures and short-term user intent. Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) . Recommender interactions form bipartite graphs $\mathcal{G} = (\mathcal{U}, \mathcal{V}, \mathcal{E})$ between user nodes $\mathcal{U}$ and item nodes $\mathcal{V}$. User Nodes (U) Item Nodes (V) ( u1 ) -------------------- ( i1 ) \ / | \ / | \ / | ---> ( u2 ) ------ ( i2 ) . GraphSAGE Neighborhood Aggregation . Aggregates representations from localized $k$-hop topological neighborhoods: . \[\mathbf{h}_{N(v)}^{(k)} = \text{AGGREGATE}_k \left( \mathbf{h}_u^{(k-1)}, \forall u \in N(v) \right)\] \[\mathbf{h}_v^{(k)} = \sigma \left( W^{(k)} \cdot \text{CONCAT} \left( \mathbf{h}_v^{(k-1)}, \mathbf{h}_{N(v)}^{(k)} \right) \right)\] PinSage (Pinterest Industrial GNN) . PinSage uses random walks to construct dynamic localized neighborhoods, running graph convolutions over the highest-visitation nodes to generate embeddings for billions of items. Transformers & Sequential Recommendation . Recurrent models like GRUs process user history linearly, whereas Transformers model explicit sequence dependencies in parallel using attention mechanisms. Behavioral Sequence Transformer (BST) . BST passes historical interaction item embeddings along with target candidate item embeddings through Transformer encoder blocks: . \[\text{Attention}(Q, K, V) = \text{softmax}\left(\frac{Q K^T}{\sqrt{d_k}}\right) V\] Position encodings incorporate temporal intervals between actions: . \[t(v_i) = t_{\text{current}} - t_{\text{action i}}\] .

590.title: Part 7: Search Systems, Exploration & Bandit Algorithms
590.content: Search and recommendation systems share similar retrieval and scoring infrastructures. Search Paradigms in RecSys . +-------------------+--------------------------------+-------------------------------------+ | Paradigm | Core Mechanism | Key Limitations | +-------------------+--------------------------------+-------------------------------------+ | Lexical Search | Sparse matching (BM25, TF-IDF) | Vocabulary mismatch; missing semantic context | Semantic Search | Dense vector search (ANN, HNSW)| Query latency; compute overhead | Hybrid Search | Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF) | Score normalization across domains | +-------------------+--------------------------------+-------------------------------------+ . Hybrid Fusion via Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF): . \[RRF_{\text{score}}(d \in D) = \sum_{m \in M} \frac{1}{k + r_m(d)}\] Where $r_m(d)$ is the rank of document $d$ in retrieval system $m$, and $k$ is a smoothing constant (typically $k=60$). Multi-Armed Bandit (MAB) Algorithms . Bandit models balance exploration of under-sampled candidates against exploitation of high-performing items. +----------------------------------+ | Select Arm (Action) based on | Exploration/Exploitation Policy | +----------------------------------+ | v +----------------------------------+ | Observe User Reward (Click/Buy) | +----------------------------------+ | v +----------------------------------+ | Update Value Distribution / UCB | +----------------------------------+ . $\epsilon$-Greedy . Selects a random item with probability $\epsilon$, and selects the item with the highest expected reward $\hat{Q}(a)$ with probability $1 - \epsilon$. Upper Confidence Bound (UCB1) . Selects arms according to potential upper confidence intervals: . \[a_t = \arg\max_a \left[ \hat{Q}_t(a) + c \sqrt{\frac{\ln t}{N_t(a)}} \right]\] Where $N_t(a)$ is the selection count of arm $a$ up to time step $t$. Thompson Sampling . Models expected reward parameters using posterior Beta distributions $\text{Beta}(\alpha_a, \beta_a)$: . | Draw sample $\theta_a \sim \text{Beta}(\alpha_a, \beta_a)$ for each candidate arm $a$. | Recommend candidate $a^* = \arg\max_a \theta_a$. | Update parameters upon interaction: $\alpha_{a^*} \leftarrow \alpha_{a^*} + r$, $\beta_{a^*} \leftarrow \beta_{a^*} + (1-r)$. | .

591.title: Part 8: Large Language Models (LLMs) in Recommender Systems
591.content: Large Language Models enhance recommender systems through zero-shot reasoning, semantic understanding, and unified sequence generation. +---------------------------------------------------------------------------------+ | LLM Recommender Paradigm Integration | +---------------------------------------------------------------------------------+ | 1. LLM as Feature Extractor: Text/Item -> LLM Embeddings -> Conventional RecSys | 2. LLM as Scoring Reranker: Prompt (User History + Candidates) -> LLM -> Ranked List | 3. Generative RecSys: Tokenized Semantic IDs -> LLM Decoder -> Next Item Tokens| +---------------------------------------------------------------------------------+ . Generative Recommendation via Semantic IDs . Instead of using randomly initialized index lookup tables for item IDs, items are mapped to semantic IDs generated via hierarchical vector quantization (e.g., RQ-VAE). Item Metadata/Image ---> [ RQ-VAE Encoder ] ---> Codebook Quantization | v Semantic ID Tuple: (3, 42, 118, 9) . The recommendation task is formulated as auto-regressive next-token prediction: . \[P(I_t \mid I_1, I_2, \dots, I_{t-1}) = \prod_{k=1}^L P\left(c_t^k \mid I_{< t}, c_t^{< k}\right)\] Where $(c_t^1, c_t^2, \dots, c_t^L)$ are the hierarchical discrete semantic tokens representing item $I_t$.

592.title: Part 9: Evaluation Metrics, Losses & Offline-Online Mismatch
592.content: Robust evaluation requires both offline statistical testing and online live-traffic experimentation. Metric Definitions . Retrieval Metrics (Top-K Candidates) . \[\text{Recall}@K = \frac{\vert{}\text{Relevant Items} \cap \text{Top-}K \text{ Recommended}\vert{}}{\vert{}\text{Total Relevant Items}\vert{}}\] \[\text{Hit Rate}@K = \mathbb{I}\left( \vert{}\text{Relevant Items} \cap \text{Top-}K\vert{} > 0 \right)\] Ranking Metrics . Mean Reciprocal Rank (MRR): . \[\text{MRR} = \frac{1}{\vert{}U\vert{}} \sum_{u=1}^{\vert{}U\vert{}} \frac{1}{\text{rank}_u^*}\] Mean Average Precision (MAP@K): . \[\text{MAP}@K = \frac{1}{\vert{}U\vert{}} \sum_{u=1}^{\vert{}U\vert{}} \left( \frac{1}{\min(m_u, K)} \sum_{k=1}^K P@k \cdot \text{rel}(k) \right)\] Normalized Discounted Cumulative Gain (NDCG@K): . \[\text{DCG}@K = \sum_{i=1}^K \frac{2^{\text{rel}_i} - 1}{\log_2(i + 1)}, \quad \text{NDCG}@K = \frac{\text{DCG}@K}{\text{IDCG}@K}\] Common Production System Failures . +---------------------------+-----------------------------------+--------------------------------------+ | Challenge | Cause | System Mitigation Strategy | +---------------------------+-----------------------------------+--------------------------------------+ | Result Reproducibility | Non-deterministic distributed ops | Standardize seed state & logging | Offline-Online Mismatch | Data leakage / Shifted distributions| Strict feature store logging time-cut| Oscillating Outputs | Feedback loops in real-time updates| Dynamic output dampening / MAB policies| Slow Convergence | Sparse gradient updates on IDs | Adagrad/FTRL for sparse embeddings | +---------------------------+-----------------------------------+--------------------------------------+ .

593.title: Part 10: Biases, Cold-Start & Content Moderation
593.content: Addressing system biases and edge cases is essential for model performance and user safety. Systemic Biases and Mitigation Strategies . Biases in RecSys | +---------------------------+---------------------------+ | | Position Bias Popularity Bias Selection Bias (Higher rank = higher CTR) (Popular items dominate) (Missing unobserved data) | | v v v Propensity Scoring Logit Correction Counterfactual Weights 1 / P(Exposed) s_adj = s - tau*log(p) Inverse Propensity Score . Position Bias Correction via Propensity Scoring . User engagement $Y$ depends on relevance $R$ and display position observation $O$: . \[P(Y=1 \mid \text{position} = k) = P(R=1) \cdot P(O=1 \mid \text{position} = k)\] Inverse Propensity Scoring (IPS) adjusts the evaluation loss: . \[\mathcal{L}_{\text{IPS}} = \sum_{i \in D} \frac{Y_i}{P(O_i = 1 \mid \text{position}_i)} \cdot \mathcal{L}_{\text{model}}(s_i, y_i)\] Popularity Bias Mitigation via Logit Adjustment . Adjusts inference logits by subtracting scaled item frequencies $P(v)$: . \[s_{\text{adjusted}}(u, v) = s(u, v) - \tau \cdot \log P(v)\] Where $\tau$ is a temperature hyperparameter controlling the degree of popularity penalization. Cold-Start Mitigation Techniques . | User Cold-Start: Use demographic priors, onboarding interest selectors, contextual bandits, and active learning queries. | Item Cold-Start: Cross-modal feature extraction (e.g., CLIP text-image embeddings), semantic IDs, and hybrid content-collaborative architectures. | System Cold-Start: Leverage domain transfer learning, heuristic rules, and metadata search indexing. | . Content Moderation Pipelines . Raw Content Stream (Video / Image / Text) | v [ Early Moderation Layer ] ---> Immediate Reject (Static Blocklists, Hashes) | v [ In-Depth Moderation ] ---> Async Multi-Modal Deep Neural Models | v [ Late Moderation Layer ] ---> Contextual Safety Filters & Policy Rules | v Safe Recommendations Delivered .

594.title: Part 11: Production Systems & Industrial Case Studies
594.content: Production architectures balance scale, latency, and business constraints across large item catalogs. Overview of Industrial Implementations . +------------------+----------------------------------+-------------------------------------+ | Company | Key Architecture Innovation | Core Technical Highlights | +------------------+----------------------------------+-------------------------------------+ | YouTube | Two-Stage DNN (Candidate + Rank) | Deep Candidate Gen + Weighted Logistic Reg | Netflix | Page Generation & Evidence Selection| Template-based row construction + Thumbnails | Instagram Explore| 3-Pass Multi-Stage Funnel Filter | Distilled model -> Fast NN -> Deep NN | Pinterest Pixie | Graph Random Walks on Pin-Board | In-memory graph traversal via Pixie | DoorDash | Store-Level Sparsity Handling | Search-Rec hybrid + Spatial constraints| Monolith (ByteDance)| Streaming Real-time Training | Collisionless Dynamic Embedding Tables| +------------------+----------------------------------+-------------------------------------+ . Instagram Explore 3-Pass Multi-Stage Ranking . Instagram reduces candidate sets through three distinct model passes: . Account Candidates (~few thousands) | v Media Candidate Sampling (~500 Items) | v +-------------------------------------------------------------+ | Pass 1: Distilled Model (Minimal features) | -> Output: Top 150 Candidates | +-------------------------------------------------------------+ | v +-------------------------------------------------------------+ | Pass 2: Lightweight NN (Full dense features) | -> Output: Top 50 Candidates | +-------------------------------------------------------------+ | v +-------------------------------------------------------------+ | Pass 3: Deep Neural Network (Full dense + sparse features) | -> Output: Top 25 Final Grid Candidates | +-------------------------------------------------------------+ .

595.title: Part 12: Hands-On Implementation: PySpark ALS Music Recommender
595.content: This section details an end-to-end implicit-feedback recommendation pipeline implemented using PySpark and Alternating Least Squares (ALS) matrix factorization. from pyspark.sql import SparkSession from pyspark.sql.functions import col, count, desc from pyspark.ml.feature import StringIndexer from pyspark.ml.recommendation import ALS from pyspark.ml.tuning import ParamGridBuilder, TrainValidationSplit from pyspark.ml.evaluation import RegressionEvaluator # 1. Initialize SparkSession spark = SparkSession.builder \ .appName("PySpark-Music-RecSys-ALS") \ .config("spark.driver.memory", "8g") \ .getOrCreate() # 2. Load Dataset file_path = "listenings.csv" df_listenings = spark.read.format("csv") \ .option("header", True) \ .option("inferSchema", True) \ .load(file_path) # 3. Clean and Preprocess Data df_cleaned = df_listenings.drop("date").na.drop() # 4. Map String Identifiers to Numerical Indices user_indexer = StringIndexer(inputCol="user_id", outputCol="user_idx") track_indexer = StringIndexer(inputCol="track", outputCol="track_idx") df_indexed = user_indexer.fit(df_cleaned).transform(df_cleaned) df_indexed = track_indexer.fit(df_indexed).transform(df_indexed) # 5. Aggregate Implicit Interaction Counts (Plays) df_interactions = df_indexed.groupby("user_idx", "track_idx") \ .agg(count("*").alias("play_count")) # 6. Split Data into Train/Test Sets train_data, test_data = df_interactions.randomSplit([0.8, 0.2], seed=42) # 7. Configure Implicit Matrix Factorization (ALS Model) als = ALS( userCol="user_idx", itemCol="track_idx", ratingCol="play_count", implicitPrefs=True, alpha=40.0, coldStartStrategy="drop", nonnegative=True ) # 8. Hyperparameter Tuning Grid param_grid = ParamGridBuilder() \ .addGrid(als.rank, [10, 50]) \ .addGrid(als.regParam, [0.01, 0.1]) \ .build() evaluator = RegressionEvaluator( metricName="rmse", labelCol="play_count", predictionCol="prediction" ) tvs = TrainValidationSplit( estimator=als, estimatorParamMaps=param_grid, evaluator=evaluator, trainRatio=0.8 ) # 9. Model Fitting model = tvs.fit(train_data) best_als_model = model.bestModel # 10. Generate Top-10 Recommendations for All Users user_recommendations = best_als_model.recommendForAllUsers(10) user_recommendations.show(5, truncate=False) .

596.title: Technical Takeaways
596.content: . | System Architecture: Production recommenders use multi-stage funnels (Retrieval $\rightarrow$ Ranking $\rightarrow$ Re-ranking $\rightarrow$ Calibration) to manage the trade-off between catalog size and computational latency. | Feature Interactions: Models like DCN-v2 and DLRM rely on explicit matrix-vector feature interactions rather than deep MLPs alone to capture cross-feature patterns efficiently. | Loss Formulations: Contrastive in-batch cross-entropy loss with logQ correction handles item frequency bias in candidate generation networks. | Bandits & Exploration: Contextual Bandits and Thompson Sampling manage exploration-exploitation trade-offs to cold-start new items and adapt to short-term user feedback. | Post-Processing Calibration: Raw neural network scores must be recalibrated using methods like Platt Scaling or Isotonic Regression before downstream multi-objective ranking or display logic. | .
